Being in a mixed-member family was always less-than-ideal. It wasn't the overt animosity you see in movies, the screaming matches and slammed doors. No, it was a more insidious kind of wrongness, a subtle dissonance that hummed beneath the surface of every interaction. My mother, a vibrant, earthy woman with a booming laugh and a penchant for bright colours, was a full-blooded witch. My father, a quiet, pragmatic accountant with a grey suit for every day of the week, was a mundane - a "no-maj," as my mother teasingly called him, knowing he hated the term.

From the start, it felt like two halves of a puzzle forced together. My mother would try to involve my father in her rituals, coaxing him to hold hands during moonlit ceremonies, only to be met with a furrowed brow and a muttered, "I'd rather be watching the news, dear." He, in turn, would try to teach me the joys of balancing a budget, lecturing me on the importance of compound interest while I was trying to levitate a dandelion.

The tension was palpable, a constant undercurrent in our lives. It manifested in awkward silences at the dinner table, in the way my mother's eyes would glaze over when my father started talking about spreadsheets, in the way my father would subtly steer me away from my mother's herb garden, muttering something about "weeds and allergies."

Growing up, I felt like I was constantly translating. I learned to filter my mother's flamboyant pronouncements about destiny and intuition into something palatable for my father's logical mind. And I learned to explain my father's rigid adherence to rules and schedules as "just his way of showing he cares."

But I couldn't bridge the gap entirely. I was caught between two worlds, belonging fully to neither. Was I supposed to embrace the magic that thrummed in my veins, or strive for the normalcy my father so desperately craved? Was I supposed to trust my intuition, or rely on cold, hard facts?

The worst part was the unspoken question hanging in the air: did they regret their choice? Did my mother ever wonder if she should have chosen a wizard, someone who truly understood her? Did my father ever wish he had married a woman who could discuss tax law instead of tarot cards?

I never dared to ask. The silence was, in its own strange way, a kind of peace. As long as we didn't talk about it, as long as we pretended everything was fine, we could maintain the illusion of a normal family. But the dissonance remained, a constant reminder that in our house, magic and mundanity were forever locked in an uneasy truce.

The light was poor, casting long shadows across her face, but I could see the faint tracery of lines etched around her eyes, lines that hadn't been there before. The vibrant red hair I remembered had faded to a dull auburn, pulled back into a tight, severe bun.

My fingers traced its length, from the barely perceptible beginning near my thumb to the slightly raised end closer to my elbow. I pulled my hand away, a sharp, involuntary movement. Enough. Dwelling on it never helped. It only dragged me back into the murky depths I’d fought so hard to escape.

I glanced at the clock on the wall. Almost time to leave for work. A mundane, ordinary task, but a lifeline nonetheless. It was a job I enjoyed, surrounded by people who, for the most part, didn’t know my story. They just saw me as… me. Not as the girl with the scars, both visible and invisible.

With a sigh, I stood up, pushing myself away from the window and its tempting shadows. Time to face the day. Time to keep moving forward, even with the weight of the past etched onto my skin. Time to prove that the scar, though a permanent fixture, didn’t define me. Not anymore.

He’s the guy you go to when you need to know the capital of Burkina Faso (Ouagadougou, obviously, he already knew you were going to ask). He’s the one who can tell you, with unnerving accuracy, what you had for breakfast three Tuesdays ago, even if you can barely remember yourself. His gaze, a steady, gentle blue, seems to pierce through pretense and uncertainty, leaving you feeling both strangely exposed and remarkably understood.

But Dave can't stop the rain. He can tell you exactly when it will start, the precise milliliter of precipitation that will fall, and even the trajectory of each individual raindrop, but he can't make it stop. He can't cure cancer, though he knows every single mutation, every failed trial, every promising lead buried in dusty research papers. He can't bring back the dead, even though he knows their every thought, every fear, every hope they held in their final moments.

This limitation, this conspicuous lack of power, is what makes him Dave. He's not a god, just a man burdened with a universe of information. He carries it with a quiet grace, offering his knowledge freely, but always with a hint of melancholy in his eyes. He knows the best way to fix your leaky faucet, but he can't fix your broken heart. He knows the winning lottery numbers, but he can't bring himself to play.

People flock to him, drawn to the promise of answers, the comfort of being seen. They ask him about the future, about the past, about the mundane and the profound. Dave answers them all, patiently, precisely, his voice a low, soothing hum. But he never offers advice. He simply presents the facts, leaving you to navigate the consequences.

He knows that knowledge, without the power to act, is a double-edged sword. It can illuminate, but it can also paralyze. And sometimes, he wonders if it wouldn’t be better to be blissfully ignorant, to live in the comfortable darkness of not knowing. But then someone asks him about the migration patterns of the Arctic Tern, or the chemical composition of a supernova, and the light in his eyes flickers again. He knows, and he can't help but share. He's Dave, after all, and that's just what he does.

Death by fulfillment, a gilded cage of our own making. Our society, drunk on the promise of individual potential, insists that every dream be chased, every ambition realized, no matter the cost. We preach a gospel of self-actualization, a relentless pursuit of passions, oblivious to the paradox that can lead to burnout, disillusionment, and ultimately, a hollow victory.

We champion the entrepreneur who sacrifices sleep and sanity for their startup, the artist who starves for their craft, the athlete who pushes their body beyond its limits for a fleeting moment of glory. We celebrate the hustle, the grind, the unwavering dedication, often romanticizing the suffering that accompanies it.

But what happens when that final goal is reached? What remains when the summit is conquered? Often, the answer is a terrifying void. The climber, having scaled the highest peak, finds themselves with no higher to climb. The artist, having achieved critical acclaim, discovers their inspiration has dried up. The entrepreneur, having built their empire, is left with a gnawing emptiness.

The problem isn't the ambition itself, but the societal pressure to define ourselves solely by our achievements. We are taught to equate success with happiness, to believe that fulfilling our ambitions will automatically lead to contentment. We neglect the importance of balance, of relationships, of finding meaning in the everyday moments that often get overshadowed by the pursuit of grander goals.

Death by fulfillment isn't always literal. It's the slow erosion of joy, the gradual loss of perspective, the creeping feeling that despite achieving everything we set out to do, we've somehow missed the point. It's the realization that the journey, not the destination, is what truly matters, and that by focusing solely on the finish line, we've sacrificed the very things that make life worth living.

Perhaps true progress lies not in enabling everyone to reach their ambitions at all costs, but in redefining what constitutes a fulfilling life. Perhaps it's time to embrace the beauty of imperfection, the value of rest, and the importance of connection, recognizing that sometimes, the most meaningful journey is the one that leads us back to ourselves.

He showed her in small gestures – a perfectly brewed cup of coffee, a meticulously curated playlist, a hand instinctively reaching for hers in a crowd. But he never said it.

She waited, patiently at first, her eyes searching his for a flicker of the emotion she felt so strongly. She gave him opportunities, leaving conversational openings like unlocked doors, hoping he'd walk through. But he remained rooted, afraid of vulnerability, afraid of shattering the carefully constructed facade he'd built.

Eventually, her patience wore thin. The unspoken words hung between them like a suffocating fog. The small gestures, once charming, now felt insufficient, like crumbs offered to a starving soul. She needed more than just actions; she needed to hear the affirmation, the validation, the simple "I love you."

One rainy afternoon, she stood by the window, her silhouette a fragile outline against the grey sky. She turned to him, her eyes filled with a weariness that cut him deeper than any shouted argument.

"I can't keep doing this," she said, her voice barely a whisper. "I need someone who can tell me what I already know to be true. Someone who isn't afraid to say the words."

He opened his mouth to speak, to finally break the dam of silence, but the words caught, choked by years of ingrained habit. He wanted to tell her, to beg her to stay, to promise he'd change. But all that came out was a weak, strangled sound.

She nodded, a single tear tracing a path down her cheek. "I'm sorry," she said, her voice thick with emotion. "I really am."

And then she was gone.

The silence that followed was deafening. He stood in the echoing emptiness of his apartment, the weight of his unspoken words crushing him. He finally understood the true cost of his fear, the devastating consequences of his silence.

He tried to call, to text, to desperately explain. But his messages went unanswered. He went to her apartment, only to find an empty mailbox and a lingering scent of her perfume, a ghost of what had been.

He was left with the wreckage of his own making, the hollow ache of regret, and the bitter realization that sometimes, the bravest thing you can do is simply speak the truth in your heart. Boy loses girl, not because he didn't love her, but because he was too afraid to say it. And now, he had all the time in the world to practice.

He pulled Whisper free, the blade slick with green blood, and turned to the boy. “Get behind the line!” he shouted, his voice hoarse from exertion. The boy, still trembling, could only nod before scrambling away, disappearing into the throng.

Kaelan knew they were losing. He could feel it in the air, in the growing desperation of his comrades, in the relentless pressure of the enemy. The banners of the King, once held high and proud, were now tattered and stained, dipping low as their bearers fell. Hope, like the setting sun, was slowly fading from the sky. He just hoped he could hold on long enough for the rest to get away.
Every day I come to work and wonder just who's in charge. The org chart says it's Mr. Henderson, but Mr. Henderson spends most of his time in meetings that seem to be about deciding which brand of coffee to order for the break room. Then there's Brenda in accounting, who, while not officially in charge, seems to have a direct line to the CEO's ear and a knack for shutting down any idea that doesn't align with her meticulously-planned budget. And let's not forget Kevin from IT, who holds the entire network hostage with his cryptic pronouncements and the password to the printer.

It's a power vacuum, really. A swirling vortex of personalities and agendas, where the actual work gets done in the cracks between the official roles. I spend half my time navigating the unspoken rules and the other half wondering if I should just start referring to Brenda as "Your Majesty." Maybe then I'd finally get my expense report approved.
The familiar fluorescent hum buzzed in my ears, a discordant symphony of cheap lighting and humming refrigerators. The air smelled of stale coffee and something vaguely chemical, like a recent spill of motor oil. I knew every chipped tile on the floor, every faded advertisement for lottery tickets and discounted cigarettes. This gas station was a recurring character in my subconscious.

I wandered through the aisles, past the dusty racks of sunglasses and the impulse-buy candy bars. The cashier, a woman with tired eyes and a nametag that read “Brenda,” didn't acknowledge me. She never did in these dreams. She was just part of the scenery, a fixture like the dented ice machine or the flickering neon sign outside.

I reached for a bag of gummy worms, the kind that were always a little too chewy, and a strange compulsion washed over me. Not to eat them, but to examine them. I poured them into my hand, a writhing mass of sugary colors. And then, I started to notice something different.

The colors weren't quite right. The red was too deep, almost crimson. The yellow was a sickly, jaundiced hue. And the green… the green was pulsing.

A low thrumming vibrated through my hand, emanating from the gummy worms. They were growing, expanding, the sugar coating cracking and flaking off. The colors intensified, becoming almost blinding. I tried to drop them, but my hand was frozen in place, clenched tight around the mutating candies.

The thrumming intensified, resonating in my chest. The gas station around me began to distort. The shelves warped, the floor buckled, and Brenda behind the counter started to blur, her features melting into a single, indistinct mass.

Panic clawed at my throat. I knew I was dreaming, but the dream was changing, evolving into something… more. Something terrifying. I had to wake up. I *needed* to wake up.

I squeezed my eyes shut, focusing all my will on escaping the suffocating reality of the gas station. I tried to scream, but no sound came out. Just the relentless thrumming, the pulsing colors, and the growing, sickening feeling that I was losing control.

Then, a voice. A whisper, barely audible above the din.

"They're not worms," it hissed. "They're seeds."
The dragon kept rising, growing to an impossible size. Scales, once individually defined, blurred into a shimmering mosaic that reflected the bruised twilight sky. Its roar, a low rumble moments before, now threatened to crack the very foundations of the world, a sound that vibrated in bone and rattled the teeth.

Below, the battlefield had fallen silent. Swords lay forgotten in the mud, shields were dropped with numbed fingers. Men, elves, dwarves, even the hulking trolls, all looked up, dwarfed into insignificance by the monstrous majesty unfolding above them. Hope, a flickering flame in their hearts, was snuffed out by the sheer, overwhelming presence of the beast.

Its eyes, twin pools of molten gold, fixed upon them. Not with rage, not with bloodlust, but with something far more terrifying: an ancient, knowing weariness. It was the gaze of a being that had seen empires rise and fall, watched civilizations bloom and wither, and understood the futility of it all.

A single, obsidian claw, longer than any siege tower, unfurled. The air crackled with energy as it descended, not with the speed of a predator, but with the deliberate, inexorable pace of a glacier. It was not a strike, but a statement. A declaration of dominance.

The claw stopped, hovering just above the petrified soldiers. A voice, ancient and resonant, echoed in their minds, bypassing ears entirely.

"Enough."

The word, simple yet imbued with unimaginable power, pressed down on them like a physical weight. The fighting, the hatred, the ambition that had driven them to this point, all seemed petty and meaningless under the dragon's gaze.

"You squabble over dust," the voice continued, laced with a profound sorrow. "You spill blood for trinkets. You forget the true enemy."

Slowly, deliberately, the dragon turned its colossal head, its gaze shifting from the battlefield to the distant horizon. A low growl, a warning this time, rumbled in its chest.

"They are coming," the dragon boomed, the words now audible, shaking the ground beneath their feet. "And when they arrive, your petty wars will seem like child's play. Unite, or perish."

With that, the claw withdrew, and the dragon, impossibly large, began to descend once more. But it wasn't shrinking. It was fading, dissolving into the twilight, leaving behind only the memory of its terrifying power and the chilling certainty of a greater threat. The battlefield remained silent, the soldiers frozen, their petty squabbles suddenly irrelevant in the face of the looming darkness. The dust, the trinkets, the blood… they were nothing. The dragon was gone, but its warning lingered, a seed of fear and a desperate, flickering hope, planted in the barren soil of their hearts.

"The price being…?" I prompted, steeling myself for the worst.

He stopped pacing and fixed me with his unsettling gaze. "The price is…comfort. You'll be…uncomfortable. Very uncomfortable. But think of the reward! Think of the life that awaits you! A life free from…constraints." He emphasized the last word with a venomous hiss.

He reached for a valve on the side of the tank. "Now, are you ready to begin your journey? There's no turning back now. Once you're in, you're in." The water began to churn, a slow, ominous whirlpool forming in the center of the tank.

I took a deep breath, the salty air burning my lungs. My heart hammered against my ribs, a frantic drumbeat against the silence of my fear. I looked back at the doorway, a sliver of light offering a tantalizing glimpse of the life I was about to abandon.

Then I looked back at the tank, at the swirling darkness, at the promise of a new life, however perilous the path. My choice was made.

"Ready," I said, my voice barely a whisper. "Let's go."

A shiver ran through Elara. This was no ordinary raven. This was a messenger. And messengers in the dead of winter rarely brought good news.

Its legs, thick and segmented, were the color of burnt caramel, tipped with wickedly curved claws. Its abdomen, a bloated sphere of mottled brown and black, pulsed slightly. And its eight eyes, oh God, its eight eyes, gleamed with an unnerving intelligence that sent a shiver down my spine.

I froze, paralyzed with a primal fear that clawed at my insides. I couldn't move, couldn't scream, couldn't even blink. It was like my entire body had decided to stage a revolt against my will, leaving me a helpless spectator in my own personal horror movie.

Slowly, deliberately, the spider shifted. One hairy leg twitched, then another. It was awakening. It was aware of me. My heart hammered against my ribs, a frantic drumbeat against the suffocating silence of the kitchen. I had to do something. I had to escape. But the spider, that eight-legged demon, had me trapped in its terrifying gaze.
"Larry?!" That voice. He knew that voice. It scraped at the back of his throat like sandpaper, a voice that brought with it a tidal wave of regret and a healthy dose of terror. He froze, hand hovering over the doorknob of his apartment, the key still clutched tight in his palm. He hadn't heard it in… how long had it been? Ten years? More?

He slowly turned, a knot tightening in his stomach. Standing on the landing above him, bathed in the dim, flickering light of the hallway, was Beatrice. Her fiery red hair, once a vibrant statement of defiance, was now streaked with silver, pulled back into a severe bun. The lines around her eyes were deeper, etched by time and, he suspected, bitterness. But those eyes, that burning, intelligent gaze, was unmistakable.

"Beatrice," he managed, the name a dry rasp. He felt like a student caught cheating on a test, exposed and utterly ashamed.

She descended the stairs, each step a measured, deliberate thud that echoed in the sterile hallway. "Larry," she repeated, the word dripping with a sarcasm that could curdle milk. "It is you. I thought I recognized the back of that balding head."

He winced. "What... what are you doing here?" he asked, his voice barely a whisper.

She stopped a few feet away, her arms crossed, a formidable barrier. "Looking for you, of course. You didn't think you could just disappear, did you, Larry? After everything?"

He swallowed hard. He had hoped. He had desperately hoped he could disappear. He had changed his name, moved across the country, built a new life. But some things, he was now painfully aware, couldn't be outrun.

"Beatrice, I..." he started, but the words caught in his throat. He knew there was no excuse he could offer, no explanation that would suffice.

"Don't bother," she cut him off, her voice hardening. "I'm not here for apologies. I'm here for what you owe."

A chill ran down his spine. He knew exactly what she meant. The past he had tried so hard to bury had just come knocking, and it was holding him accountable. He braced himself for the storm. He knew, with a sinking certainty, that his carefully constructed new life was about to be ripped apart.
...Seriously. I know, right now, it feels like everything is HUGE. Like every decision is life-altering, every mistake is a catastrophe, and every missed opportunity is a door slammed shut forever. But take a deep breath. It's not.

That embarrassing thing you said at that party? Forget about it. No one remembers. And if they do, they've probably done something equally embarrassing themselves. The test you failed? You'll retake it, study harder, and learn from it. Or maybe that subject just isn't for you, and that's okay too. The relationship that ended? Heartbreak sucks, I know. But it's also a chance to learn what you truly want and need in a partner. It’s a chance to rediscover yourself.

Right now, you're standing at the foot of a mountain range. Each peak represents a potential path, a possible future. You might feel pressured to choose the *right* one, the one that leads to success, happiness, and fulfillment. But the truth is, there is no single "right" path. There are just paths, and each one will lead you to different experiences, different challenges, and different rewards.

Don't be afraid to wander. Don't be afraid to try things and fail. Don't be afraid to change your mind. The important thing is to keep moving, keep learning, and keep growing.

That feeling of uncertainty? Embrace it. It means you're on the edge of something new, something exciting. It means you're open to possibilities.

And remember, you are stronger and more capable than you think. You have a support system, even if you don't always see it. Lean on your friends, your family, your mentors. They're there for you.

So go out there and live your life. Make mistakes, learn from them, and keep moving forward. You've got this. You've got everything you need. And you've got absolutely nothing to regret. Not yet, anyway. And even when regrets *do* come, you'll be strong enough to face them and learn from them too. Just keep going. I believe in you.

He scanned the bustling bookstore, a sudden wave of paranoia washing over him. Were people watching him? Did they know? He felt exposed, vulnerable, as if his most intimate secrets were being broadcast over the PA system.

The novel continued, venturing into the present. It described his current job, the monotony he secretly loathed, his unrequited feelings for Sarah from accounting, the recurring dream of a faceless figure chasing him through a labyrinthine city.

He stopped reading, his heart pounding in his chest. This wasn't just a biography; it was a prophecy. He hadn't told anyone about the dream. How could this author, this complete stranger, know so much?

A sense of dread settled in his stomach. He had to know what came next. He flipped forward, skipping pages, desperate to see what the future held. The words blurred, a chaotic jumble of potential outcomes. He saw a wedding, a funeral, a distant, sun-drenched beach. He saw happiness, sorrow, and a profound sense of loss.

Then, he stopped. His breath hitched in his throat. The next chapter was titled: "The Bookstore Encounter."

He read on, his hands clammy. The chapter described a man, fitting his exact description, standing in a bookstore, reading a novel about his life. It described his growing anxiety, his fear, his desperate need to know what the future held.

Little Jimmy looked into his grandma's eyes. They weren't the bright, sparkly blue he remembered from Christmas last year. Now, they were a soft, milky grey, like the fog that sometimes rolled in off the coast. He saw wrinkles crinkling around them like tiny, well-worn maps, marking the journeys she'd taken, the laughter she'd shared, and the tears she'd cried.

A flicker of recognition sparked within those foggy depths. "Jimmy?" she whispered, her voice raspy like dried leaves crunching underfoot.

A smile bloomed on Jimmy's face, chasing away the worry that had been knotting his stomach. "Hi, Grandma!" He reached out and gently took her hand, surprised by how fragile it felt.

He had been scared to visit. Momma said Grandma wasn't feeling well, that she sometimes forgot things. He'd imagined a stranger in her place, someone who wouldn't remember his silly jokes or the way he liked his toast cut into triangles.

But looking into those eyes, even with their altered landscape, he saw the familiar warmth, the unwavering love that had always been there. He saw his grandma, still.

He squeezed her hand gently. "I brought you some flowers," he said, pointing to the vase of bright yellow daffodils he'd carefully arranged. "They're your favorite."

A faint smile touched her lips. "Daffodils," she repeated, the word sounding like a forgotten melody. "Pretty... pretty like you."

Jimmy blushed, feeling a surge of happiness. He knew, in that moment, that even if the fog thickened, even if the memories faded, the love would remain, shining brightly in those gentle, grey eyes. He settled down on the chair beside her bed, ready to tell her all about his adventures, hoping to spark a little more sunshine in her day. He knew, somehow, that she would listen, even if she couldn't quite remember who he was. He was Jimmy, and he was her grandson, and that was all that mattered.
The air hung thick with a perpetual haze, a cocktail of industrial fallout and the dust of forgotten cities. The sky, once a vibrant canvas of blues and golds, was now a bruised purple, weeping acid rain on the skeletal remains of civilization. I’d seen it change, of course, felt the slow, insidious creep of decay gnawing at the world’s bones. My home was a dilapidated, reinforced concrete bunker, half-buried in the rubble of what was once Philadelphia. I called it "Fort Resilience," a pathetic attempt at injecting some semblance of hope into my desolate existence. Inside, powered by a temperamental solar array and a sputtering generator, I clung to the remnants of the old world: tattered books, cracked vinyl records, and a rusty old radio that occasionally picked up static-laced broadcasts from distant, unknown outposts.

I was a scavenger, a survivalist, a relic hunter. Every day, I ventured out into the wasteland, armed with a rusty pipe wrench and a healthy dose of cynicism, scavenging for food, fuel, and anything that might prolong my meager existence. The world outside was a dangerous place, populated by desperate gangs, mutated creatures, and the ghosts of the past.

Today, the air was particularly acrid, stinging my nostrils and making my eyes water. The Geiger counter I carried, a constant companion, clicked with increasing urgency, a grim reminder of the invisible danger that permeated everything. I was heading towards the ruins of a pharmaceutical factory, a place rumored to hold a cache of antibiotics. It was a risky venture, but my dwindling supply of medicine was running dangerously low. A cough had been rattling in my chest for days, a harbinger of something far more sinister in this poisoned world.

As I navigated the treacherous landscape, clambering over collapsed buildings and dodging pools of toxic waste, I couldn't help but wonder: what was the point? Was I simply prolonging the inevitable? Was there any hope for a future, or was I just a lonely, insignificant speck clinging to the wreckage of a dying world?

The pharmaceutical factory loomed in the distance, a skeletal behemoth against the bruised sky. It was time to find out. Time to face the dangers, to scavenge, to survive. Because even in a world consumed by decay, the instinct to live, to breathe, to simply *be*, burned bright within me. Even after 69 years, 11 months, and 29 days.

I, Ben Carter, her research assistant, stared at the data flashing across the screen. It was a chaotic mess of numbers and graphs, but even I, with my limited understanding, could see the anomaly. The signal we'd been tracking for months, a faint whisper from deep space, had suddenly amplified, bursting into a cacophony of coherent energy.

"What does it mean, Anya?" I asked, my heart pounding against my ribs.

She shook her head, her eyes wide with a mixture of awe and fear. "I don't know, Ben. It could be anything. A natural phenomenon, a cosmic fluke... or..."

She trailed off, the unspoken word hanging in the air: contact. Contact with something, someone, beyond our understanding.

We'd dedicated years of our lives to this project, scouring the heavens for any sign of intelligent life. We’d faced ridicule, funding cuts, and the crushing weight of doubt. Now, here it was, staring us in the face, and we were terrified.

The signal pulsed, a complex rhythm that seemed to bypass logic and speak directly to something primal within us. Anya began to decipher it, her fingers flying across the keyboard. Lines of code scrolled down the screen, transforming into images, symbols, and eventually, words.

Crude, rudimentary words, but words nonetheless.

"They're... they're warning us," Anya said, her voice cracking. "They're saying... 'Do not answer.'"

The storm outside intensified. The observatory creaked and groaned under the assault of the wind. The power flickered, plunging us into darkness for a heart-stopping moment before the emergency generator kicked in.

"But why?" I asked, my voice barely a whisper. "Why shouldn't we answer?"

Anya pointed to a section of the translated message. It was a single, chilling phrase: "They are coming."

We stared at each other, the weight of those words crushing us. We held the fate of humanity in our hands. Okay, a 49-year-old quarter that feels heavier than newer quarters... This strongly suggests it's likely a **silver quarter**!

Here's why and what you should do:

*   **Years to look for:** Pre-1965 US quarters (Washington quarters from 1932-1964) were made of 90% silver and 10% copper. This makes them significantly heavier and gives them a different feel.

*   **What to do:**
    1.  **Check the Date:** The most important thing is to check the date. If it's 1964 or earlier, it's almost certainly silver.
    2.  **Check for a Mint Mark:** Look for a small letter on the reverse (tails side) of the coin, usually near the bottom. This indicates which mint produced the coin (D = Denver, S = San Francisco, no mark = Philadelphia). While the mint mark itself doesn't drastically affect the value of a common silver quarter, it's good to note.
    3.  **Condition:** Examine the condition of the coin. Is it heavily worn, or does it have a lot of detail?
    4.  **Value:** Silver quarters are worth more than face value due to their silver content. The exact value fluctuates with the price of silver, but you can easily find the current spot price of silver online. Also, search eBay sold listings or a coin dealer's website to get a better idea of the value based on condition.
    5.  **Don't Clean It:** Cleaning coins can damage them and reduce their value, especially for collectible coins.

*   **What if it's post-1964?** If it's post-1964, then it shouldn't be silver. There are a few possibilities, but they are much less likely:
    *   **Error Coin:** It could be a rare error coin (e.g., a planchet error or a coin struck on the wrong metal). These are very uncommon.
    *   **Damaged:** It could be damaged or have something adhered to it, making it feel heavier.
    *   **Your Perception:** It's also possible that the difference in weight is subtle, and you're just perceiving it differently.

**In summary, check the date first and foremost. If it's pre-1965, you've likely found a silver quarter!** Good luck!

And then there are those who genuinely believe the law is unjust. They see it as an impediment to progress, a tool of oppression, a barrier to freedom. So, you create a law, you create a market for transgression. You draw a line in the sand, and someone will inevitably try to erase it, or at least see how close they can get to the edge without falling in. The question isn't whether the boundary will be tested, but *how* it will be tested, and what the consequences will be for those who dare to cross it. Because every law, every restriction, is a gauntlet thrown down, a challenge issued, an invitation to explore the limits of human ingenuity, audacity, and the ever-present tension between order and freedom.

While Einstein is the name most associated with it, the impetus and initial drafting came primarily from the physicist Leo Szilárd. Szilárd, along with other physicists like Edward Teller and Eugene Wigner, were deeply concerned about the potential for Nazi Germany to develop atomic weapons. They understood the theoretical possibility of creating an incredibly powerful bomb based on nuclear fission and were acutely aware of German progress in nuclear research.

Szilárd believed that the United States needed to be alerted to this danger and encouraged to pursue its own research into atomic weapons. He knew that Einstein, already a world-renowned and respected figure, could lend significant weight to their concerns.

The key points of the Einstein-Szilárd letter were:

*   **Warning about Uranium Fission:** The letter explained the recent discovery of nuclear fission and the possibility of creating a chain reaction in uranium, potentially leading to the construction of extremely powerful bombs.
*   **German Research:** It highlighted the fact that Germany was actively pursuing research into uranium and potentially trying to acquire uranium from Czechoslovakia (which they had occupied).
*   **Need for US Action:** It urged the US government to take action to secure uranium supplies and to accelerate experimental work in the field of nuclear research. It specifically suggested government contact with physicists working on chain reactions and providing funding for their research.

Einstein, initially hesitant to get involved in political matters, was ultimately persuaded by Szilárd's arguments. He understood the implications of a nuclear-armed Nazi regime and agreed to sign the letter.

**The Impact:**

The Einstein-Szilárd letter is widely credited with prompting Roosevelt to take the threat of atomic weapons seriously. While it didn't immediately launch the Manhattan Project, it led to the creation of the Uranium Committee, the first official US government effort to investigate the potential of atomic energy for military purposes. ## PBP-Net: Point Projection and Back-Projection Network for 3D Point Cloud Segmentation

Point cloud segmentation, a fundamental task in 3D scene understanding, often struggles with sparse and irregular data. We introduce PBP-Net, a novel neural network architecture leveraging Point Projection and Back-Projection mechanisms to address these challenges. PBP-Net operates by first projecting the sparse 3D point cloud onto a dense 2D grid using a learned projection function. This projection allows for the utilization of efficient 2D convolutional operations to capture contextual information and generate robust feature maps. Subsequently, a back-projection module transfers these learned features back to the original 3D points, enriching each point with global context and facilitating accurate segmentation. We design a specific back-projection mechanism that considers both geometric proximity and feature similarity to ensure faithful feature transfer. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that PBP-Net achieves state-of-the-art performance in 3D point cloud segmentation, surpassing existing methods, especially in handling sparse and noisy point clouds. We address the limitations of traditional sequence-to-sequence models by leveraging a modular architecture that decomposes the captioning task into a series of interconnected neural modules, each responsible for a specific subtask such as object detection, attribute recognition, and relationship understanding. Our CNMN framework learns to predict the optimal module layout for a given image, enabling the network to focus on relevant visual features and generate captions with improved accuracy and semantic coherence. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our CNMN approach outperforms existing methods, particularly in generating captions that accurately describe complex scenes with multiple objects and relationships. Furthermore, the modularity of our approach provides insights into the reasoning process behind caption generation, enhancing the interpretability of the model.
## Abstract: Guiding Global Placement With Reinforcement Learning

Global placement is a critical stage in integrated circuit design that significantly impacts performance metrics such as wirelength, congestion, and routability. Traditional placement algorithms often rely on heuristics and iterative optimization, which can be computationally expensive and may not consistently achieve optimal results. This paper explores a novel approach to global placement that leverages reinforcement learning (RL) to guide the placement process. We propose an RL framework where an agent learns to strategically manipulate the placement of circuit components based on the current state of the design. The agent is trained to optimize a reward function that balances wirelength minimization, congestion reduction, and other relevant placement objectives. We investigate various state representations, action spaces, and reward functions to effectively capture the complex interactions within the placement problem. Experimental results demonstrate that our RL-guided placement approach can achieve significant improvements in wirelength and congestion compared to conventional placement techniques, offering a promising direction for automated and intelligent design optimization.
This abstract explores the application of deep reinforcement learning (DRL) methods for optimizing processing paths in structure-guided manufacturing or material processing. Traditional approaches often rely on heuristics or computationally expensive simulations to determine optimal process sequences, especially when considering complex material microstructures and desired performance characteristics. This work proposes a novel DRL framework where the processing path is treated as a sequence of actions, and the reward function is designed to reflect the desired material properties achieved through a specific processing sequence. The DRL agent learns to navigate the high-dimensional processing parameter space, guided by the underlying material structure, to discover efficient and effective processing paths. We present preliminary results demonstrating the potential of DRL to outperform conventional methods in terms of achieving target material properties and reducing processing time. Furthermore, we discuss the challenges and future directions of applying DRL to structure-guided processing path optimization, including the development of robust reward functions, efficient state representations, and strategies for handling noisy or incomplete microstructure data.
This paper presents a novel interactive tool for robust scene segmentation and annotation, leveraging the synergy between 3D and 2D representations. Our approach addresses the limitations of purely 2D or 3D annotation methods by providing users with an intuitive interface to refine segmentation results in both 3D point clouds and corresponding 2D images. The tool incorporates robust algorithms for propagating user-defined labels across modalities, ensuring consistency and minimizing annotation effort. Specifically, we utilize a combination of geometric consistency constraints and appearance-based features to transfer annotations between 3D and 2D spaces. The interactive framework allows users to correct errors and add new labels, iteratively improving the segmentation quality. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our tool on challenging real-world datasets, showcasing its ability to generate high-quality, consistent 3D-2D annotations with significantly reduced user interaction compared to traditional methods. Our approach facilitates the creation of large-scale, accurately labeled datasets for various applications in computer vision and robotics.
This paper introduces a novel approach to semi-supervised learning with multi-view data based on Partially Shared Deep Matrix Factorization (PSDMF).  Leveraging the strengths of both deep matrix factorization and multi-view learning, PSDMF aims to effectively integrate labeled and unlabeled data across multiple views by learning a shared latent representation.  Crucially, PSDMF incorporates a partial sharing mechanism, allowing for both view-specific and shared latent factors, enabling the model to capture both view-invariant and view-specific information.  This is particularly beneficial when views exhibit varying degrees of correlation and relevance to the target task.  We develop an efficient optimization algorithm to learn the model parameters and demonstrate its superior performance compared to existing semi-supervised and multi-view learning methods on benchmark datasets across various tasks. The results highlight the effectiveness of PSDMF in leveraging unlabeled data and capturing the underlying structure of multi-view data, leading to improved prediction accuracy and robustness.
Effective robot task planning in manipulation scenarios requires reasoning about the desired outcome of actions. However, explicitly defining these goals can be challenging or impractical. This paper presents a novel approach to learning manipulation goals directly from data, enabling robots to imagine and plan towards plausible outcomes without explicit specification. We propose a model that learns a latent space of manipulation goals, conditioned on the initial state of the environment. This latent space allows the robot to sample potential goals and then utilize a learned or classical planner to generate trajectories that achieve those imagined goals. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in simulated manipulation tasks, showing that the robot can learn to generate diverse and relevant goals, leading to improved planning performance and robustness compared to methods relying on pre-defined goal specifications. Our results suggest that learning to imagine manipulation goals is a promising direction for enabling robots to autonomously solve complex tasks in unstructured environments.
Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer a biologically plausible and energy-efficient alternative to traditional Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs). However, training SNNs remains a significant challenge due to the non-differentiable nature of spike events. This work explores the use of Reinforcement Learning (RL) as a promising approach to overcome this hurdle. We investigate methods for training SNNs to perform complex tasks by rewarding desired behaviors and penalizing undesirable ones. Our focus is on developing RL algorithms specifically tailored for SNNs, considering factors such as sparse spike activity, temporal dynamics, and credit assignment across spiking neurons. We present experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach on benchmark reinforcement learning environments, showcasing the potential of RL to unlock the full computational capabilities of SNNs and paving the way for energy-efficient and adaptive intelligent systems.
This paper explores the generation of adversarial examples for machine learning models using convex programming techniques. Adversarial examples, subtly perturbed inputs that cause models to misclassify, pose a significant threat to the robustness and reliability of these systems. We propose a novel approach to crafting adversarial examples by formulating the problem as a convex optimization problem, specifically designed to minimize the perturbation required to induce misclassification. This formulation leverages the properties of convex programming to guarantee finding a globally optimal solution within a defined threat model, offering advantages in terms of solution quality and computational efficiency compared to existing methods. We analyze the effectiveness of our approach on various benchmark datasets and model architectures, demonstrating its ability to generate highly effective adversarial examples with minimal perturbation. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of different convex programming formulations and constraints on the generated adversarial examples' characteristics and the resulting model vulnerability. The findings contribute to a deeper understanding of adversarial vulnerability and provide a valuable tool for robust model evaluation and defense.
## Neural Motifs: Scene Graph Parsing with Global Context

Scene graph parsing aims to extract structured representations of visual scenes, capturing objects and their relationships. However, existing approaches often struggle with long-range dependencies and ambiguous relationships due to limited contextual information. This paper introduces "Neural Motifs," a novel scene graph parsing model that leverages global context to improve relationship prediction. Our approach incorporates a global scene representation, learned through a graph neural network, to enrich the feature representations of both individual objects and their potential relationships. This global context allows the model to disambiguate relationships based on the overall scene understanding. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Neural Motifs on standard scene graph benchmark datasets, achieving significant improvements in relationship prediction accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods. Our results highlight the importance of incorporating global context for accurate and robust scene graph parsing.
This paper presents a seamless approach for 6D object pose estimation using depth images, enabling robust robotic interaction and augmented reality applications. Our work contributes a practical and reliable solution for 6D object pose estimation, paving the way for advancements in various fields requiring precise object understanding.
This paper investigates the theoretical properties of the Lasso estimator for time series estimation under realistic conditions. We provide novel guarantees for the Lasso's performance in recovering sparse time series models when the data exhibits both subgaussian tail behavior and $β$-mixing. Unlike previous work that often relies on restrictive assumptions such as independence or strong mixing, we establish bounds on the estimation error of the Lasso under the more general and practical setting of $β$-mixing, which captures a wider range of temporal dependencies. Our results demonstrate that the Lasso can consistently estimate the true underlying model with high probability, even in the presence of noise and serial correlation, provided that the mixing coefficient decays sufficiently rapidly. We provide explicit rates of convergence that depend on the sparsity level, the mixing coefficient, and the tail behavior of the noise. These theoretical findings are supported by numerical simulations, which validate the effectiveness of the Lasso in estimating sparse time series models under the specified conditions.
Developing generalizable physiological representations from wearable sensor data is crucial for personalized health monitoring and predictive modeling. This work explores a novel approach to learning such representations from large-scale, heterogeneous wearable datasets. We leverage deep learning techniques, specifically [mention specific techniques like contrastive learning, transformers, or autoencoders, if applicable], to extract robust and invariant features from raw physiological signals like heart rate, activity, and sleep. Our methodology focuses on mitigating the challenges of data heterogeneity, including variations in sensor modalities, data quality, and individual physiological baselines. By training on diverse datasets, we aim to learn representations that capture underlying physiological principles, enabling accurate and reliable performance across different populations and sensor configurations. We evaluate the generalizability of our learned representations through transfer learning experiments on downstream tasks such as [mention specific tasks like disease prediction, stress detection, or sleep stage classification]. Results demonstrate that our approach yields significant improvements in performance compared to traditional feature engineering methods and models trained on smaller, homogeneous datasets, highlighting the potential of large-scale wearable data for learning generalizable and clinically relevant physiological representations.
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in image up-sampling, offering potential for enhancing low-resolution surveillance footage. However, the effectiveness of these "surveillance GANs" in reconstructing crucial details from extremely downsampled images remains largely unexplored. This paper proposes a novel methodology for quantitatively measuring the performance of GAN-based up-sampling algorithms specifically tailored for surveillance applications. We introduce a suite of metrics beyond standard image quality assessments (e.g., PSNR, SSIM) that focus on the fidelity of reconstructed features relevant for surveillance tasks, such as facial recognition and object detection. Our approach, "Zoom, Enhance!", involves systematically downsampling high-resolution surveillance datasets, applying various GAN-based up-sampling techniques, and then evaluating the resulting images based on these task-specific metrics. We present a comparative analysis of several state-of-the-art GAN architectures, revealing their strengths and weaknesses in recovering crucial details from severely degraded surveillance imagery. The results provide valuable insights into the practical limitations of current GAN-based up-sampling techniques for surveillance applications and highlight areas for future research to improve the utility of these methods in real-world scenarios.
Probabilistic color constancy aims to estimate the scene illuminant from a single image and correct for its influence, thereby recovering the true colors of objects. Traditional color constancy algorithms often rely on deterministic assumptions about image statistics or scene properties, which can be brittle in complex or unconstrained environments. This abstract introduces the concept of probabilistic color constancy, which embraces uncertainty in both the observed image data and the underlying illuminant. By formulating color constancy as a probabilistic inference problem, we can explicitly model the likelihood of different illuminants given the observed image and incorporate prior knowledge about plausible illuminant distributions. This allows for more robust and accurate illuminant estimation, particularly in challenging scenarios with varying lighting conditions, complex scene content, and limited prior information. This abstract highlights the potential of probabilistic approaches to advance the field of color constancy by providing a principled framework for handling uncertainty and improving the reliability of color correction.
This paper proposes a novel 3D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture for Alzheimer's Disease (AD) detection, focusing on learning effective shape features and abstractions from structural Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) data. We hypothesize that AD-related changes in brain morphology can be captured by leveraging 3D CNNs to extract intricate spatial patterns. Our approach goes beyond simple voxel-based analysis by explicitly learning shape-aware features through multi-scale convolutional filters and specialized pooling layers designed to preserve structural information. Furthermore, we incorporate abstraction mechanisms to capture higher-level representations of brain regions affected by AD. We evaluate our model on a publicly available ADNI dataset, demonstrating superior performance compared to existing methods that rely on hand-crafted features or 2D CNN approaches. The results highlight the effectiveness of learning shape-specific features and abstractions in 3D CNNs for improved AD detection accuracy and early diagnosis. This work contributes to the development of automated tools for AD diagnosis, potentially leading to earlier intervention and improved patient outcomes.
Developing effective recommendation systems is crucial for a wide range of applications, from e-commerce to personalized content delivery. However, the lack of standardized benchmarks hinders the fair comparison and advancement of machine learning (ML) models and hardware platforms for recommendation tasks. This paper proposes the development of a comprehensive recommendation benchmark suite for MLPerf Training and Inference. We outline the key considerations for selecting representative datasets, defining realistic workloads, and establishing rigorous evaluation metrics relevant to both training and inference phases of recommendation models. The proposed benchmark will encompass diverse recommendation scenarios, including collaborative filtering, content-based recommendation, and hybrid approaches, with varying data scales and complexity levels. By providing a standardized and publicly available benchmark, we aim to foster innovation in recommendation algorithms, hardware acceleration, and system design, ultimately contributing to the development of more efficient and effective recommendation systems.
This paper introduces a novel approach for fast classification using sparse decision directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). Traditional decision trees and DAGs, while interpretable, can suffer from high memory consumption and slow inference times, especially with complex datasets. Our method addresses these limitations by learning a sparse DAG structure that prioritizes crucial features and reduces redundant decision paths. We employ a regularized optimization framework to simultaneously learn the DAG topology and node parameters, promoting sparsity and minimizing prediction error. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our sparse decision DAGs achieve competitive accuracy compared to state-of-the-art classifiers, while significantly reducing model size and inference time. This makes our approach particularly suitable for resource-constrained environments and applications requiring rapid classification.
Understanding the dynamic relationships between diseases (comorbidities) is crucial for personalized medicine and predicting disease progression. Traditional comorbidity network analysis often relies on static co-occurrence patterns, neglecting the temporal evolution and individual variations in disease trajectories. This paper introduces a novel approach, leveraging Deep Diffusion Processes, to learn dynamic and personalized comorbidity networks from event data (e.g., medical records). Our method models the progression of patients through disease states as a diffusion process, where the transition probabilities between diseases are learned through a deep neural network. This allows us to capture the dynamic interplay of diseases over time and personalize the network structure based on individual patient histories. We evaluate our approach on real-world medical datasets, demonstrating its ability to accurately predict future disease occurrences and uncover clinically relevant, dynamic comorbidity patterns compared to existing static and dynamic network learning methods. The personalized comorbidity networks learned offer valuable insights into individual disease risks and can potentially improve patient-specific treatment strategies.
This paper presents a novel approach for fish recognition that leverages the synergy between robust feature selection, image segmentation, and geometrical parameter extraction techniques, coupled with Artificial Neural Network (ANN) and Decision Tree (DT) classifiers. The proposed method initially employs image segmentation to isolate individual fish from background clutter, followed by the extraction of a comprehensive set of geometrical parameters. To mitigate the impact of redundant and irrelevant features, a robust feature selection algorithm is implemented to identify the most discriminative parameters for fish species identification. The selected features are then used to train both an ANN and a DT classifier. The performance of the proposed method is evaluated on a diverse dataset of fish images, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness in accurately recognizing different fish species. A comparative analysis between the ANN and DT classifiers reveals their respective strengths and weaknesses in this context. This research contributes to the development of automated fish recognition systems with applications in aquaculture, fisheries management, and biodiversity monitoring.
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as a powerful tool for representation learning on graph-structured data. However, designing effective GNN architectures often requires significant expertise and manual experimentation. This paper introduces Auto-GNN, a novel framework for automatically searching for optimal GNN architectures. Auto-GNN leverages neural architecture search (NAS) techniques to explore a vast design space of GNN components, including aggregation functions, message passing mechanisms, and layer connectivity patterns. We propose a differentiable search space that allows for efficient gradient-based optimization of the GNN architecture. Furthermore, we introduce a performance prediction model to further accelerate the search process and prune unpromising architectures early on. Experimental results on various benchmark datasets demonstrate that Auto-GNN can discover GNN architectures that outperform manually designed models, achieving state-of-the-art performance and demonstrating the potential of automated GNN architecture design.
Searching for optimal object detector architectures within a vast design space is computationally expensive. This paper introduces a novel representation sharing approach to significantly accelerate this search process. Our method leverages the observation that different detector architectures often share common feature extraction modules. Instead of training each candidate architecture from scratch, we train a shared feature representation that can be efficiently adapted and fine-tuned for various detector heads and backbones. This representation sharing drastically reduces the training time required for each candidate, enabling a faster and more thorough exploration of the detector architecture space. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a diverse set of object detection benchmarks, showcasing significant speedups in architecture search without compromising detection accuracy. Furthermore, we explore the potential of our shared representation beyond architecture search, demonstrating its applicability to transfer learning and domain adaptation, highlighting its versatility and broad applicability.
This paper introduces the Graph Learning Network (GLN), a novel algorithm for structure learning from data. GLN aims to automatically discover the underlying graph structure that best represents the relationships and dependencies within a dataset. Unlike traditional methods that rely on pre-defined graph structures or require significant domain knowledge, GLN learns the graph directly from the data through an iterative process of edge pruning and addition based on a learned scoring function. This scoring function leverages node features and potential edge relationships to evaluate the importance of each connection. We demonstrate the effectiveness of GLN on both synthetic and real-world datasets, showing its ability to accurately recover ground truth graph structures and improve performance in downstream tasks such as node classification and link prediction compared to existing structure learning techniques and methods relying on pre-defined graph structures. The results highlight GLN's potential for applications in various domains where understanding underlying relationships is crucial, including social network analysis, biological network discovery, and knowledge graph construction.
This paper addresses the challenging problem of parsing surveillance videos into meaningful events without relying on costly and time-consuming frame-level annotations. We propose a novel approach that leverages single frame supervision to learn to understand complex activities within surveillance footage. Our method focuses on [mention the core technique - e.g., learning temporal relationships, identifying key objects, or using weakly supervised learning]. By only requiring annotations for a single representative frame within each event, we significantly reduce the annotation burden while still achieving effective event detection and classification. Experimental results on [mention datasets used] demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, showing competitive performance compared to methods requiring more extensive supervision and highlighting the potential for practical application in real-world surveillance systems. We further analyze the impact of different single frame selection strategies and provide insights into the challenges and future directions of single frame supervised surveillance video parsing.
Understanding the complex dynamics of the human cardiovascular system is crucial for diagnosis, treatment planning, and personalized medicine. While traditional mechanistic models offer high fidelity, they can be computationally expensive and require extensive parameter identification. In contrast, data-driven models, such as neural networks, can learn complex relationships from data but often lack interpretability and generalizability. This work proposes a hybrid modeling approach, leveraging Neural Functional Mock-up Units (NeuralFMUs), to combine the strengths of both methodologies. We integrate a simplified, physics-based cardiovascular model with a neural network trained to capture unmodeled dynamics and patient-specific variations. The NeuralFMU framework allows for seamless co-simulation of the mechanistic and data-driven components, enabling efficient and accurate prediction of cardiovascular behavior. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through simulations, showing improved accuracy compared to purely mechanistic models while maintaining interpretability and enabling efficient exploration of different physiological scenarios. This hybrid modeling approach offers a promising avenue for developing personalized cardiovascular models with enhanced predictive capabilities and reduced computational burden.
Predicting future events from time-series data is a critical task in various domains. This paper introduces a novel approach, Time-Series Event Prediction with Evolutionary State Graph (TSEP-ESG), which leverages a dynamically evolving state graph to model complex temporal dependencies and predict future events. TSEP-ESG represents the system's state as a node in the graph, with edges representing transitions between states triggered by observed events. The graph evolves over time, adapting to new event sequences and capturing long-range dependencies. We propose an evolutionary mechanism that allows the graph to grow, merge, and prune nodes and edges based on event frequencies and transition probabilities. This evolutionary process enables the model to adapt to non-stationary time-series data and mitigate the impact of noise.  Furthermore, we develop a prediction algorithm that utilizes the evolved state graph to estimate the likelihood of future events based on the current system state and historical event sequences.  Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate that TSEP-ESG outperforms existing methods in terms of prediction accuracy and robustness, highlighting its effectiveness in capturing complex temporal patterns and predicting future events in dynamic environments.
This paper introduces a novel approach for high-dimensional nonlinear profile monitoring using Deep Probabilistic Autoencoders (DPAEs). Traditional profile monitoring techniques often struggle with high-dimensional data and nonlinear relationships. The proposed method leverages the ability of DPAEs to learn a low-dimensional latent representation that captures the essential nonlinear features of the profiles. By modeling the latent space with a probabilistic distribution, we can establish control limits based on the reconstruction probability of new profiles. This allows for more robust and accurate detection of process shifts compared to methods relying on linear assumptions or distance-based metrics. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our DPAE-based profile monitoring approach through simulations and real-world case studies, showcasing its superior performance in detecting subtle and complex process deviations in high-dimensional nonlinear environments. The results highlight the potential of DPAEs as a powerful tool for process monitoring and quality control in modern manufacturing and industrial applications.
## DISK: Learning Local Features with Policy Gradient

This paper introduces DISK, a novel approach for learning local feature detectors and descriptors using policy gradient reinforcement learning. Traditional feature learning methods often rely on hand-crafted loss functions or proxy tasks, limiting their adaptability to diverse downstream applications. DISK overcomes these limitations by formulating feature extraction as a sequential decision-making process. An agent, represented by a neural network, learns a policy to select keypoints and generate corresponding descriptors. The policy is trained directly on downstream tasks, such as image matching or visual localization, using policy gradient methods. We demonstrate that DISK can learn robust and task-specific local features that outperform existing hand-crafted and learned features on challenging benchmarks. The flexibility of the policy gradient framework allows for easy adaptation to various downstream tasks and offers a promising direction for developing more intelligent and adaptable local feature representations.
Perceptual image super-resolution aims to generate high-resolution (HR) images that are not only visually pleasing but also perceptually realistic. This paper proposes Bi-GANs-ST, a novel framework leveraging Bidirectional Generative Adversarial Networks (Bi-GANs) and Spatial Transformers (ST) to achieve superior perceptual image super-resolution. Our approach employs a Bi-GAN architecture, where the generator upscales the low-resolution (LR) input and the encoder maps the generated HR image back to a latent space, encouraging consistency between the generated and real HR distributions. We further enhance the perceptual quality by incorporating Spatial Transformers within the generator, enabling it to selectively focus on and refine salient regions within the image. This allows the network to better reconstruct fine-grained details and reduce artifacts. Experimental results demonstrate that Bi-GANs-ST outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of both perceptual metrics and visual quality, generating HR images with sharper details and more realistic textures while maintaining high fidelity to the original LR input.

Distributed Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is a prevalent approach for training large-scale machine learning models. However, the communication of gradients between workers and the parameter server can become a significant bottleneck, especially with high-dimensional models and large datasets. This paper proposes a communication-efficient distributed SGD algorithm that leverages sketching techniques to reduce the communication overhead.
