## SPSG: Self-Supervised Photometric Scene Generation from RGB-D Scans

This paper introduces SPSG, a novel self-supervised approach for photometric scene generation from RGB-D scans. Our method leverages the abundance of readily available RGB-D data to learn a generative model capable of producing realistic and photometrically consistent novel views of a scene. Unlike existing methods that rely on explicit geometric proxies or require paired data, SPSG learns directly from raw RGB-D scans by formulating a photometric consistency loss between generated and observed images. This self-supervised learning framework enables the model to implicitly learn scene geometry and appearance representations, leading to high-quality novel view synthesis. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SPSG through quantitative and qualitative evaluations on benchmark datasets, showing that our method achieves competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art supervised approaches while requiring no labeled data. Furthermore, we analyze the learned representations and demonstrate their potential for downstream tasks such as scene understanding and relighting.
Conditional Teacher-Student Learning (CTSL) is a novel framework for knowledge transfer that extends traditional teacher-student learning by incorporating conditional information. Unlike standard approaches where the student learns directly from the teacher's outputs, CTSL leverages contextual information to guide the learning process. This contextual information, represented as conditions, modulates the relationship between the teacher and student, allowing the student to learn different aspects of the teacher's knowledge based on the specific context. This approach enables the student to acquire a more nuanced and adaptive understanding of the target task, potentially exceeding the performance of the teacher under specific conditions. We explore various implementations of CTSL, including methods for conditioning the student's learning objective, the teacher's output, and the knowledge distillation process itself. We demonstrate the effectiveness of CTSL in several challenging domains, showcasing its ability to improve student performance, enhance generalization, and enable specialization based on contextual cues. Our results highlight the potential of CTSL as a powerful tool for knowledge transfer in dynamic and complex environments.
This paper explores the creation of knowledge graph (KG)-based world models for navigating and interacting with textual environments. We propose a novel approach to learn structured representations of textual environments by extracting entities and relations from text and constructing a KG that captures the state and dynamics of the environment. This KG serves as a world model that agents can use to reason about the environment, predict future states, and plan actions. The results highlight the potential of KG-based world models for improving reasoning, planning, and exploration in complex, text-based environments.
Risk-sensitive reinforcement learning aims to optimize policies that not only maximize expected returns but also account for the uncertainty and potential variability in those returns. This paper introduces Distributional Soft Actor-Critic (DSAC), a novel algorithm that combines the benefits of distributional reinforcement learning with the exploration and stability of Soft Actor-Critic (SAC). DSAC learns a categorical distribution over returns, allowing for a richer representation of uncertainty compared to traditional value-based methods. By integrating this distributional perspective into the SAC framework, DSAC enables risk-sensitive control by directly influencing the learned return distribution through a risk-sensitive temperature parameter. We demonstrate that DSAC outperforms standard SAC and other risk-sensitive RL algorithms on a range of challenging continuous control tasks, showcasing its ability to effectively learn policies that prioritize either risk-aversion or risk-seeking behavior, depending on the specified risk preferences. Our results highlight the effectiveness of distributional representations for incorporating risk sensitivity into off-policy actor-critic methods.
Additive Manufacturing (AM) processes offer unprecedented design freedom but are often characterized by complex relationships between process parameters and resulting material properties. Efficiently exploring this parameter space to optimize desired outcomes is crucial for realizing the full potential of AM. This work investigates the application of Bayesian Optimization (BO) as a sequential experimental design strategy for AM process optimization. BO leverages Gaussian Process (GP) surrogates to model the unknown objective function and an acquisition function to intelligently select the next experiment, balancing exploration of the parameter space with exploitation of promising regions. Integrating external knowledge into neural networks is crucial for enhancing performance in various tasks. Accurate prediction of traffic signal timings is crucial for intelligent transportation systems, enabling optimized routing, reduced congestion, and improved overall network efficiency. This paper presents a novel approach for predicting traffic signal states on transportation networks by leveraging spatio-temporal correlations represented on graphs. We model the transportation network as a graph, where nodes represent intersections and edges represent road segments. By capturing the spatial dependencies between neighboring intersections and the temporal evolution of signal timings, we develop a model that learns complex patterns and predicts future signal states. We evaluate the performance of our model on [mention dataset used] and demonstrate its superiority over baseline methods in terms of prediction accuracy and responsiveness to dynamic traffic conditions. The results highlight the potential of our spatio-temporal graph-based approach for real-time traffic signal prediction and its contribution to the development of more efficient and sustainable transportation systems.
## LEAF-QA: Locate, Encode & Attend for Figure Question Answering

Figure Question Answering (FigureQA) presents a unique challenge, requiring models to understand both visual information within figures and complex natural language questions. We introduce LEAF-QA, a novel approach that explicitly addresses the crucial aspects of this task: **L**ocating relevant regions within the figure, **E**ncoding both the figure and question effectively, and **A**ttending to the most informative visual features for answering the question. Our model first employs a region proposal network to identify potential areas of interest within the figure. These regions, along with the question, are then encoded using a combination of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs). Finally, an attention mechanism dynamically focuses on the most pertinent visual regions based on the encoded question, allowing the model to reason about the figure and generate an accurate answer. We demonstrate the efficacy of LEAF-QA through extensive experiments on benchmark FigureQA datasets, achieving state-of-the-art results and demonstrating its ability to effectively integrate visual and textual information for accurate question answering.
This paper presents a novel approach for human extraction and scene transition leveraging the capabilities of Mask R-CNN.  We propose a system that accurately identifies and segments human figures within images or video frames using Mask R-CNN.  This allows for precise extraction of the human subject from the original background.  Furthermore, we explore the application of this extracted human mask in creating seamless scene transitions.  By intelligently compositing the extracted human onto a new background, we demonstrate the potential for generating visually compelling and realistic transitions between different scenes.  The effectiveness of the proposed method is evaluated on [mention datasets used, e.g., a dataset of diverse scenes and human poses], demonstrating its ability to achieve accurate human extraction and facilitate smooth scene transitions with minimal artifacts. This work offers a valuable tool for various applications, including video editing, augmented reality, and virtual environment creation.
Sample efficiency remains a significant challenge in reinforcement learning (RL). While much research focuses on algorithm design, the quality of the state representation significantly impacts learning speed. This work investigates the central question: "Is a good representation sufficient for sample efficient reinforcement learning?" We explore the interplay between representation learning and RL algorithms, examining whether a representation capturing the essential task-relevant information can drastically reduce the sample complexity of subsequent policy learning. We analyze various notions of "good" representations, including those that are disentangled, predictive, and informative about rewards and transitions. Through theoretical analysis and empirical evaluations on benchmark environments, we investigate the conditions under which a high-quality representation enables sample-efficient learning, even with relatively simple RL algorithms. Our findings suggest that while a good representation can significantly improve sample efficiency, it is often not sufficient on its own. Factors such as the exploration strategy, the complexity of the policy space, and the presence of non-Markovian dynamics can still limit performance. We conclude by discussing the implications of our findings for future research directions, emphasizing the need for a holistic approach that combines effective representation learning with robust RL algorithms and exploration strategies to achieve truly sample-efficient learning.
This paper presents a novel Bayesian Decision Tree (BDT) algorithm for classification and regression tasks. Traditional decision tree algorithms often suffer from overfitting and instability due to their greedy tree-growing approach. To address these limitations, we propose a fully Bayesian framework that leverages prior distributions over tree structures and node parameters. This allows us to quantify uncertainty in the model and obtain a posterior distribution over possible decision trees. Our algorithm employs Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods to sample from this posterior, effectively averaging over a diverse set of trees. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our BDT algorithm through empirical evaluations on various benchmark datasets, showing significant improvements in predictive accuracy, robustness to noise, and uncertainty quantification compared to traditional decision tree algorithms and other state-of-the-art methods. The Bayesian approach also provides a natural framework for handling missing data and incorporating prior knowledge, further enhancing the algorithm's applicability in real-world scenarios.
Log data is a valuable resource for monitoring and diagnosing system anomalies. However, the high volume and complexity of log data present significant challenges for effective anomaly detection. Existing log anomaly detection methods often struggle with noisy data, subtle anomaly patterns, and the intricate relationships between log events. This paper introduces A2Log, an **A**ttentive **A**ugmented Log Anomaly Detection framework designed to address these limitations. A2Log leverages log parsing to extract event templates and then employs a novel **attentive sequence-to-sequence model** to learn normal log patterns. To further enhance detection accuracy, A2Log incorporates an **augmentation strategy** that generates synthetic log sequences representative of normal behavior, enriching the training data and improving the model's ability to distinguish subtle anomalies. The attention mechanism allows the model to focus on the most relevant log events within a sequence, capturing nuanced contextual information. Experimental results on real-world log datasets demonstrate that A2Log significantly outperforms state-of-the-art log anomaly detection methods in terms of precision, recall, and F1-score, showcasing its effectiveness in detecting a wide range of anomalies while minimizing false positives.
Arbitrary style transfer aims to render a content image in the style of any given style image. While existing approaches have achieved impressive results, they often neglect the spatial relationships and structural information present in the content image, leading to artifacts and inconsistencies, especially in scenes with significant depth variations. This paper introduces a novel depth-aware arbitrary style transfer method that leverages instance normalization (IN) to better preserve content structure and enhance stylistic fidelity. We incorporate depth information, estimated from a single image or provided externally, to modulate the IN parameters within a convolutional neural network. Specifically, we propose a depth-modulated instance normalization (DMIN) layer that adaptively adjusts the normalization statistics based on the depth map. This allows the network to preserve the original content structure at different depth levels while effectively transferring the style.  Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the visual quality of stylized images, yielding more realistic and coherent results compared to state-of-the-art methods, particularly in scenes with complex depth cues. We further validate the effectiveness of our DMIN layer through ablation studies and qualitative comparisons.
This paper proposes a scalable approach to centralized deep multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) using policy gradients. Centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE) offers improved stability and performance in cooperative MARL scenarios by leveraging global state information during training. However, naively scaling centralized training to large agent populations can become computationally intractable due to the exponentially growing joint action space. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel policy gradient method that decomposes the joint action selection process, enabling efficient exploration and learning in high-dimensional action spaces. Our approach leverages a centralized critic that conditions on the global state and individual agent policies to estimate the joint action-value function. We then use this estimate to guide individual agent policy updates. We demonstrate the scalability and effectiveness of our method in challenging cooperative MARL environments with a large number of agents, showing significant performance improvements compared to existing decentralized and centralized MARL algorithms. Our results highlight the potential of centralized deep MARL with policy gradients for solving complex, large-scale multi-agent problems.
## GMAT: Global Memory Augmentation for Transformers

Transformers excel at capturing local dependencies within sequences, but struggle with long-range dependencies and maintaining a coherent global context, particularly in lengthy inputs. This paper introduces Global Memory Augmentation for Transformers (GMAT), a novel architecture that explicitly augments the Transformer with a learnable global memory module. GMAT iteratively updates this global memory based on the current input and previous memory state, allowing the model to accumulate and maintain a comprehensive representation of the entire input sequence. This global memory is then incorporated into the Transformer's attention mechanism, enabling the model to attend to both local context and the globally aggregated information. We evaluate GMAT on a range of tasks requiring long-range dependency modeling, including document summarization, question answering, and language modeling. Experimental results demonstrate that GMAT significantly improves performance compared to standard Transformers and other memory-augmented architectures, highlighting its ability to effectively capture and utilize global context for enhanced sequence modeling.
Subgraph Federated Learning (SubFL) offers a promising approach to address data heterogeneity and privacy concerns in graph neural networks (GNNs) by training GNNs on local subgraphs at each client. However, real-world graph data often suffers from missing neighbor information, which can significantly degrade the performance of GNNs in SubFL. To mitigate this issue, we propose a novel SubFL framework with Missing Neighbor Generation. Our approach enables clients to generate plausible missing neighbors based on their local subgraph structure and attributes before participating in the federated learning process. This generation process is integrated into the local training loop, allowing the GNN to learn to leverage both observed and generated neighbors. Furthermore, we introduce a federated aggregation strategy that considers the uncertainty associated with generated neighbors, preventing the propagation of potentially noisy information across clients. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework through extensive experiments on various benchmark datasets, showing significant performance improvements compared to existing SubFL methods, especially in scenarios with high degrees of missing neighbor information. Our results highlight the importance of addressing missing data issues in federated graph learning and the potential of our approach to improve the robustness and accuracy of SubFL systems.
Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) suffer from performance degradation due to inter-subject variability and the challenge of extracting discriminative features for different brain states. This paper proposes a novel deep learning framework for BCI that learns subject-invariant and class-relevant representations based on mutual information (MI) maximization and minimization. Specifically, we maximize the MI between the learned representation and the task labels to ensure class-relevance, while simultaneously minimizing the MI between the representation and subject-specific information to achieve subject-invariance. This encourages the network to learn features that are highly predictive of the intended brain state but less sensitive to individual differences. We evaluate the proposed approach on multiple BCI datasets and demonstrate its superior performance compared to existing methods in terms of classification accuracy and generalization ability across subjects. The results highlight the effectiveness of utilizing MI as a guiding principle for learning robust and generalizable BCI representations.
Visual navigation is a critical capability for autonomous unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs), enabling them to traverse complex environments without relying solely on GPS or pre-mapped routes. This paper explores the application of machine learning techniques to enhance visual navigation for UGVs. We review various machine learning approaches, including supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning, and their specific applications in areas such as visual perception, path planning, and control. We discuss the advantages and limitations of each approach, focusing on their performance in challenging scenarios involving dynamic environments, varying lighting conditions, and limited computational resources. Furthermore, we examine the challenges associated with data acquisition, model training, and real-time deployment of machine learning algorithms on UGVs. Finally, we present potential future research directions in this rapidly evolving field, highlighting opportunities for improving the robustness, efficiency, and adaptability of machine learning-based visual navigation systems for UGVs.
This paper explores the generation of the Near-Infrared (NIR) spectral band for satellite imagery using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). NIR data is crucial for various applications, including vegetation monitoring, land cover classification, and water resource management. However, access to NIR bands is often limited due to sensor availability or cost constraints. This research investigates the feasibility of synthesizing the NIR band from readily available visible bands (Red, Green, and Blue) using a deep learning approach. We propose a CNN architecture specifically designed to learn the complex relationships between visible and NIR spectral information. The model is trained on a dataset of paired visible and NIR satellite images and evaluated based on its ability to accurately reconstruct the NIR band. The results demonstrate the potential of CNNs to generate high-quality NIR data, offering a cost-effective and efficient solution for enhancing satellite image analysis and expanding the applicability of remote sensing technologies.
## Abstract: Machine Learning Classifications of Coronary Artery Disease

Coronary Artery Disease (CAD) remains a leading cause of mortality and morbidity worldwide. Early and accurate diagnosis is crucial for effective management and improved patient outcomes. This study explores the application of machine learning (ML) algorithms for the classification of CAD based on various clinical and demographic features. We investigate the performance of several ML models, including [mention specific models used, e.g., Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines, Random Forest, and Neural Networks], in classifying individuals as having CAD or not. The models are trained and validated on a dataset of [mention dataset size and key characteristics, e.g., patient records from a hospital database containing risk factors, ECG results, and angiographic findings]. We evaluate the models using metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC to identify the most effective algorithm for CAD classification. Furthermore, we analyze feature importance to identify the key predictors contributing to the models' performance. The findings demonstrate the potential of ML techniques to assist clinicians in early CAD detection, leading to improved diagnostic accuracy and potentially facilitating more timely and personalized treatment strategies. This research contributes to the growing body of evidence supporting the use of ML in cardiovascular disease management.
Point cloud registration, a fundamental task in computer vision and robotics, aims to find the optimal transformation that aligns two or more point clouds. Existing approaches often rely on point-to-point or point-to-plane distances within a least-squares framework. However, these methods are susceptible to outliers, noise, and variations in point density, leading to inaccurate registration results. This paper introduces a novel and robust loss function specifically designed to mitigate the impact of these challenges. Our loss function leverages [mention key idea, e.g., a re-weighted M-estimator or a robust error norm] to effectively downweight outliers and noisy correspondences, thereby improving the accuracy and stability of the registration process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, showcasing its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods, particularly in scenarios with significant noise and outlier contamination. Our results indicate that the proposed loss function significantly enhances the robustness and reliability of point cloud registration, making it a valuable tool for various applications.
Irregular time series data, characterized by non-uniform sampling intervals and missing values, pose significant challenges for traditional time series models. This paper introduces Multi-FIT (Multi-resolution Networks For Flexible Irregular Time Series Modeling), a novel approach that leverages multi-resolution analysis to effectively capture temporal dependencies in such data. Multi-FIT employs a hierarchical network architecture to represent the time series at different levels of granularity, allowing it to adaptively focus on relevant temporal patterns regardless of the irregularity. Specifically, the model utilizes learnable aggregation functions to consolidate information across resolutions and incorporates a novel imputation mechanism to handle missing values without relying on predefined interpolation strategies. We demonstrate the efficacy of Multi-FIT on various benchmark datasets, showcasing its superior performance compared to existing methods in tasks such as classification, forecasting, and imputation. Our results highlight the advantages of multi-resolution representations in capturing complex temporal dynamics within irregular time series data, offering a flexible and robust solution for real-world applications.
This paper explores the application of a plugin procedure for hyperspectral image segmentation. Hyperspectral images, with their rich spectral information, offer significant potential for accurate and detailed segmentation. However, their high dimensionality presents challenges for traditional segmentation algorithms. The proposed approach leverages a plugin procedure, a technique that estimates parameters and substitutes them into a predefined classifier or segmentation model. This allows for efficient and adaptable segmentation by decoupling the parameter estimation from the classification process. We investigate the effectiveness of this plugin procedure using various parameter estimation techniques and segmentation models, highlighting its potential for improving segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency in hyperspectral image analysis. The performance of the proposed method is evaluated on real-world hyperspectral datasets, demonstrating its advantages in terms of both segmentation quality and computational cost compared to existing approaches.
## GaussiGAN: Controllable Image Synthesis with 3D Gaussians from Unposed Silhouettes

This paper introduces GaussiGAN, a novel framework for controllable image synthesis from unposed silhouettes using 3D Gaussians.  Leveraging the expressive power and differentiability of 3D Gaussian splatting, GaussiGAN learns to reconstruct and render realistic images given only silhouette masks as input. Our approach combines a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) with a 3D Gaussian rasterizer, enabling the generation of diverse and high-quality images with explicit 3D structure learned from 2D supervision. We demonstrate that by conditioning the GAN on silhouette information, we can effectively control the shape and pose of the generated objects. Furthermore, we explore strategies for disentangling appearance and geometry within the 3D Gaussian representation, allowing for fine-grained control over the synthesized images.  Experiments on various datasets demonstrate GaussiGAN's ability to generate compelling and controllable images from unposed silhouettes, achieving state-of-the-art results in silhouette-based image synthesis and offering a promising avenue for 3D-aware generative modeling from limited supervision.
This paper proposes a novel approach for selective network discovery using deep reinforcement learning (DRL) operating on embedded spaces. Traditional network discovery methods often exhaustively explore all possible connections, leading to significant overhead in resource-constrained environments, particularly in embedded systems. Our method addresses this challenge by learning a policy that selectively explores the network, prioritizing potentially valuable connections while minimizing unnecessary probing. We first embed network entities into a high-dimensional space, capturing their inherent relationships and characteristics.  Then, a DRL agent learns to navigate this embedded space, making informed decisions about which connections to investigate based on the current state representation and a learned reward function that balances discovery efficiency with accuracy.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through simulations and experiments, showing that it significantly reduces the discovery overhead compared to traditional methods while maintaining a high level of network coverage and accuracy, making it particularly suitable for resource-limited embedded environments.
Time series data, characterized by its sequential and temporal dependency, is prevalent in various domains. However, real-world time series are often incomplete due to missing values arising from sensor failures, data corruption, or irregular sampling. Accurate imputation of these missing values is crucial for reliable downstream analysis and forecasting. In recent years, deep learning techniques have emerged as powerful tools for time series imputation, demonstrating superior performance compared to traditional statistical methods. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of deep learning approaches for time series data imputation, categorizing them based on their underlying architectures, including Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Transformers, and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). We discuss the strengths and weaknesses of each approach, highlighting their suitability for different types of missing data patterns (e.g., Missing Completely At Random, Missing At Random, Missing Not At Random) and time series characteristics (e.g., seasonality, trend). Furthermore, we examine commonly used evaluation metrics and benchmark datasets for comparing imputation performance. Finally, we identify open challenges and future research directions in the field, focusing on areas such as handling long-range dependencies, incorporating domain knowledge, and developing robust imputation methods for complex and high-dimensional time series data.
This paper investigates the application of the Network Lasso for semi-supervised regression, a machine learning paradigm where a model is trained using both labeled and unlabeled data. We focus on leveraging the network structure, represented as a graph connecting data points, to improve regression performance in scenarios with limited labeled data. The Network Lasso incorporates a regularization term that encourages similar regression coefficients for connected nodes in the network, effectively propagating information from labeled to unlabeled instances. We present a detailed analysis of the Network Lasso's theoretical properties and demonstrate its effectiveness through numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets. Our results demonstrate that the Network Lasso can significantly outperform traditional supervised regression methods, particularly when the network structure accurately reflects the underlying relationships between data points and the amount of labeled data is scarce. We further explore the impact of different network construction methods and regularization parameters on the performance of the Network Lasso, providing insights into its practical application for semi-supervised regression tasks.
Structured output prediction, where the goal is to predict complex, interrelated output structures, poses significant generalization challenges. Traditional generalization bounds often provide limited insight into the performance of models on specific substructures or under particular data distributions. This work presents a fine-grained generalization analysis of structured output prediction, moving beyond global error bounds to offer a more nuanced understanding of model behavior. We leverage techniques from learning theory and structural risk minimization to derive bounds that are sensitive to the complexity of individual substructures within the output space. Our analysis considers factors such as the frequency of specific substructures in the training data, their inherent complexity, and the model's ability to capture their dependencies. We demonstrate how these fine-grained bounds can be used to identify potential failure modes of structured prediction models and guide model design for improved performance on targeted substructures. Furthermore, we provide empirical validation of our theoretical results on benchmark structured prediction tasks, highlighting the practical benefits of this fine-grained generalization perspective.
Graph embedding aims to represent graph structures as low-dimensional vectors, enabling efficient analysis and prediction. However, many existing methods rely on carefully tuned hyperparameters, requiring significant computational effort and expertise. Furthermore, the lack of transparency in the embedding process hinders understanding and trust in the resulting representations. This paper introduces a novel **hyperparameter-free and explainable whole graph embedding** approach. Our method leverages intrinsic structural properties of the graph, specifically its spectral characteristics, to generate embeddings without requiring user-defined hyperparameters. Crucially, we provide mechanisms to interpret the contribution of individual nodes and edges to the overall graph embedding, offering insights into the reasoning behind the learned representations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on various graph datasets, showing competitive performance compared to hyperparameter-dependent methods while providing significantly enhanced explainability. Our approach facilitates broader adoption and deeper understanding of graph embedding techniques, especially in domains where interpretability is paramount.
## Abstract: Context-Aware Generative Adversarial Privacy

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have shown promise in generating synthetic data for privacy-preserving data sharing and analysis. However, traditional GAN-based privacy mechanisms often overlook the contextual information inherent within the data, leading to potential privacy leakage and reduced utility. This paper introduces Context-Aware Generative Adversarial Privacy (CAGAP), a novel framework that leverages contextual information during the GAN training process to enhance both privacy and utility. CAGAP incorporates a context encoder that captures relevant contextual attributes and integrates them into both the generator and discriminator of the GAN. By conditioning the generated data on these contextual features, CAGAP ensures that the synthetic data reflects the underlying data distribution more accurately, while simultaneously obfuscating sensitive individual information through context-aware generation. We evaluate CAGAP on real-world datasets, demonstrating its superior performance compared to existing GAN-based privacy mechanisms in terms of both privacy metrics (e.g., membership inference attack success rate) and utility metrics (e.g., classification accuracy on synthetic data). Our results highlight the importance of considering context in generative adversarial privacy and demonstrate the potential of CAGAP to create more effective and practical privacy-preserving data sharing solutions.
Multiplicative noise, where noise is scaled by the input signal, is increasingly recognized as a powerful regularizer and uncertainty estimator in neural networks. This work provides a novel perspective on multiplicative noise models by framing them as scale mixtures. We demonstrate that common multiplicative noise distributions, such as Gaussian and Bernoulli, can be viewed as arising from specific scale mixtures of simpler distributions. This perspective offers several advantages: (1) it provides a unified framework for understanding different multiplicative noise strategies; (2) it facilitates the development of new and potentially more effective multiplicative noise models by leveraging the rich literature on scale mixtures; and (3) it allows for improved inference and learning algorithms by exploiting the conditional conjugacy often present in scale mixture representations. We illustrate the utility of this framework through theoretical analysis and empirical evaluations, demonstrating that the scale mixture perspective can lead to improved performance and interpretability in neural networks with multiplicative noise.
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable success in various graph-related tasks. However, their inherent complexity often results in opaque decision-making processes, hindering trust and hindering their adoption in critical applications. This paper addresses the challenge of explainability in GNNs by exploring techniques towards **self-explainable GNNs**. We aim to develop GNN architectures that inherently provide explanations for their predictions, eliminating the need for post-hoc explanation methods. We investigate strategies to integrate explanation mechanisms directly into the GNN training process, focusing on methods that highlight relevant features, subgraphs, or node relationships contributing to a specific prediction. Our approach aims to improve model transparency, enhance user understanding, and ultimately foster greater trust and reliability in GNN-based systems. We will present preliminary results demonstrating the feasibility of self-explainable GNNs, highlighting their potential to provide intrinsic insights into the reasoning process behind GNN predictions.
Catastrophic forgetting, the abrupt and severe loss of previously learned information when training on new tasks, poses a significant challenge to the development of robust and lifelong learning artificial intelligence systems. This study investigates the hypothesis that providing explanations for decisions during training can mitigate catastrophic forgetting. We propose that explanations, by forcing the model to represent underlying causal relationships and generalize beyond superficial correlations, lead to more stable and transferable knowledge representations. Through experiments on benchmark continual learning datasets, we demonstrate that models trained with explanation mechanisms exhibit significantly reduced catastrophic forgetting compared to baseline models. Furthermore, we analyze the learned representations to show that explanation-augmented models develop more robust and generalizable knowledge, allowing them to retain performance on previously learned tasks while adapting to new information. These findings suggest that incorporating explanation capabilities is a promising approach for building AI systems that can learn continuously and avoid catastrophic forgetting.
Large-scale graph neural networks (GNNs) are prone to overfitting, especially when trained on imbalanced or noisy datasets. Label smoothing, a regularization technique that softens hard labels, has shown promise in mitigating this issue. However, a fixed smoothing rate may not be optimal for all nodes and training stages. This paper proposes an adaptive label smoothing (ALS) approach that dynamically adjusts the smoothing rate based on the uncertainty and confidence of the GNN's predictions during training. Our method leverages the network's output distribution to estimate the reliability of its predictions for each node and adapts the smoothing rate accordingly, smoothing more aggressively for uncertain predictions and less for confident ones. We demonstrate the effectiveness of ALS on several large-scale graph datasets, showing that it consistently outperforms traditional label smoothing and other regularization techniques in terms of generalization performance and robustness to noisy labels. Our results highlight the benefits of adapting regularization strategies to the specific characteristics of the graph data and the GNN's learning process.
This paper presents a realistic approach to generate masked faces for training and evaluating masked face recognition (MFR) systems. Recognizing the limitations of existing MFR datasets, which often rely on simplistic mask application, we propose a method to realistically synthesize masked faces by considering factors such as mask shape, texture, and placement variations. Our approach leverages [mention key techniques, e.g., image blending, GANs, or 3D modeling, if applicable]. We then introduce two novel masked face datasets, constructed using [mention how the datasets were created and what makes them unique, e.g., different mask types, diverse demographics, varying lighting conditions]. We evaluate the performance of several state-of-the-art face recognition models on these datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of our realistic mask generation approach in improving the robustness of MFR systems. The datasets and code will be made publicly available to facilitate further research in this critical area.
Developing robust and plannable representations is crucial for effective decision-making and control in complex environments. This paper proposes a novel approach, **Mutual Information Maximization for Robust Plannable Representations (MIM-RPR)**, which learns representations that are both informative about the environment and conducive to downstream planning. We achieve this by maximizing the mutual information between the learned representation and relevant aspects of the environment, while simultaneously encouraging smoothness and predictability with respect to future states. This dual objective promotes representations that capture salient environmental features and facilitate efficient planning by enabling accurate state prediction and consistent action sequencing. We demonstrate the effectiveness of MIM-RPR on challenging reinforcement learning tasks, showing that it outperforms existing methods in terms of robustness to environmental noise and planning efficiency, leading to improved overall performance. Our results highlight the benefits of directly optimizing for mutual information as a means to learn representations that are both informative and amenable to planning.
Rotation averaging is a fundamental problem in robotics, computer vision, and structure-from-motion, aiming to estimate a globally consistent set of rotations from noisy and potentially outlier-corrupted relative rotation measurements. This paper introduces NeuRoRA, a novel neural network architecture for robust rotation averaging. NeuRoRA leverages the power of deep learning to learn robust aggregation functions directly from data, effectively mitigating the impact of outliers and noise. Our approach combines a graph neural network (GNN) for message passing between rotations with a differentiable robust loss function, enabling end-to-end training. We demonstrate that NeuRoRA outperforms traditional robust rotation averaging methods on both synthetic and real-world datasets, achieving higher accuracy and robustness, particularly in the presence of significant outlier ratios. Our results highlight the potential of learned robust aggregation strategies for solving challenging geometric estimation problems.
Time series data often exhibits variable dimensionality, posing challenges for traditional time series analysis methods. This variability can arise from missing sensors, dynamic selection of relevant features, or the inherent nature of the observed system. This paper presents a novel approach for handling variable-dimensional time series data using Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). We propose a framework that represents time series data as a graph, where nodes correspond to individual time series dimensions and edges capture relationships between them, enabling the network to adapt to varying dimensionality. By leveraging GNNs, our method can effectively learn from and generalize across time series with different numbers of dimensions. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on [mention specific applications or datasets, e.g., multivariate sensor data classification, traffic flow prediction with dynamic road networks], showing improved performance compared to existing methods that either require fixed dimensionality or rely on imputation techniques. Our results highlight the potential of GNNs for analyzing and modeling complex, variable-dimensional time series data.
Cloud-based image classification services are increasingly relied upon across various domains due to their accessibility, scalability, and purported accuracy. However, their robustness to simple image transformations, a fundamental requirement for real-world deployment, is often overlooked. This paper investigates the vulnerability of popular cloud-based image classification services to basic transformations such as slight rotations, shifts, and changes in brightness. Our experiments demonstrate that these services, despite achieving high accuracy on standard benchmark datasets, can exhibit significant performance degradation when presented with images subjected to seemingly inconsequential alterations. This highlights a critical gap between reported accuracy and real-world applicability, suggesting that the "battlefield" of image classification robustness, particularly concerning simple transformations, remains largely forgotten in the rush towards achieving high accuracy on curated datasets. We conclude by discussing the implications of these findings for practical applications and proposing potential avenues for improving the robustness of cloud-based image classification services.
## Abstract: Dense xUnit Networks

This paper introduces Dense xUnit Networks, a novel architecture that enhances the performance of xUnit networks by promoting dense connectivity. Traditional xUnit networks, while offering modularity and interpretability, can suffer from limitations due to sparse connections between units. Dense xUnit Networks address this by establishing direct connections between all xUnits within a specified layer or module, enabling richer information flow and improved feature representation. We demonstrate that this dense connectivity, coupled with the inherent advantages of xUnits, leads to significant performance gains across a range of tasks. The proposed architecture retains the modular structure of xUnit networks, allowing for easier understanding and debugging, while simultaneously leveraging the benefits of dense connections often found in deep neural networks. Experimental results on [mention specific datasets/tasks, e.g., image classification, natural language processing tasks] demonstrate that Dense xUnit Networks outperform traditional xUnit networks and achieve competitive results compared to other state-of-the-art architectures, showcasing the effectiveness of our approach in improving both performance and interpretability.
This paper explores the application of Partial Optimal Transport (POT) to the problem of Positive-Unlabeled (PU) learning. PU learning deals with the challenge of training classifiers when only positive examples and unlabeled data are available. We leverage the inherent flexibility of POT to handle the noise and incompleteness inherent in unlabeled data by allowing for the transportation of only a subset of the unlabeled data distribution to the positive distribution. This approach mitigates the risk of erroneously mapping negative examples to positive ones, a common issue in traditional Optimal Transport-based PU learning methods. We propose a novel PU learning framework based on POT, offering theoretical justification for its effectiveness. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical utility of our method through extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, showcasing its superior performance compared to existing PU learning techniques, particularly in scenarios with high label noise and a large proportion of negative examples within the unlabeled set. Our results highlight the potential of POT as a robust and effective tool for addressing the challenges of PU learning.
## Abstract: Learnability for the Information Bottleneck

The Information Bottleneck (IB) principle provides a framework for learning compressed representations that are sufficient for predicting a target variable. This work investigates the learnability of IB-based representations. We analyze the conditions under which representations learned through the IB objective can be reliably generalized from a finite sample of data. We explore theoretical bounds on the sample complexity required to achieve a desired trade-off between compression and prediction accuracy, taking into account factors such as the complexity of the input and target distributions, the capacity of the representation space, and the specific IB objective function used. Our results provide insights into the statistical properties of the IB principle and offer guidance for its effective application in practical learning scenarios. We discuss the implications of our findings for designing IB-based algorithms and understanding their generalization performance.
This paper presents a scene perception system designed to aid visually impaired individuals in understanding their surroundings. The system leverages a multi-modal Deep Convolutional Neural Network (DCNN) architecture for robust object detection and classification. By integrating visual and potentially other sensory data (e.g., depth, audio), the system aims to overcome the limitations of relying solely on visual input. The proposed DCNN is trained to identify and categorize common objects in everyday environments, providing users with detailed scene information through audio feedback or other accessible output modalities. The system's performance is evaluated on a benchmark dataset, demonstrating its potential to improve spatial awareness and navigation for visually impaired users. We discuss the challenges and future directions of multi-modal scene perception for assistive technology.
High-fidelity simulations are increasingly used for design and verification in complex systems. However, identifying failure-inducing scenarios within the vast input space remains a significant challenge. This paper presents a novel approach combining Adaptive Stress Testing (AST) with the Backward Algorithm (BA) to efficiently uncover failures in high-fidelity simulations. AST guides the search towards regions of the input space likely to trigger failures, leveraging a tailored fitness function that incorporates domain knowledge and observed simulation behavior. The BA then complements this by exploring the immediate vicinity of identified failure points. Starting from a known failure state, the BA iteratively modifies input parameters in reverse simulation steps to identify the minimal set of conditions required to induce the failure. This synergistic combination allows for both efficient exploration of the input space and precise characterization of failure root causes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on a representative high-fidelity simulation, showcasing its ability to uncover failures and identify critical input parameters more effectively than traditional random testing or AST alone. The results highlight the potential of this technique to improve the robustness and reliability of complex systems designed and verified using high-fidelity simulations.
This study investigates the challenges and opportunities in Machine Translation (MT) from code-mixed Modern Standard Arabic (MSA)-Egyptian Arabic (EA) to English. Code-mixing, the interweaving of multiple languages within a single utterance, presents a significant hurdle for current MT systems often trained on monolingual or parallel data. This research explores the impact of MSA-EA code-mixing on translation accuracy, focusing on the types of code-switching patterns observed in real-world data. We analyze the effectiveness of different MT approaches, including fine-tuning pre-trained multilingual models and exploring novel techniques to handle the complexities of code-mixed input. The study aims to identify the specific linguistic features of MSA-EA code-mixing that pose the greatest difficulty for MT and to propose strategies for improving translation quality in this challenging domain. Ultimately, this research contributes to the development of more robust and accurate MT systems capable of handling the increasing prevalence of code-mixing in online communication and other real-world scenarios.
Offline reinforcement learning (RL), which learns policies from previously collected datasets without further environment interaction, offers a promising avenue for applying RL in real-world settings where online data collection is expensive or dangerous. However, progress in offline RL has been hampered by the lack of standardized benchmarks and datasets. This paper introduces RL Unplugged, a comprehensive suite of diverse and challenging offline RL benchmarks. This suite comprises datasets collected from various environments, including simulated locomotion tasks, robotics manipulation, and recommender systems, generated using a range of policy types and data collection strategies. RL Unplugged aims to provide a unified platform for evaluating and comparing offline RL algorithms, facilitating reproducible research and accelerating the development of more robust and practical offline RL solutions. We detail the structure of the benchmark, discuss the challenges posed by each dataset, and provide baseline results for several existing offline RL algorithms. This work serves as a valuable resource for the offline RL community, enabling more rigorous evaluation and ultimately driving progress towards real-world applications.
Offline Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning (DOCTR-L) offers a powerful framework for learning optimal control policies from previously collected, potentially suboptimal, trajectory data in continuous-time domains. However, challenges remain in effectively handling distributional shifts between the offline data and the target environment. This paper introduces SciPhy RL for DOCTR-L, a novel approach that integrates Neural Physics-Informed Partial Differential Equations (Neural PDEs) into the distributional actor-critic framework. By leveraging Neural PDEs, we explicitly model and constrain the learned dynamics to adhere to underlying physical laws, thereby improving generalization and robustness to distributional shifts. Our approach not only learns a policy but also simultaneously learns and validates the underlying physics governing the system, leading to more accurate value function estimation and improved policy performance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SciPhy RL for DOCTR-L on various benchmark tasks, highlighting its ability to achieve superior performance and generalization compared to existing DOCTR-L methods, especially in scenarios with significant distributional discrepancies between the offline dataset and the test environment.
This paper proposes a novel framework for Facial Action Unit (AU) Recognition that leverages multi-level adaptive Region of Interest (ROI) detection and graph learning. Recognizing the varying importance of different facial regions for specific AUs, our method adaptively identifies and extracts ROIs at multiple scales. A novel graph neural network is then employed to learn relationships between these ROIs, capturing both local and global dependencies. This graph learning component explicitly models the co-occurrence and interaction of AUs, addressing the challenges posed by subtle expressions and inter-AU correlations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on benchmark datasets, showing significant improvements in AU recognition performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Our results highlight the benefits of adaptively focusing on relevant facial regions and explicitly modeling the underlying relationships between them for accurate and robust AU recognition.
This work explores the potential of training face verification models using synthetic face identity data. We propose a novel approach that leverages generative adversarial networks (GANs) to create a large-scale dataset of diverse and realistic facial images, each labeled with a unique synthetic identity. By training a face verification model on this generated data, we aim to alleviate the reliance on real-world identity labels, which can be expensive and difficult to obtain. We investigate the performance of models trained solely on synthetic data and compare it against models trained on real-world datasets. Furthermore, we explore techniques for domain adaptation to bridge the gap between the synthetic and real face distributions, improving the generalization ability of the trained models on unseen real-world faces. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of training effective face verification models using generated face identity data, offering a promising avenue for reducing data dependency and enhancing privacy in face recognition systems.
This paper explores the use of intrinsic motivation, specifically curiosity, to drive the exploration of learned, disentangled goal spaces in reinforcement learning. We propose a novel approach where an agent learns a latent goal space with disentangled factors and uses a curiosity-driven reward signal based on prediction error within this space to guide exploration. By incentivizing the agent to visit states that lead to unpredictable changes in the disentangled goal representations, we encourage exploration of diverse and meaningful goals. We demonstrate that our approach allows the agent to discover and master a wider range of behaviors compared to traditional exploration strategies and those operating directly in the state space. Furthermore, we show that the disentangled representation facilitates more efficient learning and generalization to new tasks within the learned goal space. Our results suggest that combining curiosity with disentangled goal spaces offers a promising direction for addressing the exploration problem in complex environments and for learning reusable skills.
Vision Transformers (ViTs) have demonstrated remarkable success in computer vision, yet their global attention mechanism can be computationally expensive and may overlook crucial local details. This paper introduces RegionViT, a novel architecture that leverages a regional-to-local attention strategy to improve efficiency and capture fine-grained features. RegionViT initially divides the input image into non-overlapping regions and applies self-attention within each region, fostering regional context understanding. Subsequently, it introduces a novel attention mechanism that allows information to flow from these regional representations to individual local patches. This regional-to-local attention allows the model to efficiently leverage broader contextual information from regions while simultaneously focusing on specific local details. We demonstrate the effectiveness of RegionViT through extensive experiments on image classification tasks, showing that it achieves competitive performance compared to standard ViTs while significantly reducing computational cost. Our results suggest that RegionViT offers a promising approach for building more efficient and effective Vision Transformers.
This paper proposes a novel approach for 3D shape classification using collaborative representation based projections. We leverage the power of collaborative representation (CR) to learn discriminative features from 3D shape data by projecting the high-dimensional shape descriptors into a lower-dimensional subspace. Instead of relying on individual shape descriptors, we explore the collaborative information among multiple descriptors, allowing for a more robust and accurate representation of the 3D shape. Specifically, we project each shape descriptor onto a collaborative representation subspace constructed using training samples from different classes. The reconstruction coefficients obtained from this projection are then used as features for classification. We evaluate the proposed method on benchmark 3D shape datasets and demonstrate its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods that rely on individual shape descriptors or other dimensionality reduction techniques. The results highlight the effectiveness of collaborative representation in capturing essential shape information and improving the accuracy of 3D shape classification.
## MIA-Prognosis: A Deep Learning Framework to Predict Therapy Response

Predicting patient response to therapy is crucial for personalized medicine, enabling informed treatment decisions and improved outcomes. This paper introduces MIA-Prognosis, a novel deep learning framework designed to predict therapy response based on multi-modal patient data. MIA-Prognosis leverages a modular architecture capable of integrating diverse data types, such as genomic profiles, clinical features, and imaging data, through modality-specific encoders. These encoded representations are then fused using an attention mechanism to capture the complex interplay between different modalities and identify the most relevant features for prediction. We demonstrate the efficacy of MIA-Prognosis on [mention specific dataset, e.g., a cancer therapy dataset], showing significant improvements in prediction accuracy compared to traditional machine learning methods and single-modality deep learning approaches. Our results highlight the potential of MIA-Prognosis to assist clinicians in making data-driven decisions regarding therapy selection and ultimately improve patient care. Furthermore, we provide interpretability analysis of the model, shedding light on the key features driving the prediction of therapy response.
Accurate left atrial (LA) segmentation in 3D Gadolinium-Enhanced Magnetic Resonance Imaging (GE-MRI) is crucial for planning and guiding catheter ablation procedures for atrial fibrillation. However, the complex and variable LA anatomy presents a significant challenge. This paper investigates the application of dilated convolutions within a neural network architecture for improved LA segmentation in 3D GE-MRI. Dilated convolutions, with their ability to increase the receptive field without increasing the number of parameters, are employed to capture both local fine-grained details and global contextual information relevant for accurate segmentation. We propose a [Specify Architecture - e.g., 3D U-Net based] network incorporating dilated convolutional layers to effectively learn the LA boundaries from the complex 3D GE-MRI data. The proposed method is evaluated on [Specify Dataset] and compared against [Specify Baseline Methods]. Experimental results demonstrate that the incorporation of dilated convolutions leads to [Quantifiable Improvement - e.g., significant improvements in Dice score, Hausdorff distance] compared to traditional convolutional approaches, highlighting the effectiveness of this technique for robust and accurate LA segmentation in 3D GE-MRI.
## RUM: Network Representation Learning through Multi-Level Structural Information Preservation

Network representation learning (NRL) aims to embed nodes in a network into a low-dimensional space while preserving the network's inherent structure. Existing approaches often focus on preserving either local (e.g., neighborhood) or global (e.g., community) structures, neglecting the importance of integrating multi-level structural information. This paper proposes RUM, a novel NRL framework that leverages **R**epresentation learning thro**U**gh **M**ulti-level structural information preservation. RUM simultaneously captures and preserves structural information at multiple granularities, including node proximity, local neighborhood similarity, and global community affiliations. We achieve this by designing a novel objective function that incorporates multiple loss terms, each tailored to a specific structural level. The proposed method learns node embeddings that effectively reflect the network's complex organization. Extensive experiments on various real-world networks demonstrate that RUM consistently outperforms state-of-the-art NRL methods in tasks such as node classification, link prediction, and network visualization, highlighting the benefits of integrating multi-level structural information for effective network representation learning.
Accurate 3D vehicle detection is crucial for autonomous driving systems. While LiDAR-based methods have shown promising results, they often suffer from high false positive rates due to the sparsity and irregularity of point clouds, particularly in complex urban environments. This paper proposes MAFF-Net, a novel 3D vehicle detection network designed to effectively filter false positives through Multi-modal Adaptive Feature Fusion. MAFF-Net leverages both LiDAR point cloud and RGB image data to enrich the feature representation and improve detection accuracy. The core of our approach lies in an adaptive feature fusion module that learns to dynamically weight and combine features from both modalities based on their relevance to the current scene context. This allows the network to prioritize more reliable features and suppress noise, leading to a significant reduction in false positives. We evaluate MAFF-Net on the challenging KITTI benchmark, demonstrating its superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, particularly in reducing the number of false positive detections while maintaining high recall. Our results highlight the effectiveness of adaptive multi-modal feature fusion for robust and reliable 3D vehicle detection.
Pixel-wise regression, crucial for tasks like depth estimation and semantic segmentation, often suffers from limitations in capturing long-range dependencies and distinguishing between relevant and irrelevant features. This paper introduces Polarized Self-Attention, a novel self-attention mechanism designed to enhance the quality of pixel-wise regression. Unlike traditional self-attention, Polarized Self-Attention explicitly encourages the network to focus on both global context and local details. We achieve this by introducing a polarized attention map that separately attends to foreground (relevant) and background (irrelevant) features. This polarization allows the network to effectively suppress noise and focus on informative regions, leading to more accurate and robust pixel-wise predictions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Polarized Self-Attention on challenging pixel-wise regression tasks. Experimental results show significant improvements in performance compared to existing self-attention mechanisms and state-of-the-art methods, highlighting the potential of our approach for achieving high-quality pixel-wise regression.
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are notoriously difficult to train due to the unstable dynamics of the adversarial minimax game. The generator and discriminator often engage in oscillatory behavior, leading to mode collapse and poor sample quality. This paper introduces Lookahead-Minmax (LaMM), a novel training algorithm designed to stabilize GAN training by explicitly considering the future impact of each player's updates. LaMM employs a lookahead step where each player anticipates the opponent's best response to their proposed update, thereby enabling more conservative and stable parameter adjustments. By approximating the minmax objective with a lookahead strategy, LaMM mitigates oscillatory behavior and encourages convergence towards a stable Nash equilibrium. We demonstrate the effectiveness of LaMM on several benchmark datasets, showing improved training stability, reduced mode collapse, and enhanced sample quality compared to existing GAN training techniques. Our results highlight the potential of lookahead strategies for taming the adversarial dynamics in GANs and improving their overall performance.
This paper introduces a novel Learnable Sampling 3D Convolution (LS-Conv3D) designed for both video enhancement and action recognition tasks. Existing 3D convolutional approaches often rely on fixed sampling patterns, limiting their adaptability to complex and dynamic video content. LS-Conv3D addresses this limitation by learning dynamic offsets for sampling points within the 3D convolutional kernel. This allows the network to focus on the most relevant spatio-temporal information, leading to improved feature representation. We propose a dedicated module that predicts these offsets based on the input video features, enabling adaptive sampling based on the local context. We demonstrate the effectiveness of LS-Conv3D through extensive experiments on video enhancement and action recognition benchmarks. Our results show that LS-Conv3D significantly outperforms traditional 3D convolutional methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance, highlighting its ability to capture fine-grained spatio-temporal dependencies and adapt to diverse video characteristics.
Person re-identification (Re-ID) is a challenging task due to variations in viewpoint, pose, illumination, and background clutter. This paper presents R-FCN-3000, a novel approach to object detection that significantly improves upon the original Region-based Fully Convolutional Network (R-FCN) architecture, achieving a processing speed of 30 frames per second (fps). Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have emerged as a promising approach for generating synthetic time series data. However, evaluating the quality and utility of these generated time series remains a significant challenge. Traditional evaluation metrics often fail to capture the complex temporal dependencies and subtle statistical properties inherent in time series. This paper focuses on visual evaluation techniques for assessing the performance of GANs in generating realistic and useful time series data. We explore a range of visualization methods, including time series plots, autocorrelation functions, periodograms, and dimensionality reduction techniques, to provide a comprehensive visual assessment of the generated data. These visualizations allow for a qualitative comparison between the generated and real time series, highlighting similarities and discrepancies in their temporal dynamics, statistical distributions, and overall structure. By leveraging visual insights, we aim to complement quantitative metrics and provide a more intuitive and insightful understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of GAN-based time series generation, ultimately guiding the development of improved models and evaluation strategies.
Accurate color correction is crucial for image processing pipelines in various applications. ColorChecker charts provide a standardized reference for color calibration, but their manual detection is time-consuming. This paper proposes a fast and robust method for detecting multiple ColorChecker charts within an image using deep convolutional neural networks. Our approach leverages a two-stage architecture: first, a custom-designed convolutional neural network efficiently identifies potential ColorChecker regions. Second, a regression network refines the bounding box predictions and estimates the pose of each detected chart. By combining efficient feature extraction with robust regression, our method achieves high detection accuracy and speed even under challenging conditions such as varying illumination, partial occlusions, and complex backgrounds. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of both detection accuracy and processing time, making it suitable for real-time color calibration applications.
## WaterGAN: Unsupervised Generative Network to Enable Real-time Color Correction of Monocular Underwater Images

Underwater images often suffer from color distortion and low contrast due to light absorption and scattering. This hinders visual perception and subsequent image analysis tasks. We propose WaterGAN, an unsupervised generative adversarial network (GAN) for real-time color correction of monocular underwater images. WaterGAN leverages a novel architecture that learns a mapping from distorted underwater images to visually appealing, color-corrected counterparts without requiring paired training data. The generator network utilizes a convolutional encoder-decoder structure with skip connections to preserve high-frequency details. The discriminator network distinguishes between real, well-lit images and generated, corrected images, driving the generator to produce realistic and visually plausible outputs. We introduce a specialized loss function combining adversarial loss, perceptual loss, and color constancy loss to enforce color balance and structural similarity. Experimental results demonstrate that WaterGAN effectively restores color, enhances contrast, and reduces artifacts in underwater images, achieving superior performance compared to state-of-the-art unsupervised underwater image enhancement techniques. Furthermore, WaterGAN's efficient architecture enables real-time processing, making it suitable for applications such as underwater robotics, marine life monitoring, and underwater surveillance.
This paper presents a novel semi-supervised, data-driven method for chiller fault diagnosis that effectively leverages both labeled and unlabeled data to improve diagnostic accuracy and robustness. Traditional fault diagnosis methods often rely on extensive labeled data, which can be expensive and time-consuming to acquire in real-world chiller systems.
