Generative models of time series data have seen significant advancements, yet often struggle to capture long-range temporal dependencies crucial for realistic sequence generation. This paper introduces a novel approach leveraging temporal autoencoding to enhance the performance of existing generative models. We propose pre-training an autoencoder specifically designed to capture temporal structure through a bottleneck representation that summarizes the sequential information. This encoded representation is then used to condition the generative model, guiding its generation process to better adhere to the learned temporal dynamics. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on diverse time series datasets, showing that incorporating temporal autoencoding leads to improved sample quality, enhanced long-term consistency, and superior performance compared to state-of-the-art generative models trained independently. Our findings highlight the importance of explicitly modeling temporal structure for generating realistic and coherent time series data.
Vision Transformers (ViTs) have demonstrated remarkable performance in image classification, but their vulnerability to adversarial attacks remains a significant concern. While adversarial training can improve robustness, the adversarial examples often fail to transfer effectively across different ViT architectures or to other model families. This paper investigates methods for improving the adversarial transferability of ViTs. We explore techniques focusing on manipulating the attention mechanisms, input perturbations, and training objectives to generate more transferable adversarial examples. Specifically, we propose [mention key approach, e.g., a novel regularization technique for attention diversity or a modified input transformation strategy]. Our experiments on benchmark datasets and diverse ViT architectures demonstrate that the proposed method significantly enhances the transferability of adversarial examples while maintaining competitive attack success rates against the source model. The findings of this work contribute to a deeper understanding of the adversarial landscape of ViTs and pave the way for developing more robust and reliable vision systems.
Deep Transfer Learning (DTL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for leveraging knowledge learned from one or more source domains to improve the performance of deep learning models in target domains with limited labeled data. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the advancements in DTL, categorizing existing approaches based on their underlying principles and mechanisms. We examine techniques such as instance-based transfer, feature-based transfer, parameter-based transfer, and adversarial transfer, highlighting their strengths, weaknesses, and applicability to various tasks. Furthermore, we discuss the key challenges in DTL, including negative transfer, domain adaptation, and the selection of appropriate source domains. Finally, we explore potential future research directions in this rapidly evolving field, focusing on areas such as meta-learning for transfer, unsupervised domain adaptation, and the development of more robust and generalizable DTL frameworks. This survey aims to serve as a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners seeking to understand the landscape of DTL and its potential for solving real-world problems.
## AASeg: Attention Aware Network for Real Time Semantic Segmentation

Real-time semantic segmentation is crucial for various applications, including autonomous driving, robotics, and augmented reality. However, achieving high accuracy and speed simultaneously remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces AASeg, an Attention Aware Network designed for efficient and accurate real-time semantic segmentation. AASeg leverages a novel attention mechanism integrated within a lightweight network architecture to selectively focus on salient features, enhancing representational power without significantly increasing computational cost. Specifically, we propose an Attention Refinement Module (ARM) that adaptively refines feature maps by emphasizing important regions while suppressing irrelevant background noise. Furthermore, we incorporate a Spatial Attention Module (SAM) to capture long-range dependencies and improve spatial context understanding. We evaluate AASeg on benchmark datasets such as Cityscapes and CamVid, demonstrating its superior performance compared to existing real-time semantic segmentation models, achieving competitive accuracy with significantly improved inference speed. Our results show that AASeg provides a promising solution for real-time semantic segmentation, offering a favorable trade-off between accuracy and speed.
Dynamic Label Dictionary Learning (DLDL) addresses the challenge of learning discriminative and compact dictionaries for multi-label classification in dynamic environments where new labels and instances continuously arrive. Existing dictionary learning methods often struggle with this dynamic nature, requiring retraining from scratch or failing to effectively leverage label correlations. This paper proposes a novel DLDL framework that incorporates hypergraph regularization to capture complex, high-order relationships between labels. Specifically, the proposed method dynamically updates the label dictionary by incorporating new labels and adapting existing atoms to maintain discriminative power. The hypergraph regularization term enforces smoothness and consistency among related labels, promoting a more robust and generalizable representation. Experimental results on several benchmark multi-label datasets demonstrate that our DLDL method achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art dynamic and static dictionary learning algorithms in terms of classification accuracy, dictionary compactness, and computational efficiency. The results highlight the effectiveness of hypergraph regularization in capturing label dependencies and the adaptability of our method in evolving multi-label environments.
## Abstract: Transferring Knowledge across Learning Processes

The ability to transfer knowledge acquired in one learning context to novel, related situations is a cornerstone of intelligent behavior. This abstract explores the multifaceted nature of knowledge transfer across different learning processes, encompassing both theoretical frameworks and practical implications. We examine how knowledge representation, encoding strategies, and contextual similarity impact the effectiveness of transfer. Furthermore, we investigate diverse learning paradigms, including supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning, highlighting the challenges and opportunities for facilitating knowledge transfer between them. This abstract also considers the role of meta-learning and domain adaptation techniques in enabling robust and efficient transfer across varying task domains and learning objectives. Ultimately, understanding the mechanisms underlying knowledge transfer is crucial for developing more adaptable, efficient, and generalizable learning systems that can leverage prior experience to accelerate learning and improve performance in new environments.
This paper proposes a novel cascaded deep learning framework for video deblurring, leveraging a temporal sharpness prior to improve performance.  Traditional video deblurring methods often struggle with complex motion blur and noise. Our approach addresses this by employing a cascaded architecture where an initial network coarsely deblurs the input video, followed by subsequent networks that refine the result and enforce temporal consistency.  Crucially, we introduce a temporal sharpness prior, learned from unblurred video sequences, which guides the refinement networks to prioritize sharp regions and minimize flickering artifacts across frames. This prior is incorporated into the loss function, encouraging temporal coherence and preventing over-sharpening. We demonstrate through extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets that our cascaded approach, incorporating the temporal sharpness prior, significantly outperforms state-of-the-art video deblurring methods, producing visually superior results with reduced noise and improved temporal stability.
Autonomous driving systems require robust and reliable pedestrian detection and tracking for safe navigation in complex urban environments. This paper presents a novel pedestrian detection and tracking framework designed for autonomous cars, leveraging the complementary strengths of camera and LiDAR data. Our approach focuses on efficient fusion of these modalities to improve detection accuracy and robustness, particularly in challenging conditions such as varying lighting, occlusions, and cluttered scenes.  We propose a multi-stage architecture that first extracts pedestrian proposals from both camera images and LiDAR point clouds.  These proposals are then fused using a learned feature fusion mechanism, enhancing discrimination between pedestrians and background.  Finally, a Kalman filter-based tracker maintains pedestrian identities and provides trajectory predictions.  Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our framework achieves state-of-the-art performance in pedestrian detection and tracking, offering a significant improvement in accuracy and robustness compared to single-modality approaches, while maintaining computational efficiency suitable for real-time autonomous driving applications.
This paper proposes a novel Label Refinement Network (LRN) for semantic segmentation, designed to address the challenges of achieving fine-grained segmentation accuracy when starting from coarse initial predictions. The LRN adopts a coarse-to-fine approach, iteratively refining initially coarse semantic labels through a dedicated network architecture. This network leverages contextual information and spatial relationships to progressively enhance the label precision. Specifically, the LRN employs a multi-stage refinement process, where each stage incorporates features from the input image and the previous stage's refined labels to predict a more accurate segmentation map. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our LRN on benchmark datasets, showcasing significant improvements in segmentation accuracy compared to existing methods, particularly in refining object boundaries and recovering fine details. Our results highlight the potential of iterative label refinement as a powerful strategy for achieving high-quality semantic segmentation.
## Hcore-Init: Neural Network Initialization based on Graph Degeneracy

Neural network initialization is a critical factor influencing training convergence and final performance. This paper introduces Hcore-Init, a novel initialization scheme leveraging the concept of graph degeneracy to guide parameter setting. Hcore-Init represents the neural network architecture as a computational graph and decomposes it into its k-core structure, where the k-core represents the densest subgraph with minimum degree k. By initializing weights based on the k-core number of each neuron, Hcore-Init aims to promote efficient information propagation and mitigate the vanishing/exploding gradient problem. Neurons in higher k-cores, representing more densely connected regions, are initialized with smaller variances to prevent saturation, while neurons in lower k-cores are initialized with larger variances to encourage exploration. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Hcore-Init across various network architectures and datasets, showing improved training speed, stability, and generalization performance compared to traditional initialization methods like Xavier and He initialization. Our results suggest that leveraging graph degeneracy provides a valuable perspective for designing more effective and robust neural network initialization strategies.
## ShapeConv: Shape-aware Convolutional Layer for Indoor RGB-D Semantic Segmentation

RGB-D semantic segmentation in indoor environments benefits from both rich visual appearance and accurate 3D geometric information. While conventional convolutional neural networks (CNNs) effectively capture visual features, they often struggle to fully leverage the complex 3D shapes present in depth data. To address this limitation, we propose ShapeConv, a novel shape-aware convolutional layer designed to explicitly integrate 3D shape information into the feature extraction process. ShapeConv utilizes a local shape encoding module that captures geometric cues within the receptive field, such as surface normals and curvature, and fuses them with the convolutional features. This allows the network to learn shape-sensitive representations that are more robust to variations in viewpoint and lighting. We integrate ShapeConv into a deep CNN architecture and evaluate its performance on benchmark indoor RGB-D semantic segmentation datasets, demonstrating significant improvements over existing methods. Our results highlight the effectiveness of explicitly incorporating 3D shape information into convolutional layers for enhanced indoor scene understanding.
## Abstract: Interactive Illumination Invariance

Achieving illumination invariance in image processing and computer vision remains a significant challenge due to the complex interplay between light sources, surface properties, and camera characteristics. This paper introduces a novel approach to illumination invariance by leveraging interactive user input to guide the process. Our method moves beyond purely automated techniques by allowing users to selectively identify and correct for illumination variations, leading to more robust and accurate results. We present an interactive framework that enables users to: (1) intuitively specify regions affected by non-uniform illumination, (2) provide local constraints based on perceived surface albedo or shading variations, and (3) visualize the effects of illumination correction in real-time. The system then utilizes these user-defined constraints within an optimization framework to estimate and compensate for the underlying illumination field. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our interactive approach through a variety of experiments, showcasing its ability to improve image segmentation, object recognition, and relighting tasks, particularly in challenging scenarios where purely automated methods falter. Our results highlight the potential of combining human intuition with computational methods to achieve robust illumination invariance.
This paper explores the integration of human gaze data into attention mechanisms for improved egocentric activity recognition. Egocentric vision, captured from a first-person perspective, presents unique challenges due to camera motion, cluttered scenes, and limited field of view. We hypothesize that human gaze, reflecting the user's attentional focus, can provide valuable contextual information to guide the attention mechanism and improve the accuracy of activity recognition. We propose a novel architecture that incorporates gaze information directly into the attention weights, allowing the model to prioritize relevant features within the egocentric video stream. Our experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed gaze-aware attention mechanism significantly outperforms existing methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance in egocentric activity recognition. This work highlights the importance of leveraging human attention signals in egocentric perception and offers a promising direction for future research in this domain.
Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming drug discovery, offering the potential to accelerate the identification of novel therapeutic targets, optimize drug candidates, and reduce the overall cost and time associated with bringing new drugs to market. This review explores the diverse applications of AI across the drug discovery pipeline, encompassing target identification and validation, hit discovery, lead optimization, preclinical testing, and clinical trial design. We delve into key AI techniques including machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and natural language processing (NLP), highlighting their specific contributions to different stages of drug development. Furthermore, we discuss the challenges and opportunities associated with integrating AI into drug discovery, including data availability and quality, algorithm interpretability, and regulatory considerations. By providing an overview of current applications and techniques, this review aims to illuminate the transformative potential of AI in revolutionizing the future of drug development.
Anderson Acceleration (AA) is a powerful sequence acceleration technique that has shown promise in accelerating iterative algorithms across various fields. This work explores the application of AA to reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms, specifically focusing on accelerating the convergence of policy evaluation and policy improvement steps. We investigate the theoretical properties of AA when applied to common RL updates, analyzing its potential for improving convergence rates compared to standard iterative approaches like value iteration and policy iteration. Furthermore, we present empirical results on benchmark RL environments, demonstrating the effectiveness of AA in accelerating learning and achieving higher performance with fewer iterations. Our findings suggest that AA offers a practical and efficient method for enhancing the performance of RL algorithms, making it a valuable tool for tackling complex reinforcement learning problems.
Large-scale semi-supervised learning (SSL) presents significant challenges due to the computational complexity of processing massive datasets and the need for effective label propagation techniques. This paper introduces a novel local label propagation (LLP) approach designed to address these challenges. Unlike traditional global label propagation methods, LLP focuses on propagating labels within local neighborhoods, thereby reducing computational overhead and improving scalability. We propose a localized propagation scheme that leverages the inherent structure of the data to iteratively refine label assignments based on the similarity between neighboring instances. The effectiveness of our LLP method is demonstrated through extensive experiments on several large-scale benchmark datasets, showcasing significant improvements in classification accuracy compared to state-of-the-art SSL algorithms while maintaining comparable or superior computational efficiency. Our results highlight the potential of local label propagation for efficiently leveraging unlabeled data in large-scale learning scenarios.
Causality inference in complex systems is often hampered by the presence of feedback loops and confounding factors. Memory-less transition networks, where future states depend solely on the current state, offer a simplified framework for studying causal relationships. This work revisits the problem of causality inference in such networks, focusing on the challenges and opportunities presented by the memory-less assumption. We critically examine existing methods for identifying causal links from observational data generated by these networks, including constraint-based and score-based approaches. We then explore the potential for leveraging the memory-less property to improve the accuracy and efficiency of causal discovery, potentially through novel algorithms or by refining existing techniques. Furthermore, we investigate the limitations of causality inference in memory-less transition networks, particularly concerning the identification of genuine causal mechanisms versus spurious correlations. This work contributes to a deeper understanding of the theoretical foundations and practical limitations of causality inference in simplified dynamical systems, providing insights relevant to broader applications in fields such as robotics, control theory, and network analysis.
Semi-supervised object detection (SSOD) aims to leverage unlabeled data to improve the performance of object detectors trained with limited labeled data. This paper presents an end-to-end SSOD framework based on a "Soft Teacher" approach. The framework employs a teacher-student paradigm where a teacher model, which is an exponentially moving average of the student model, generates pseudo-labels for unlabeled data. Unlike traditional SSOD methods that rely on hard pseudo-labels, our approach utilizes soft pseudo-labels, representing the confidence distribution over object categories and bounding box locations. This allows the student model to learn from richer and more informative signals, reducing the impact of noisy pseudo-labels. Furthermore, the end-to-end training eliminates the need for separate pre-training or fine-tuning stages, simplifying the training pipeline and enabling more efficient knowledge transfer from unlabeled data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our "Soft Teacher" approach on benchmark datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance compared to existing SSOD methods, showcasing its ability to effectively utilize unlabeled data and improve object detection accuracy with limited labeled examples.
## Autobahn: Automorphism-based Graph Neural Nets

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable success in various graph-related tasks. However, many GNN architectures struggle to distinguish between non-isomorphic graphs, limiting their expressive power. This paper introduces Autobahn, a novel GNN architecture that leverages graph automorphisms to improve its expressive capabilities. Autobahn explicitly incorporates automorphism information by constructing permutation-equivariant features that are invariant to automorphism transformations. These features are then integrated into the GNN message passing scheme, allowing the network to effectively differentiate between graphs with differing automorphism structures. We demonstrate theoretically that Autobahn can distinguish between certain non-isomorphic graphs that are indistinguishable by standard GNNs. Furthermore, empirical results on various graph classification and regression benchmarks show that Autobahn consistently outperforms existing GNN architectures, particularly on datasets where distinguishing between graphs with subtle structural differences is crucial. Our results highlight the significant potential of incorporating automorphism information into GNNs for enhancing their expressive power and performance.
This paper introduces a novel framework for multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) that leverages centralized training and exploration while ensuring decentralized execution through policy distillation.  Our approach addresses the challenges of non-stationarity and exploration inherent in MARL by training a centralized critic that has access to the global state information, facilitating effective credit assignment and coordinated exploration.  During training, agents learn individual policies based on their local observations, guided by the centralized critic's insights. Crucially, we employ policy distillation to transfer the knowledge acquired by the centralized critic to these decentralized agent policies, enabling them to approximate the optimal joint action even with limited local information at execution time.  This distillation process ensures that the decentralized policies inherit the coordinated strategies learned during centralized training. We demonstrate the efficacy of our framework on several benchmark MARL environments, showing significant improvements in performance and stability compared to existing decentralized and centralized MARL algorithms.  Our results highlight the benefits of combining centralized training and exploration with decentralized execution via effective policy distillation for achieving robust and scalable multi-agent learning.
Safe exploration in Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) is crucial for deploying reinforcement learning agents in real-world scenarios where violating safety constraints can have significant consequences. This work presents a novel approach for safe exploration in finite MDPs using Gaussian Processes (GPs). We leverage GPs to model the unknown transition dynamics and reward function of the MDP, enabling us to quantify uncertainty and predict potential constraint violations. Our algorithm integrates GP predictions with a risk-aware exploration strategy that actively seeks to improve the model while ensuring the agent remains within predefined safety bounds. We propose a novel safety criterion based on the GP uncertainty and a pre-defined confidence level, allowing the agent to confidently explore while minimizing the probability of unsafe actions. Through theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in achieving safe and efficient learning in finite MDPs, outperforming existing methods in terms of constraint satisfaction and reward acquisition.
Moving vehicle license plate recognition (MVLPR) presents a significant challenge due to factors like motion blur, varying lighting conditions, and diverse plate styles. Traditional training datasets often lack sufficient representation of these challenging scenarios, limiting the performance of MVLPR systems. This paper explores the use of adversarial generation of training examples to augment existing datasets and improve the robustness of MVLPR models. We propose a novel approach that leverages generative adversarial networks (GANs) to create synthetic license plate images exhibiting realistic artifacts commonly encountered in moving vehicles, such as motion blur and perspective distortions. These adversarially generated examples are then incorporated into the training process of a license plate recognition model. We demonstrate through experimental evaluation that training with the augmented dataset leads to significant improvements in recognition accuracy, particularly in challenging scenarios with significant motion blur and varying lighting conditions. Our results highlight the effectiveness of adversarial training data generation as a valuable technique for enhancing the performance and robustness of MVLPR systems.
This paper proposes a novel framework, DCNN-GAN (Deep Convolutional Neural Network - Generative Adversarial Network), for reconstructing realistic images from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data. Current approaches often struggle to generate high-fidelity images, producing blurry or semantically inaccurate representations. Our DCNN-GAN leverages the strengths of both architectures: a DCNN is trained to decode fMRI activity into a latent image representation, which is then fed into a GAN. The GAN, composed of a generator and a discriminator, is trained adversarially to refine the image representation and generate photorealistic images that align with the original visual stimuli encoded in the fMRI data. The DCNN acts as an encoder, bridging the gap between neural activity and image features, while the GAN ensures the generated images are perceptually realistic. We evaluate the performance of DCNN-GAN on a benchmark dataset, demonstrating its superior ability to reconstruct visually compelling and semantically coherent images compared to existing methods, as evidenced by both quantitative metrics and qualitative assessments. This work represents a significant step towards accurately decoding visual experiences from brain activity, with potential applications in understanding visual processing, brain-computer interfaces, and visual prosthesis development.
Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) is a popular technique for explaining the decisions of neural networks by tracing the contribution of each input feature to the final prediction. While LRP has demonstrated its effectiveness in various applications, questions remain regarding its optimal configuration and the reliability of the resulting explanations. This paper explores critical aspects of applying LRP to achieve robust and meaningful explanations. We investigate the impact of different LRP propagation rules, network architectures, and training methodologies on the quality and interpretability of the explanations generated. Through empirical analysis, we identify best practices for implementing LRP, highlighting the importance of careful rule selection, network design considerations, and validation strategies. Our findings contribute towards a more principled and reliable application of LRP, paving the way for increased trust and adoption of neural network models in critical domains.
Foreground object detection, the task of identifying salient objects in an image or video, is traditionally approached using supervised learning methods requiring extensive labeled data. This paper presents a novel unsupervised learning framework for foreground object detection, eliminating the need for manual annotation. Our approach leverages inherent image characteristics and statistical properties to learn a robust representation of foreground objects. We explore techniques that exploit image priors such as color contrast, motion cues, and background complexity to automatically generate pseudo-labels for training. The learned model can then effectively segment foreground objects from unseen images without requiring any prior knowledge of specific object classes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our unsupervised approach through comprehensive experiments on benchmark datasets, showcasing its ability to achieve competitive performance compared to weakly supervised methods and highlighting its potential for applications where labeled data is scarce or unavailable. This work opens new avenues for developing more adaptable and scalable foreground object detection systems.
Tensor completion aims to recover missing entries in a multi-dimensional array (tensor) given a subset of observed values.  PARAFAC decomposition is a powerful tool for tensor analysis and has been successfully applied to tensor completion. However, standard PARAFAC methods can be sensitive to noise and may produce non-smooth factor matrices, leading to suboptimal completion performance. This paper introduces a novel approach, **Smooth PARAFAC Decomposition for Tensor Completion (Smooth PARAFAC-TC)**, which incorporates smoothness constraints on the factor matrices during the PARAFAC decomposition process.  By promoting smoothness, we aim to obtain more robust and interpretable factor matrices, leading to improved completion accuracy, especially in noisy environments. We achieve this by adding regularization terms to the PARAFAC objective function that penalize deviations from smoothness based on finite difference approximations.  Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world tensor datasets demonstrate that Smooth PARAFAC-TC outperforms state-of-the-art tensor completion methods, achieving superior accuracy and robustness while maintaining reasonable computational efficiency.  Our approach provides a promising solution for tensor completion tasks where smoothness of the underlying data structure is expected.
Generating high-resolution images with intricate details remains a computational challenge for Transformers due to their quadratic complexity with respect to input size. This paper introduces Grid Partitioned Attention (GPA), an efficient Transformer approximation designed to address this issue. GPA incorporates an inductive bias by partitioning the input image into non-overlapping grids and restricting attention within each grid. This significantly reduces computational cost while simultaneously allowing for the capture of local dependencies crucial for generating fine-grained details. We demonstrate that GPA effectively approximates global attention while maintaining computational efficiency, enabling the generation of high-resolution images with improved fidelity and detail compared to standard Transformers and other attention approximation methods. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of GPA in tasks such as image generation and super-resolution, showcasing its potential for efficient and high-quality detail generation in high-resolution settings.
This paper introduces Sparse-MLP, a novel neural network architecture that leverages the inherent strengths of multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) while incorporating conditional computation for improved efficiency and performance.  Unlike traditional MLPs with dense connections, Sparse-MLP employs a sparse connectivity pattern, dynamically activated based on the input. A routing mechanism learns to selectively activate relevant neurons within the MLP, effectively creating a conditional computation path tailored to each input sample. This approach allows the model to focus computational resources on the most important features, reducing redundancy and enabling scalability to larger models. We demonstrate that Sparse-MLP achieves competitive performance on benchmark datasets while significantly reducing computational cost compared to dense MLPs and other established architectures. Our results highlight the potential of sparse conditional computation within fully-MLP architectures for efficient and scalable machine learning.
## EVOQUER: Enhancing Temporal Grounding with Video-Pivoted BackQuery Generation

Temporal grounding aims to locate the temporal extent of a target event described by a natural language query within a video. While existing methods primarily focus on matching the query with video content, we propose EVOQUER, a novel approach that enhances temporal grounding by leveraging video-pivoted backquery generation. EVOQUER generates counterfactual queries based on the video content, aiming to describe what is *not* happening in the video segments that are considered negative examples. By training the model to distinguish between the original query and these generated backqueries, we effectively sharpen the boundaries of relevant segments and improve the discriminative power of the model. Our experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that EVOQUER consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, highlighting the effectiveness of video-pivoted backquery generation in enhancing temporal grounding performance. Furthermore, we provide ablation studies to analyze the impact of different components within our proposed framework.
## Abstract: Feature Importance Ranking for Deep Learning

Deep learning models, while achieving state-of-the-art performance across various domains, often operate as "black boxes," making it challenging to understand which input features are most influential in driving their predictions. This lack of interpretability hinders trust, debugging, and domain-specific knowledge discovery. This work explores and compares various techniques for ranking feature importance in deep learning models. We investigate methods ranging from gradient-based approaches and perturbation-based techniques to model-agnostic methods like SHAP and LIME. We analyze their strengths and weaknesses, considering factors such as computational cost, sensitivity to hyperparameters, and ability to capture complex feature interactions. Through empirical evaluation on benchmark datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods in identifying salient features and providing insights into the decision-making processes of deep learning models. Our findings highlight the importance of selecting appropriate feature importance techniques based on the specific characteristics of the model and the application domain, ultimately contributing to more transparent and reliable deep learning systems.
Generating realistic and coherent images from text descriptions remains a challenging task. While recent advances have shown promise, current methods often struggle to accurately represent complex relationships between objects in a scene. This paper proposes a novel approach to image generation that leverages scene graph context to improve visual fidelity and semantic consistency. We argue that explicitly modeling the relationships between objects, as represented in a scene graph, allows for more informed and structured image synthesis. Our method incorporates scene graph information to guide the generative process, enabling the model to better understand and reproduce the intricate dependencies within the described scene. We demonstrate through quantitative and qualitative evaluations that our approach generates images with improved object arrangements, relationship accuracy, and overall visual quality compared to existing text-to-image generation techniques. This highlights the significant potential of scene graph context in enhancing the realism and coherence of generated images.
This paper presents a novel self-supervised multi-view learning framework that leverages auto-encoding 3D transformations to learn robust and informative representations. Our approach aims to learn feature embeddings from multiple views of an object or scene without relying on manual annotations. We achieve this by training an autoencoder that predicts the 3D transformation (rotation and translation) required to align different views of the same object. This process forces the encoder to learn view-invariant features that capture the underlying 3D structure. By minimizing the reconstruction error of the 3D transformation, we implicitly learn consistent feature representations across different viewpoints. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several benchmark datasets, showing that our self-supervised learned representations outperform state-of-the-art self-supervised methods on downstream tasks such as object classification and 3D shape retrieval. Our results highlight the power of leveraging 3D geometric constraints for self-supervised learning from multi-view data.
This paper proposes a novel semi-supervised dimensionality reduction method for hyperspectral imagery called Joint and Progressive Subspace Analysis (JPSA) with Spatial-Spectral Manifold Alignment. JPSA aims to effectively leverage both labeled and unlabeled data while preserving the underlying manifold structure of the data. The method first constructs a spatial-spectral neighborhood graph to capture the local manifold structure within the hyperspectral data cube. Then, a joint subspace learning framework is introduced that simultaneously learns a global subspace from all data and a class-specific subspace from labeled data. This allows for effective exploitation of labeled information while maintaining the overall data structure. Furthermore, a progressive learning strategy is adopted to iteratively refine the subspace by incorporating more unlabeled data based on their manifold alignment with the learned subspaces. This iterative refinement enhances the robustness and accuracy of the dimensionality reduction, particularly in scenarios with limited labeled data. Experimental results on benchmark hyperspectral datasets demonstrate that the proposed JPSA method achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art dimensionality reduction techniques in terms of classification accuracy and visual interpretation.
This paper proposes a novel framework for interactive reinforcement learning (RL) that combines learning from demonstration (LfD) with human evaluative feedback, leveraging generative adversarial networks (GANs).  Our GAN-based approach addresses the limitations of traditional LfD methods by generating diverse and realistic demonstrations, allowing the RL agent to efficiently explore the state space and learn a robust policy.  Furthermore, we incorporate human evaluative feedback on the agent's behavior, guiding the learning process towards desirable outcomes and correcting potential biases introduced by the demonstrations. The GAN acts as a demonstration generator, providing a rich source of data for imitation learning, while the human evaluator provides scalar rewards or preferences that are integrated into the RL objective.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments in simulated environments, showing that it outperforms existing LfD and human-in-the-loop RL algorithms in terms of learning speed, policy quality, and robustness to noisy or incomplete demonstrations.  Our results highlight the potential of GANs to facilitate interactive RL by generating high-quality training data and enabling efficient incorporation of human expertise.
Vector fields, representing direction and magnitude at every point in space, are fundamental in various scientific and engineering disciplines. Effective data modelling of vector fields is crucial for tasks such as visualization, analysis, simulation, and prediction. This short review provides an overview of common data modelling techniques for vector fields, encompassing both discrete and continuous representations. We examine methods for storing and manipulating vector field data, including structured grids, unstructured meshes, and particle-based approaches. Furthermore, we discuss interpolation techniques like linear, higher-order polynomial, and radial basis function methods used to estimate vector values at arbitrary locations. Finally, we briefly touch upon advanced modelling approaches such as vector field decomposition and feature extraction, highlighting their potential for extracting meaningful insights from complex vector field data. This review aims to provide a concise introduction to the key concepts and techniques in vector field data modelling, serving as a starting point for researchers and practitioners working with this important type of data.
This paper introduces a novel salient object detection method, termed "Inner and Inter Label Propagation," designed for robust performance in complex, uncontrolled "in the wild" scenarios. Recognizing the limitations of existing label propagation approaches that often focus solely on pixel-level relationships, our method leverages both **inner label propagation** within salient regions and **inter label propagation** between salient and non-salient regions. Inner label propagation reinforces the consistency and completeness of detected salient objects by propagating labels within confidently identified salient areas, effectively filling gaps and refining boundaries. Simultaneously, inter label propagation leverages the contrast and contextual information between salient and non-salient regions to suppress false positives and enhance the precision of salient object boundaries. We achieve this by constructing a graph-based representation that explicitly models both intra- and inter-region relationships, and then employ an iterative propagation scheme to refine the saliency map. Extensive experimental results on challenging benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, particularly in handling complex backgrounds, cluttered scenes, and low-contrast objects, highlighting the effectiveness of integrating both inner and inter label propagation for robust salient object detection in the wild.
Detecting objects in urban scenes is crucial for various applications, including autonomous driving and robotics. However, heavy occlusion, where objects are significantly obscured by other objects, poses a significant challenge. This paper introduces a novel approach, "Learning to Separate," that specifically addresses the problem of detecting heavily-occluded objects in urban environments.  Our method focuses on learning to disentangle overlapping object features, effectively "separating" the occluded object from its surroundings. Experimental results on benchmark urban scene datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing object detection methods in handling heavy occlusion, leading to improved recall and precision, particularly for occluded objects. We further analyze the effectiveness of our method through ablation studies, highlighting the contribution of each component in achieving robust object detection under challenging occlusion conditions.
Estimating the 3D pose of multiple people from monocular videos is a challenging task due to ambiguity in depth perception and occlusions. This paper proposes a novel approach leveraging Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) and Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) to address these challenges. First, we employ a 2D pose detector to obtain initial 2D pose estimates for each person in each frame. Then, a GCN is used to model the spatial relationships between body joints within each frame, refining the 2D poses and implicitly learning the 3D structure. Subsequently, a TCN is applied to capture temporal dependencies across frames, smoothing the pose trajectories and disambiguating depth information. By integrating GCNs for spatial reasoning and TCNs for temporal modeling, our method effectively leverages both spatial and temporal context to improve the accuracy and robustness of 3D multi-person pose estimation from monocular videos. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on benchmark datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance and showcasing its ability to handle occlusions and complex interactions.
Semantic segmentation, the task of assigning a semantic label to each pixel in an image, has become a cornerstone of computer vision applications ranging from autonomous driving to medical image analysis. While significant progress has been made in improving the accuracy of semantic segmentation models, understanding *why* these models fail remains a critical challenge. This abstract focuses on the importance of diagnostics in semantic segmentation. We argue that simply evaluating overall performance metrics like Intersection over Union (IoU) is insufficient for identifying and addressing the nuanced weaknesses of segmentation models. This abstract highlights the need for diagnostic techniques that can pinpoint specific failure modes, such as confusion between classes, sensitivity to image artifacts, or poor generalization to unseen data. We explore various diagnostic approaches, including visualization techniques, error analysis frameworks, and attribution methods, that offer insights into model behavior and inform targeted improvements. By emphasizing the role of diagnostics, we aim to promote the development of more robust, reliable, and interpretable semantic segmentation models for real-world applications.
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable success in graph classification tasks, often attributed to their sophisticated architectures and ability to learn complex node and edge representations. However, the question remains: are these powerful GNNs always necessary? This work presents a critical dissection of the role of GNN architecture in graph classification. We systematically investigate the performance of various GNN models, ranging from simple message-passing networks to more advanced architectures with attention mechanisms and higher-order connectivity, across a diverse set of benchmark datasets. Our analysis reveals that the effectiveness of a GNN is often highly dependent on the characteristics of the graph dataset, with simpler models sometimes outperforming complex ones. Furthermore, we explore the impact of crucial factors such as node feature initialization, graph pre-processing techniques, and the inherent structural properties of the graphs themselves. Through this comprehensive evaluation, we aim to provide insights into the conditions under which powerful GNNs are truly essential and identify scenarios where simpler, more efficient approaches can achieve comparable or even superior performance in graph classification. This understanding can guide the selection of appropriate GNN models and contribute to the development of more efficient and interpretable graph learning techniques.
Automated part assembly is a challenging task requiring reasoning about complex relationships between parts and their evolving configurations. This paper introduces RGL-NET, a novel Recurrent Graph Learning framework designed for progressive part assembly. RGL-NET leverages a graph neural network to represent the assembly state, where nodes represent parts and edges represent their spatial relationships. A recurrent architecture allows the network to iteratively refine the assembly by predicting which part to add next and where to place it, based on the current assembly configuration. Crucially, the graph learning component dynamically updates edge weights to capture the evolving importance of part relationships during the assembly process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of RGL-NET on a variety of assembly tasks, showing its ability to generate valid and efficient assembly sequences compared to existing methods. Our results highlight the benefits of recurrent processing and dynamic graph learning for tackling the complexities of progressive part assembly.
This paper presents an empirical study of graph-based approaches for semi-supervised time series classification (TSC).  While labeled time series data is often scarce and expensive to obtain, unlabeled data is usually more readily available.  Semi-supervised learning leverages both labeled and unlabeled data to improve model performance.  We investigate the effectiveness of several graph-based techniques, including label propagation and graph convolutional networks, within the context of TSC. These methods represent time series data as nodes in a graph, with edges capturing similarity relationships between them.  We explore different graph construction strategies and node feature engineering techniques to optimize performance.  Our experiments, conducted on a diverse set of benchmark time series datasets, demonstrate the potential of graph-based approaches to enhance classification accuracy when labeled data is limited. We also analyze the impact of graph structure and feature representation on the performance of these methods, providing insights into their strengths and limitations for semi-supervised TSC. The results highlight the promise of graph-based techniques for addressing the challenges of limited labeled data in time series analysis.
Concrete petrographic analysis, a crucial tool for assessing concrete durability and performance, is traditionally a time-consuming and labor-intensive process involving manual image segmentation of microstructural features. This paper presents a novel deep learning-based approach for automated image segmentation of concrete petrographic images. We leverage convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to accurately delineate key features such as air voids, cement paste, aggregates, and microcracks, significantly reducing the reliance on manual interpretation. The proposed model is trained and validated on a comprehensive dataset of annotated concrete thin-section images acquired under polarized light microscopy. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by comparing its segmentation performance against manual segmentation by experienced petrographers, achieving high accuracy and efficiency in identifying and quantifying critical microstructural components. The automated segmentation capabilities enabled by this deep learning approach offer the potential to revolutionize concrete petrography, facilitating faster, more objective, and cost-effective analysis for improved concrete quality control and durability assessment.
Image captioning, the task of generating natural language descriptions for images, has seen significant progress with the advent of deep learning. However, many existing models still struggle with capturing fine-grained details and generating captions that are both accurate and contextually relevant. This paper introduces the Reflective Decoding Network (RDN), a novel architecture that enhances the decoding process by incorporating a reflective mechanism. RDN leverages a feedback loop that allows the decoder to iteratively refine its understanding of the image and its generated caption. Specifically, the model uses the generated caption to re-attend to the image, extracting more relevant visual features for subsequent decoding steps. This reflective process enables the decoder to identify and correct errors, leading to more accurate and informative captions. We evaluate RDN on benchmark datasets such as COCO and demonstrate its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. The experimental results highlight the effectiveness of the reflective mechanism in improving caption quality and generating more descriptive and contextually aware image captions.
Histopathology image analysis is crucial for cancer diagnosis and prognosis, but automated methods face challenges due to significant appearance variability arising from factors like staining protocols, scanner variations, and tissue preparation. This heterogeneity can severely degrade the performance of models trained on data from a single domain when applied to data from a different domain. To mitigate this issue, we propose a domain-adversarial neural network (DANN) approach for histopathology image analysis. The DANN architecture aims to learn domain-invariant features by simultaneously optimizing for a classification task and minimizing the ability of a domain discriminator to distinguish between different image domains. This encourages the feature extractor to learn representations that are informative for the diagnostic task while being robust to domain-specific variations. We evaluate the effectiveness of our approach on [mention specific datasets or tasks, e.g., a multi-center dataset of breast cancer histopathology images for tumor detection]. Results demonstrate that the DANN significantly improves the generalization performance of the classifier across different domains compared to models trained without domain adaptation, suggesting its potential for developing more robust and reliable automated histopathology image analysis systems.
Brain aging is a complex process characterized by structural and functional changes that can lead to cognitive decline. This study introduces a novel approach for modeling and analyzing brain aging using normalizing flows. Our method leverages the powerful density estimation capabilities of normalizing flows to learn a bidirectional mapping between chronological age and brain imaging data. This allows us to not only predict chronological age from brain scans, providing a "brain age" estimate, but also to generate synthetic brain images conditioned on specific ages, enabling the exploration of age-related brain changes. Furthermore, the learned latent space provides a valuable representation for identifying key biomarkers and trajectories associated with healthy and accelerated aging. We evaluate the performance of our model on a large neuroimaging dataset, demonstrating its ability to accurately predict age and generate realistic brain images. The results highlight the potential of normalizing flows for understanding the complex relationship between brain structure and aging, and for identifying individuals at risk of age-related cognitive decline.
## Explaining Knowledge Distillation by Quantifying the Knowledge

Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used technique for transferring knowledge from a large, complex "teacher" model to a smaller, more efficient "student" model. While KD's effectiveness is well-established, a comprehensive understanding of *what* knowledge is being transferred and *how* it contributes to the student's performance remains elusive. This work proposes a novel framework for explaining KD by explicitly quantifying the knowledge transferred. We define knowledge as the information gain about the data distribution achieved by observing the teacher's output, and introduce metrics to measure this knowledge in terms of both **generalization ability** and **feature representation quality**. By quantifying these aspects of knowledge before, during, and after distillation, we can identify the specific benefits imparted by the teacher. We demonstrate the applicability of our framework through experiments on image classification datasets, revealing that KD not only improves the student's classification accuracy but also enhances its feature representations, leading to better generalization. Furthermore, we show how our knowledge quantification framework can be used to optimize KD parameters, such as the temperature parameter, for maximizing the transfer of specific types of knowledge. Our findings provide a deeper understanding of the mechanisms underlying KD and offer valuable insights for designing more effective knowledge transfer strategies.
## GNN-FiLM: Graph Neural Networks with Feature-wise Linear Modulation

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as powerful tools for representation learning on graph-structured data. However, effectively incorporating node and edge features into message passing remains a challenge. This paper introduces GNN-FiLM, a novel GNN architecture that leverages Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) to dynamically modulate node features during message aggregation. GNN-FiLM allows for adaptive feature scaling and shifting based on incoming messages, enabling a more nuanced and expressive integration of information from neighboring nodes and edges. We demonstrate the effectiveness of GNN-FiLM on a variety of graph-based tasks, including node classification, graph classification, and link prediction. Experimental results show that GNN-FiLM consistently outperforms existing GNN architectures, particularly in scenarios with complex feature interactions and heterogeneous graph structures. This highlights the potential of FiLM as a powerful mechanism for enhancing the representational capacity of GNNs.
Visual Relation Detection (VRD) aims to identify semantic relationships between objects in an image. Existing methods often struggle with effectively capturing and reasoning about the complex interplay between object features and their spatial configurations. This paper introduces a Visual Translation Embedding Network (VTEN) designed to explicitly model the translational relationships between objects to improve VRD performance. VTEN utilizes a novel translation embedding module that learns to represent the spatial displacement between object pairs as a learned translation vector. This vector is then integrated with object features and contextual information to predict the relationship. By explicitly encoding the spatial translation, VTEN enhances the network's ability to understand the relative positions and orientations of objects, leading to a more accurate and robust representation of visual relations. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that VTEN achieves significant performance gains compared to state-of-the-art methods, highlighting the effectiveness of the proposed translation embedding approach for visual relation detection.
This paper introduces MiniVLM, a novel vision-language model designed for resource-constrained environments. While large-scale vision-language models have demonstrated impressive performance on a variety of tasks, their computational demands often limit their deployment on edge devices and in real-time applications. MiniVLM addresses this limitation by employing a combination of model compression techniques and architectural optimizations to achieve a significant reduction in model size and inference latency without sacrificing performance. We present a detailed description of the model architecture, training methodology, and experimental results. Our evaluations on benchmark datasets demonstrate that MiniVLM achieves comparable or superior performance to existing smaller vision-language models, while exhibiting substantially faster inference speeds and lower memory footprint. This makes MiniVLM a practical and efficient solution for a wide range of applications where computational resources are limited.
This paper presents a novel unsupervised learning framework that combines disentangled representation learning with nonlinear dynamics modeling. Our model, designed for unsupervised learning, aims to simultaneously discover meaningful, independent factors of variation in data and learn the underlying dynamics governing their evolution. We achieve this by utilizing a disentangled recognition network to map raw observations into a latent space where each dimension represents a distinct generative factor. This latent representation is then fed into a nonlinear dynamics model, such as a recurrent neural network, to predict future states based on the learned dynamics. By imposing disentanglement constraints during training, we encourage the dynamics model to operate on interpretable, independent factors, leading to improved prediction accuracy and a more structured understanding of the data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on both synthetic and real-world datasets, showing its ability to learn disentangled representations, accurately model complex dynamics, and generate realistic future states in an unsupervised manner. The results highlight the potential of our model for tasks such as anomaly detection, state prediction, and causal inference in various domains.
Modern motion sensors, such as accelerometers and gyroscopes embedded in smartphones and wearables, generate high-resolution time-series data that capture intricate details of human movement and activity. This abundance of data presents a significant opportunity for advanced motion and time analysis, enabling applications ranging from healthcare monitoring and sports performance optimization to security and human-computer interaction. This paper explores the application of data science techniques to extract meaningful insights from motion sensor data. We discuss key data science methodologies including signal processing for noise reduction and feature extraction, machine learning algorithms for activity recognition and anomaly detection, and time series analysis for identifying temporal patterns and trends. We highlight the challenges associated with processing large volumes of noisy, heterogeneous motion sensor data and discuss strategies for addressing these challenges. Furthermore, we showcase the potential of data science to unlock valuable information about human behavior and movement patterns, ultimately contributing to the development of intelligent and personalized applications in various domains.
This paper explores a novel approach to accelerating neural network inference by directly leveraging the JPEG compression format. Instead of decoding JPEG images to raw pixel data, our method extracts and utilizes the Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) coefficients inherent in the JPEG structure to directly feed a tailored neural network. This "JPEG-to-Network" paradigm bypasses the computationally expensive decoding step, significantly reducing processing time and memory bandwidth requirements. We propose a specialized neural network architecture designed to operate efficiently on DCT coefficients, demonstrating that surprisingly accurate and fast inference can be achieved with substantially less computational overhead. Our experiments show that this "less is more" approach, by processing the compressed JPEG data directly, can achieve comparable accuracy to networks trained on raw pixels while offering significant speedups, paving the way for efficient deployment of deep learning models on resource-constrained devices and in latency-sensitive applications.
This paper proposes a novel one-stage inpainting network leveraging bilateral attention and a pyramid filling block to address the challenges of generating coherent and visually plausible content for missing regions in images. Existing one-stage methods often struggle with capturing long-range dependencies and generating fine-grained details. To mitigate these issues, we introduce a bilateral attention mechanism that effectively aggregates contextual information from both spatial and channel dimensions, allowing the network to better understand the global structure and semantic relationships. Furthermore, we present a pyramid filling block that progressively fills the missing regions at multiple scales, enabling the generation of high-resolution and detailed textures. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance, significantly improving image quality and perceptual realism compared to existing one-stage inpainting methods. The proposed network generates visually compelling inpainting results with improved structural consistency and finer details, showcasing the effectiveness of the bilateral attention and pyramid filling strategy.
Video smoke detection is crucial for early fire warning systems, yet its performance suffers significantly due to domain shift between training data and real-world scenarios. While deep learning models excel with large datasets, acquiring sufficient labeled real-world smoke videos is challenging. This paper explores domain adaptation techniques to bridge the gap between synthetically generated smoke datasets and real-world video data. We propose a novel domain adaptation approach that focuses on adapting a single smoke detection model trained solely on synthetic data to perform effectively on real-world smoke videos. Domain shift, the discrepancy between training and testing data distributions, significantly degrades the performance of deep learning models, particularly in medical image analysis. This study investigates the anatomy of domain shift impact on U-Net, a widely used architecture for medical image segmentation, specifically focusing on Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI). We analyze the performance degradation across individual layers of the U-Net architecture when applied to out-of-distribution MRI data. By examining layer-wise feature representations, activation distributions, and gradient magnitudes, we identify specific layers most susceptible to domain shift. Our findings reveal that domain shift disproportionately affects the shallow encoder layers, impacting feature extraction and generalization ability. Furthermore, we observe altered feature representations and increased instability in gradient flow within these affected layers. These insights provide a deeper understanding of how domain shift propagates through the U-Net architecture, paving the way for targeted domain adaptation strategies and robust model development for MRI segmentation across diverse clinical settings.
This paper addresses the challenge of multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) in environments with hybrid action spaces, where agents must simultaneously choose discrete and continuous actions. Such hybrid action spaces are common in real-world scenarios but pose significant difficulties for existing MARL algorithms. We propose a novel deep MARL framework that effectively handles discrete-continuous hybrid action spaces by employing separate neural networks for discrete and continuous action selection, leveraging the strengths of both policy gradient and value-based methods. Specifically, we utilize a policy gradient method for discrete action selection and a deep Q-network (DQN) variant for continuous action selection, ensuring compatibility and stability within the multi-agent setting. We also introduce a novel coordination mechanism to enable effective collaboration among agents with hybrid action capabilities. We evaluate our approach on a suite of challenging benchmark environments with hybrid action spaces, demonstrating significant performance improvements compared to existing MARL algorithms and ablation studies. Our results highlight the effectiveness of our framework in learning complex multi-agent policies in environments with discrete-continuous hybrid action spaces.
Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) have proven effective in learning latent representations of data, but often struggle to capture underlying group symmetries present in the data generating process. Capsule networks offer a promising alternative for encoding geometric relationships and equivariance, but lack the probabilistic framework of VAEs. This work introduces **Topographic VAEs learn Equivariant Capsules**, a novel architecture that integrates the strengths of both approaches. By leveraging a topographic latent space in the VAE framework, we encourage the emergence of organized and interpretable representations. Simultaneously, we incorporate capsule networks in the decoder, forcing the latent space to encode parameters that control the capsules. This design enables the model to learn **equivariant capsules**, where transformations in the input space are reflected in corresponding transformations within the capsule parameters in the latent space. We demonstrate that our model learns structured latent spaces that capture meaningful variations in the data, while also exhibiting strong equivariance properties compared to standard VAEs and other related methods. Our experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that Topographic VAEs learn Equivariant Capsules achieves superior performance in reconstruction, disentanglement, and downstream tasks requiring sensitivity to geometric transformations.
This paper presents a novel approach to learning deep analysis dictionaries, specifically focusing on the convolutional variant. Building upon the foundation of deep analysis dictionaries, we introduce a framework for learning convolutional filters organized in a hierarchical manner. This "Convolutional Deep Analysis Dictionary" (CDAD) leverages convolutional operations to efficiently capture spatial dependencies and extract meaningful features from input data. We propose an optimization algorithm that jointly learns the convolutional filters and the associated non-linear activation functions at each layer of the CDAD. This joint learning process allows for the discovery of task-specific features and improves the overall representation power of the dictionary. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed CDAD on several benchmark datasets, showcasing its superior performance in tasks such as image denoising and classification compared to traditional shallow dictionaries and other deep learning architectures. The results highlight the benefits of learning convolutional filters within a deep analysis dictionary framework for achieving robust and efficient data representation.
## DNN2LR: Interpretation-inspired Feature Crossing for Real-world Tabular Data

Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have demonstrated impressive performance on tabular data, but often suffer from a lack of interpretability. Conversely, Logistic Regression (LR) offers high interpretability but struggles to capture complex non-linear relationships. This paper introduces DNN2LR, a novel approach that bridges this gap by leveraging the interpretability of LR to guide feature crossing within a DNN framework. DNN2LR first trains a DNN on the tabular data and then extracts important feature interactions based on the learned DNN weights. These interactions are then encoded as explicit feature crosses, which are combined with the original features as input to a simplified DNN architecture. This process effectively transfers knowledge from the complex DNN to a more interpretable model while retaining the DNN's ability to capture non-linear relationships. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DNN2LR on several real-world tabular datasets, showing that it achieves competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art DNN models while significantly improving interpretability by highlighting crucial feature interactions. The proposed method provides a practical solution for scenarios where both accuracy and interpretability are paramount.
This paper proposes a novel approach for segmenting camera-trap images using multi-layer robust principal component analysis (ML-RPCA). Camera-trap images, crucial for wildlife monitoring, often suffer from noise and clutter, including variations in illumination, vegetation, and background. These factors hinder accurate object detection and species identification. Traditional segmentation methods struggle to effectively handle these complexities. Our proposed ML-RPCA framework decomposes the image data into multiple layers, allowing for the separation of foreground objects (animals) from background clutter and noise in a robust manner. Each layer leverages RPCA to identify and isolate low-rank (background) and sparse (foreground) components. By iteratively applying RPCA across multiple layers, we effectively refine the segmentation, isolating the animal of interest while mitigating the impact of challenging environmental conditions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on a diverse set of camera-trap images, showing improved segmentation accuracy compared to existing techniques. The results highlight the potential of ML-RPCA for automating the analysis of camera-trap data, ultimately contributing to more efficient and reliable wildlife monitoring.
This paper explores unsupervised speech representation learning using WaveNet autoencoders. We propose a novel approach that leverages the powerful generative capabilities of WaveNet to learn meaningful representations directly from raw audio waveforms without relying on labeled data. The autoencoder architecture consists of a WaveNet encoder that maps the input speech signal to a lower-dimensional latent space, and a corresponding WaveNet decoder that reconstructs the original signal from this latent representation. By training the autoencoder to minimize reconstruction error, the encoder learns to capture salient acoustic features and temporal dependencies present in speech. We evaluate the learned representations on downstream tasks such as phoneme classification and speaker identification, demonstrating their effectiveness in capturing relevant speech information. Results indicate that our WaveNet autoencoder-based approach achieves competitive performance compared to existing unsupervised speech representation learning methods, highlighting the potential of WaveNet architectures for learning robust and informative representations directly from raw speech.
Oriented object detection, which aims to precisely locate objects with arbitrary orientations, has recently gained increasing attention. However, deep features extracted from convolutional neural networks (CNNs) often lack orientation awareness and exhibit misalignment with oriented bounding boxes, leading to performance degradation. This paper proposes a novel approach to **align deep features for oriented object detection**.
