Our results highlight the importance of feature alignment for accurate oriented object detection and validate the effectiveness of our proposed solution.
This paper explores the application of Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (Neural ODEs) to control the dynamics of systems evolving on graphs. We propose a novel framework that leverages the continuous-time nature of Neural ODEs to learn and control complex, non-linear dynamics defined on graph structures. The model learns a continuous-time representation of the graph's state, allowing for precise control through learned control inputs injected at specific nodes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several challenging tasks, including stabilization of unstable graph systems and targeted state transfer, showing superior performance compared to discrete-time control methods and traditional graph neural networks. The continuous-time formulation offers advantages in terms of robustness to sampling frequency and adaptability to varying graph topologies, paving the way for more efficient and flexible control of complex systems represented as graphs.
This paper introduces an Explainable Ordinal Factorization Model (EOFM) that leverages piece-wise linear approximation to decipher the effects of attributes on ordinal data. Traditional matrix factorization methods often struggle to provide clear, interpretable explanations for their predictions, particularly when dealing with ordinal ratings. EOFM addresses this limitation by representing the latent factors associated with users and items as linear combinations of attribute-specific basis functions. These piece-wise linear functions allow us to model non-linear relationships between attributes and latent factors, while simultaneously providing a readily understandable representation of the influence of each attribute on the final ordinal prediction. We demonstrate the effectiveness of EOFM on real-world ordinal datasets, showcasing its ability to achieve comparable or superior predictive performance compared to existing methods, while offering significantly improved interpretability. The resulting models provide insights into how specific attributes influence user preferences and item characteristics, facilitating a deeper understanding of the underlying factors driving ordinal ratings.
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have traditionally relied on convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for their generator and discriminator architectures. However, the inductive bias of CNNs can limit the expressiveness and scalability of GANs. In this paper, we introduce TransGAN, a novel GAN architecture where both the generator and discriminator are built purely from Transformers. By leveraging the global receptive field and attention mechanisms inherent in Transformers, TransGAN overcomes the limitations of local convolutions, leading to improved image generation quality and training stability. We demonstrate that this seemingly simple replacement of CNNs with Transformers yields surprisingly strong GAN performance. Furthermore, we show that TransGAN's inherent scalability allows it to effectively leverage larger datasets and higher resolution image generation, pushing the boundaries of GAN capabilities. Our results demonstrate that two pure Transformers can indeed make one strong GAN, and that this approach offers a promising avenue for scaling up GANs for future advancements in generative modeling.
Accurate neuron segmentation in electron microscopy (EM) images is crucial for reconstructing neural circuits. Traditional segmentation methods often struggle with challenges such as weak boundaries, topological errors, and high computational cost. We propose a novel approach that leverages the power of graph neural networks to learn a metric graph representation from EM images for improved neuron segmentation. Our method learns to embed image patches into a high-dimensional space where distances reflect the likelihood of belonging to the same neuron. We then construct a graph based on these embeddings and utilize graph-based clustering algorithms to generate neuron segmentations. This approach allows us to effectively capture long-range dependencies and address common segmentation errors. We evaluate our method on benchmark EM datasets and demonstrate significant improvements in segmentation accuracy compared to state-of-the-art techniques, particularly in resolving challenging boundaries and reducing topological errors. Our results highlight the potential of metric learning and graph neural networks for robust and efficient neuron segmentation in EM images.
Understanding how image transformations influence human gaze behavior is crucial for developing robust and adaptable computer vision systems. This paper investigates the impact of various image transformations on gaze patterns using a novel dataset and a deep learning model. We present a comprehensive dataset of eye-tracking data collected while participants viewed images subjected to a range of transformations, including geometric distortions (e.g., rotation, scaling, cropping) and photometric alterations (e.g., brightness, contrast, noise). We then introduce a convolutional neural network (CNN) model trained to predict gaze locations based on the transformed images. The model incorporates transformation-specific features to capture the unique visual cues introduced by each transformation. Our results demonstrate that different image transformations significantly alter gaze distributions and that the proposed model can effectively predict gaze behavior under various transformation conditions. The dataset and model contribute to a deeper understanding of the relationship between image transformations and human attention, paving the way for improved saliency prediction and gaze-contingent applications.
Hidden Tree Markov Networks (HTMNs) offer a powerful approach for modeling complex structured data by combining the strengths of tree-structured graphical models with the representational capacity of deep learning. This work introduces a novel HTMN architecture that leverages both deep and wide learning principles to capture intricate dependencies within structured data. The "deep" component utilizes multiple layers of non-linear transformations to learn hierarchical feature representations from the input, enabling the model to automatically extract relevant features for prediction. Simultaneously, the "wide" component directly incorporates raw features and their interactions, providing a complementary path for learning explicit relationships and enhancing model interpretability. We demonstrate that this hybrid approach allows the HTMN to effectively model complex dependencies beyond the limitations of traditional tree-based models while retaining the computational efficiency and structural advantages of a tree architecture. Experimental results on [mention relevant datasets, e.g., benchmark structured prediction datasets] showcase the superior performance of our deep and wide HTMN compared to existing methods, highlighting its potential for a wide range of applications involving structured data.
Machine learning (ML) is increasingly being integrated into smart healthcare systems, enabling advancements in diagnostics, treatment planning, and patient monitoring. However, the reliance on data-driven models makes these systems vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where carefully crafted input perturbations can cause misclassifications and potentially lead to incorrect medical decisions. This paper explores the potential impact of adversarial attacks on ML-based smart healthcare systems. We review various attack strategies, including white-box and black-box attacks, and their effectiveness against common ML models used in healthcare applications such as image-based diagnostics, predictive analytics, and anomaly detection. We discuss the unique challenges and ethical considerations associated with adversarial attacks in healthcare, highlighting the potential for patient harm and the need for robust defense mechanisms. Finally, we outline current defense strategies and suggest future research directions to mitigate the risks posed by adversarial attacks, ensuring the safety and reliability of ML-driven smart healthcare systems.
## Abstract: Assessing Capsule Networks With Biased Data

Capsule Networks (CapsNets) have shown promise in capturing hierarchical relationships and spatial information in data, offering potential advantages over traditional Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). However, their performance and robustness in real-world scenarios where data is often biased or imbalanced remain relatively unexplored. This study investigates the impact of biased data distributions on the performance of CapsNets across different tasks and architectures. We explore various types of data bias, including class imbalance, feature bias, and sample selection bias, and evaluate their influence on the accuracy, generalization ability, and robustness of CapsNets compared to benchmark CNN models. Our findings reveal the susceptibility of CapsNets to specific forms of data bias and highlight potential strategies for mitigating these effects, such as data augmentation, re-weighting schemes, and specialized loss functions. This work provides crucial insights into the practical limitations of CapsNets in biased data settings and offers valuable guidance for developing more robust and reliable capsule-based systems.
Self-supervised learning (SSL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for learning representations from unlabeled data. This paper explores SSL from a multi-view perspective, highlighting how leveraging multiple, often complementary, views of the same underlying data can significantly enhance the quality and robustness of learned representations. We argue that the core principle behind many successful SSL methods lies in enforcing consistency or predictability across different views. This involves either explicitly constructing multiple views through data augmentation, implicitly exploiting inherent multi-view characteristics of the data (e.g., image and text descriptions), or learning to generate new views from existing ones. We review a range of multi-view SSL techniques, categorized by the nature of the views and the consistency objectives employed. Furthermore, we discuss the benefits of this approach, including improved feature disentanglement, increased robustness to noise and adversarial attacks, and enhanced generalization performance. Finally, we identify challenges and future directions for multi-view SSL, such as developing more effective view generation strategies and exploring adaptive view weighting schemes. This work provides a comprehensive overview of the multi-view perspective in SSL and its potential to unlock more powerful and generalizable representations.
This paper presents a novel approach for reconstructing physical fields obtained from simulations using a Reconstruction Neural Network (RNN) method. Simulation-based physical fields often suffer from limitations such as computational cost, limited resolution, or noise, hindering their direct application in downstream tasks. To address this, we propose an RNN architecture trained to learn the underlying structure and relationships within the simulated data. The RNN leverages its ability to process sequential or spatially correlated data to effectively reconstruct the physical field, enhancing its resolution, reducing noise, and potentially extrapolating beyond the original simulation domain. We demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method on [mention specific type of physical field, e.g., fluid flow, temperature distribution, stress field] datasets, comparing its performance against traditional interpolation and regression techniques. Results show that the RNN-based reconstruction significantly improves the accuracy and visual quality of the physical field, offering a promising alternative for enhancing simulation data and enabling more reliable downstream analyses. This approach holds potential for applications in various fields, including engineering design, scientific visualization, and data-driven modeling.
Efficient exploration in reinforcement learning remains a significant challenge, particularly in sparse reward environments. This paper proposes a novel exploration strategy, **State Entropy Maximization with Random Encoders (SEME-RE)**, which leverages the principle of information gain to drive the agent towards novel and informative states. SEME-RE utilizes a randomly initialized, fixed encoder to extract features from observed states. By maximizing the entropy of the encoded state representations, the agent is incentivized to visit regions of the state space that are poorly represented by the encoder, indicating novelty. This approach offers a computationally efficient alternative to learning intrinsic reward functions, as it avoids the need for online training of the encoder. We demonstrate empirically that SEME-RE outperforms existing exploration methods, including count-based and prediction-error based approaches, on a suite of benchmark environments. Our results suggest that maximizing state entropy with fixed, random encoders provides a powerful and efficient mechanism for driving effective exploration in reinforcement learning.
Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents often struggle to generalize to unseen environments or tasks, particularly when faced with variable-sized or permutation-invariant inputs. This work explores the application of Deep Sets, a powerful framework for learning functions on sets, to improve generalization in RL. We propose integrating Deep Sets architectures into various components of RL agents, such as state representation learning and policy parameterization, allowing them to effectively process set-structured data. We hypothesize that this approach enables the agent to learn representations that are invariant to the order of elements within the set and adaptable to varying set sizes, ultimately leading to improved generalization performance across diverse RL tasks. We present empirical results on benchmark environments demonstrating the effectiveness of our Deep Sets-based RL agents in generalizing to novel configurations and unseen task instances compared to traditional RL methods. Our findings suggest that Deep Sets provide a promising avenue for building more robust and generalizable RL agents capable of handling complex, set-structured environments.
Stereo matching, the task of estimating disparity maps from stereo image pairs, is highly sensitive to domain shifts between training and testing data. Performance degrades significantly when models trained on synthetic datasets are applied to real-world scenarios, or when encountering unseen environments. Our results highlight the effectiveness of our approach in learning robust representations, leading to more reliable disparity estimation in diverse and challenging environments.
Time series classification (TSC) is a critical task in various domains, from healthcare to finance. Dictionary-based classifiers, which leverage the frequency of occurrence of short, discriminative subsequences (words) within time series, have shown promising accuracy. However, their computational complexity often hinders their scalability to large datasets and high-dimensional time series. This paper addresses the scalability limitations of dictionary classifiers for TSC. Our results highlight the potential of scalable dictionary classifiers for tackling large-scale TSC problems in real-world applications.
This paper explores the vulnerability of deep learning models for 3D point cloud classification to adversarial attacks and investigates potential defense mechanisms. While adversarial attacks have been extensively studied in 2D image classification, their application to 3D point cloud data remains relatively less explored. We extend existing adversarial attack techniques, such as gradient-based methods and optimization-based approaches, to the 3D domain, adapting them to the unique characteristics of point cloud data, including sparsity and permutation invariance. Furthermore, we evaluate the transferability of these attacks across different 3D point cloud classifiers. We also investigate several defense strategies against these attacks, including adversarial training, input denoising techniques, and robust feature learning. Our experiments on benchmark 3D point cloud datasets demonstrate the significant vulnerability of state-of-the-art classifiers to adversarial perturbations and provide insights into the effectiveness and limitations of different defense mechanisms. These findings highlight the need for developing more robust and reliable deep learning models for 3D point cloud processing in safety-critical applications.
Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is a ubiquitous optimization algorithm in machine learning, yet a complete understanding of its dynamics remains elusive. This work investigates the landscape traversed by SGD and its implications for escape from local minima. We demonstrate that the optimization landscape exhibits a logarithmic structure, characterized by progressively flatter regions as training progresses. This logarithmic landscape, coupled with the inherent stochasticity of SGD, leads to a power-law decay in the probability of remaining trapped in local minima. Specifically, we derive a theoretical framework that connects the scaling exponent of the power-law escape rate to the properties of the logarithmic landscape and the noise level of SGD. Our findings provide novel insights into the long-time behavior of SGD and offer a potential explanation for its ability to escape suboptimal solutions and achieve good generalization performance. We validate our theoretical predictions with empirical experiments on various machine learning tasks, highlighting the practical relevance of the logarithmic landscape and power-law escape rate in understanding the optimization dynamics of SGD.

Our results highlight the potential of Safe DRL to enable the deployment of robust and reliable autonomous agents in complex, real-world MAS with continuous action spaces.
Anticipating driving maneuvers is crucial for advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS) and autonomous vehicles to ensure safety and efficiency. This work addresses the challenge of building robust and subject-independent maneuver anticipation models. We propose a Domain-Adversarial Recurrent Neural Network (DANN) architecture to mitigate the effects of inter-subject variability and improve generalization across different drivers. By incorporating a domain discriminator within a recurrent neural network framework, our model learns maneuver-related features that are invariant to driver-specific characteristics. We evaluate the proposed approach on a real-world driving dataset, demonstrating its superior performance in terms of accuracy and robustness compared to traditional recurrent models and domain adaptation techniques. Our results highlight the potential of DANN-based models for building reliable and personalized ADAS that can effectively anticipate driving maneuvers across diverse driver populations.
Causal mediation analysis is a powerful tool for understanding the mechanisms through which an exposure influences an outcome, by decomposing the total effect into direct and indirect (mediated) effects. However, the presence of unmeasured confounding variables that affect both the mediator and the outcome (hidden confounders) can bias traditional mediation estimates. This work addresses the challenges posed by hidden confounders in causal mediation analysis. We explore and compare various approaches for identifying and mitigating the bias introduced by such confounders, including sensitivity analysis techniques, instrumental variable methods, and methods leveraging observed proxies for the unmeasured confounders. We discuss the assumptions underlying each approach and their limitations, highlighting the importance of careful consideration of the causal structure and available data when conducting mediation analysis in the presence of potential hidden confounding. Furthermore, we propose potential extensions and improvements to existing methods to enhance their robustness and applicability in real-world scenarios. This research contributes to a more reliable and valid understanding of causal pathways in complex systems where hidden confounding is a significant concern.
This paper investigates the problem of Robust Principal Component Analysis (RPCA) through the lens of bilinear factor matrix norm minimization. Traditional RPCA methods often rely on convex relaxation techniques that can be computationally expensive and may not always yield optimal solutions. We propose a novel approach based on directly minimizing a non-convex objective function involving bilinear factor matrix norms, offering potential advantages in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. We develop efficient alternating minimization algorithms with provable convergence properties for solving the resulting optimization problem. Furthermore, we analyze the robustness of our approach to outliers and noise. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods through extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, including image denoising and background subtraction, showcasing its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art RPCA algorithms in terms of both accuracy and computational time.
Approximate Bayesian Reinforcement Learning (ABRL) aims to efficiently learn optimal policies under uncertainty by maintaining a posterior distribution over the environment's dynamics. However, traditional reward functions often provide insufficient signal for effective posterior exploration, especially in complex or sparse-reward environments. This paper proposes a novel variance-based reward shaping technique to address this challenge. Our approach leverages the posterior variance over value functions to incentivize exploration and reduce uncertainty about the optimal policy. By augmenting the original reward with a term proportional to the variance of the estimated value function, we encourage the agent to explore states and actions where the posterior is uncertain, leading to more informative updates and improved learning performance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on several benchmark reinforcement learning tasks, showing that variance-based rewards significantly accelerate learning, improve sample efficiency, and achieve higher asymptotic performance compared to traditional ABRL approaches. Our results highlight the potential of variance as a powerful signal for exploration in Bayesian reinforcement learning.
Neural networks, despite their powerful predictive capabilities, are often treated as black boxes, hindering trust and widespread adoption. Model interpretation techniques aim to shed light on the inner workings of these networks, providing explanations for their predictions. However, the explanations generated can be highly sensitive to minor input perturbations, rendering them unreliable and potentially misleading, especially when applied to inherently unstable or unreliable neural networks. This paper investigates the problem of building robust and reliable explanations for unreliable models. We propose a novel approach based on a locally smoothing perspective of model interpretation. By leveraging the inherent stability of smoothed representations, we demonstrate that locally smoothing the model's input space leads to more consistent and reliable explanations, mitigating the impact of noise and instability. We empirically validate our approach on various datasets and model architectures, demonstrating that our method significantly improves the robustness of explanations without sacrificing their fidelity. Our findings contribute to a more trustworthy understanding of neural network behavior, particularly in scenarios where model reliability is a concern.
Remote sensing image super-resolution (SR) aims to enhance the spatial resolution of low-resolution (LR) images, enabling more detailed analysis and applications. Traditional SR methods often rely on paired LR-HR training data, which is challenging to acquire in remote sensing due to the inherent difficulties in obtaining perfectly aligned HR images. To address this challenge, we propose a novel unsupervised remote sensing SR method leveraging a **Migration Image Prior (MIP)**. Our approach exploits the inherent statistical similarities between different regions within the LR image itself, allowing the network to learn high-frequency details without requiring external HR training data. Specifically, we formulate a loss function that encourages the super-resolved output to exhibit self-similarity with migrated patches from the LR input, effectively transferring texture and structural information to reconstruct finer details. This self-supervised learning strategy enables the network to learn a powerful image prior directly from the input data, leading to enhanced SR performance, particularly in challenging remote sensing scenarios with limited or no paired training data. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our unsupervised MIP-based approach achieves competitive performance compared to existing unsupervised and even some supervised SR methods, highlighting its potential for practical remote sensing applications.
Estimating node importance within knowledge graphs (KGs) is crucial for various downstream tasks, including knowledge graph completion, entity recommendation, and information retrieval. Traditional methods often rely on handcrafted features or computationally expensive graph traversal algorithms. This paper proposes a novel approach leveraging Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to effectively estimate node importance in KGs. We develop a GNN-based model that learns node embeddings reflecting their structural significance within the graph. The model aggregates information from neighboring nodes and edges, capturing complex relationships and dependencies that influence node importance. We explore different GNN architectures and training strategies to optimize performance. Empirical evaluations on benchmark KG datasets demonstrate that our GNN-based approach achieves superior performance compared to existing methods in predicting node importance, showcasing its ability to capture intricate graph structures and effectively identify influential nodes. The proposed model offers a scalable and efficient solution for estimating node importance in large-scale knowledge graphs.
Human Activity Recognition (HAR) plays a crucial role in various applications, including healthcare monitoring, smart home environments, and security systems. This paper presents a novel approach for HAR utilizing the Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT) in conjunction with Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). The CWT is employed to transform raw sensor data into time-frequency representations, capturing both temporal and spectral characteristics of human activities. These time-frequency representations are then fed as input to a CNN, which automatically learns hierarchical features and effectively classifies different activities. The combination of CWT and CNN leverages the strengths of both techniques: CWT provides robust signal processing capabilities for feature extraction, while CNN offers powerful pattern recognition and classification abilities. Experimental results on benchmark HAR datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, achieving competitive accuracy compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches. This research highlights the potential of utilizing CWT and CNNs for robust and accurate human activity recognition.
Multivariate time series data is ubiquitous across various domains, demanding robust and interpretable models for effective analysis and prediction. While deep learning models, particularly temporal networks, have demonstrated superior performance on such data, their inherent complexity often hinders understanding the reasoning behind their predictions. This paper introduces an Instance Explainable Temporal Network (IETN) for multivariate time series, designed to provide instance-specific explanations for model outputs. IETN leverages attention mechanisms within a temporal network architecture to identify salient features and time steps that contribute most significantly to the prediction for each individual instance. We propose a novel explanation method that aggregates attention weights to generate a concise and intuitive explanation highlighting the influential variables and temporal segments driving the model's decision. We evaluate IETN on benchmark multivariate time series datasets, demonstrating its ability to achieve competitive predictive performance while simultaneously providing meaningful and actionable explanations for individual predictions, enhancing trust and facilitating deeper insights into the underlying dynamics of the time series.
Correlative microscopy techniques, combining modalities such as light microscopy (LM) and electron microscopy (EM), offer powerful insights into biological structures and processes. A critical step in these workflows is the accurate registration of data acquired from different modalities. This paper presents a novel cross-modal registration approach leveraging point clouds extracted from LM and EM images, coupled with a graph-matching algorithm. We construct point clouds representing salient features in each modality and then formulate the registration problem as a graph-matching task, where nodes represent points and edges encode spatial relationships. By optimizing for a consistent transformation that aligns the graph structures, we achieve robust and accurate registration despite differences in resolution, contrast, and inherent distortions between modalities. We evaluate the performance of our method on synthetic and real correlative microscopy datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in achieving sub-pixel registration accuracy and its potential for automating correlative microscopy workflows. This approach offers a valuable tool for researchers seeking to integrate multi-modal microscopy data and gain a deeper understanding of complex biological systems.
Learning without forgetting (LwF) enables models to incrementally learn new tasks without catastrophically forgetting previously learned knowledge. This is particularly challenging for 3D point cloud object recognition due to the inherent complexity and sparsity of point cloud data. This paper proposes a novel LwF approach tailored specifically for 3D point cloud object recognition. We address the challenges of preserving knowledge in the point cloud domain by introducing a [**mention specific technique(s) used, e.g., knowledge distillation strategy based on feature similarity and a novel regularization term that encourages the model to maintain consistent representations across different tasks.**] This allows the model to effectively transfer knowledge from old tasks to new tasks while mitigating the negative impact of forgetting. We evaluate our method on [**mention datasets used, e.g., ModelNet40 and ScanObjectNN**] and demonstrate significant improvements over existing LwF approaches in terms of both forward transfer and backward compatibility. Our results show that the proposed method enables effective incremental learning for 3D point cloud object recognition, paving the way for more robust and adaptable 3D perception systems.
Robust body-pose estimation in challenging scenarios, such as occlusion, variations in clothing, and complex environments, remains a significant hurdle. We introduce "Skeletor," a novel approach leveraging skeletal transformers to achieve robust and accurate body-pose estimation. Unlike traditional methods that directly regress joint coordinates, Skeletor operates on a skeletal representation of the human body, encoding the relationships between joints through a transformer architecture. This allows the model to reason about the overall body structure and infer the location of occluded or ambiguous joints based on the context provided by visible joints. By transforming the skeletal representation through the transformer layers, Skeletor learns to effectively propagate information across the skeleton, mitigating the impact of noisy or incomplete input. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Skeletor on challenging benchmark datasets, showing significant improvements in robustness and accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods, particularly in scenarios with significant occlusion and complex poses. Our results highlight the potential of skeletal transformers for learning robust and generalizable representations for body-pose estimation.
Reinforcement learning (RL), a computational framework for learning optimal behavior through trial-and-error interactions with an environment, has emerged as a powerful tool in artificial intelligence. Beyond its applications in robotics and game playing, RL has also garnered significant attention for its potential to provide insights into the neural and psychological mechanisms underlying learning and decision-making. This abstract explores the connections between RL and these fields, focusing on how RL algorithms can be used to model and understand behavioral phenomena observed in humans and animals, such as reward-based learning, habit formation, and cognitive control. Furthermore, it examines the neural substrates implicated in RL processes, highlighting the role of brain regions like the basal ganglia and prefrontal cortex. By bridging the gap between computational modeling, neuroscience, and psychology, this research aims to illuminate the fundamental principles governing adaptive behavior and pave the way for more biologically plausible artificial intelligence systems.
## Abstract: Image Transformer

The Image Transformer leverages the Transformer architecture, originally designed for sequence-to-sequence tasks in natural language processing, to address computer vision problems. This approach moves beyond traditional convolutional neural networks (CNNs) by treating images as sequences of patches, enabling the Transformer's inherent ability to model long-range dependencies and global context. This abstract outlines the fundamental principles of the Image Transformer, highlighting its ability to capture complex relationships between image regions through self-attention mechanisms. We explore how this architecture can be adapted and applied to various vision tasks, such as image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation, demonstrating its potential to achieve state-of-the-art performance and offering a promising alternative to CNN-based methodologies. Furthermore, we discuss the advantages and challenges associated with using the Transformer architecture for image processing, including computational complexity and data requirements, paving the way for future research and development in this rapidly evolving field.
## GuidedStyle: Attribute Knowledge Guided Style Manipulation for Semantic Face Editing

Semantic face editing aims to manipulate specific facial attributes while preserving identity. However, existing methods often struggle with disentangling attribute manipulation from identity preservation, leading to undesired artifacts or identity leakage. This paper introduces GuidedStyle, a novel framework that leverages attribute knowledge to guide style manipulation for more precise and controllable semantic face editing. GuidedStyle employs a two-stage approach. First, an attribute prediction network learns to extract attribute representations from input faces. Second, a style manipulation network uses these attribute representations to guide the generation of style codes, which are then injected into a pre-trained StyleGAN generator. By explicitly encoding attribute information into the style space, GuidedStyle enables targeted attribute manipulation while minimizing unintended changes to other facial features and preserving identity. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that GuidedStyle achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of attribute editing accuracy, identity preservation, and visual quality, surpassing existing methods in generating realistic and semantically consistent edited faces.
## HandFoldingNet: A 3D Hand Pose Estimation Network Using Multiscale-Feature Guided Folding of a 2D Hand Skeleton

This paper introduces HandFoldingNet, a novel deep learning approach for 3D hand pose estimation from a single depth image. Our method leverages the efficiency of 2D hand skeleton detection and then "folds" this 2D representation into a 3D pose through a learned folding process.  HandFoldingNet utilizes a 2D hand pose estimator to generate an initial 2D skeleton.  This skeleton is then fed into a novel network architecture that employs multiscale features extracted from the depth image to guide the 3D reconstruction.  The multiscale features capture both local and global context, enabling the network to accurately resolve ambiguities inherent in the 2D-to-3D lifting process.  Specifically, we learn a mapping that deforms and positions the 2D skeleton in 3D space, effectively "folding" it into a plausible 3D configuration.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of HandFoldingNet on challenging benchmark datasets, showing competitive performance and highlighting the benefits of leveraging 2D skeleton priors and multiscale feature guidance for robust and accurate 3D hand pose estimation. Our results demonstrate that HandFoldingNet offers a promising alternative to direct 3D pose regression methods, particularly in scenarios with occlusions and noise.
This paper introduces a novel transformer-based framework for learning robust and informative representations of multivariate time series data. Traditional approaches often struggle to capture complex temporal dependencies and inter-variable relationships inherent in such data. Our framework leverages the attention mechanism of transformers to effectively model both local and global dependencies across time steps and variables. We propose a specific architecture that incorporates [mention key architectural components, e.g., positional encoding modifications, variable embedding strategies, or pre-training objectives]. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework through extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets, showcasing its superiority over existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and robustness. The results highlight the potential of transformer-based architectures for capturing complex patterns in multivariate time series data and facilitating downstream analysis.
## Abstract: Unsupervised Features Learning for Sampled Vector Fields

This paper presents a novel unsupervised approach for learning feature representations from sampled vector fields. Vector fields, prevalent in diverse domains such as fluid dynamics, climate modeling, and medical imaging, are often represented by discrete samples.  Extracting meaningful features from these samples is crucial for various downstream tasks like anomaly detection, clustering, and prediction.  Our method leverages [mention specific technique, e.g., autoencoders, generative adversarial networks, etc.] to learn a low-dimensional latent space that captures the underlying structure and patterns within the vector field data. By training without explicit labels, the model discovers inherent relationships between neighboring vectors and identifies salient features reflecting the global flow characteristics.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on synthetic and real-world vector field datasets, showcasing its ability to generate informative features that improve the performance of downstream tasks compared to traditional feature engineering methods.  The learned features provide a compact and efficient representation of the vector field, enabling scalable analysis and facilitating a deeper understanding of complex flow phenomena.
Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has achieved remarkable success in various domains, but its performance often hinges on effective state representation. Traditional methods rely on fixed-size vectors or images, which can struggle to capture complex relationships and relational structures inherent in many environments. This paper explores the use of graph-based state representations for DRL. We propose a novel framework that leverages graph neural networks (GNNs) to encode state information represented as graphs, where nodes represent entities and edges encode their interactions. This allows the agent to learn representations that are sensitive to the relational structure of the environment, enabling more efficient learning and improved generalization. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our graph-based approach on benchmark tasks with complex relational dynamics, showing that it outperforms traditional DRL methods that utilize fixed-size state representations. Our results highlight the potential of GNNs and graph-based representations for enhancing the capabilities of DRL agents in environments with intricate relationships and dependencies.
## Abstract: Rethinking ImageNet Pre-training

ImageNet pre-training has become a cornerstone of modern computer vision, enabling significant performance gains across a wide range of downstream tasks. However, the reliance on ImageNet raises several critical questions regarding its relevance, efficiency, and potential biases. This work critically re-examines the role of ImageNet pre-training in light of recent advancements. We explore alternative pre-training strategies, including self-supervised learning, multi-modal pre-training, and task-specific pre-training, evaluating their effectiveness in comparison to traditional ImageNet pre-training. We analyze the limitations of ImageNet, such as its dataset bias and the discrepancy between ImageNet's object-centric focus and the requirements of more complex downstream tasks. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of scaling laws and efficient fine-tuning techniques on the necessity of large-scale pre-training. Our findings provide a nuanced perspective on the future of pre-training in computer vision, highlighting the potential of alternative approaches to surpass ImageNet pre-training in specific scenarios and ultimately leading to more robust, efficient, and generalizable vision models.
This paper explores the use of graphs as a powerful and versatile representation for deep learning models. Traditional deep learning architectures primarily operate on data structured as sequences, grids, or volumes. However, many real-world datasets are inherently relational and best represented as graphs, capturing complex dependencies and interactions between entities. This abstract outlines the benefits of leveraging graph-based representations within deep learning, focusing on techniques such as Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and their ability to learn node embeddings, graph-level representations, and perform tasks like node classification, link prediction, and graph classification. We discuss various GNN architectures, including convolutional, recurrent, and attention-based approaches, highlighting their strengths and limitations. Furthermore, we explore applications of graph-based deep learning across diverse domains, such as social network analysis, drug discovery, knowledge graph reasoning, and recommendation systems. Finally, we address key challenges in this field, including scalability to large graphs, handling dynamic graphs, and developing robust and interpretable GNN models, paving the way for future research directions in graph-based deep learning.
Accurate prediction of significant wave height (SWH) is crucial for coastal engineering, maritime operations, and offshore energy applications. Traditional statistical and numerical models often struggle to capture the complex spatiotemporal dependencies inherent in wave dynamics. This paper introduces a novel approach, the Wavelet Graph Neural Network (WaveGNN), for SWH prediction. WaveGNN leverages the power of graph neural networks (GNNs) to model the spatial relationships between wave measurement locations, while incorporating wavelet decomposition to extract multi-scale temporal features from wave time series data. Specifically, wavelet analysis decomposes the SWH time series into different frequency bands, capturing both long-term trends and short-term fluctuations. These features, combined with spatial information encoded in the graph structure, are fed into a GNN to predict future SWH values. Experimental results on [Mention specific datasets/regions used, e.g., a real-world buoy dataset] demonstrate that WaveGNN outperforms state-of-the-art SWH prediction models, exhibiting superior accuracy and robustness in capturing complex wave patterns. The proposed WaveGNN offers a promising framework for improved SWH forecasting, potentially leading to enhanced coastal management and safer maritime activities.
## SegCodeNet: Color-Coded Segmentation Masks for Activity Detection from Wearable Cameras

Activity detection from wearable cameras faces challenges due to egocentric perspective, dynamic backgrounds, and privacy concerns. This paper introduces SegCodeNet, a novel approach that leverages color-coded segmentation masks to represent and abstract visual information for robust activity detection while mitigating privacy risks. SegCodeNet consists of two key modules: a lightweight semantic segmentation network that generates pixel-level segmentation masks of the wearer's surroundings, and a color-coding scheme that encodes semantic classes into distinct color channels. These color-coded masks serve as a simplified, privacy-preserving representation of the scene, effectively reducing the complexity of the visual input while retaining crucial contextual information relevant to activity recognition. We train and evaluate SegCodeNet on a challenging egocentric activity dataset, demonstrating that our approach achieves competitive accuracy compared to methods operating directly on raw images, while offering inherent privacy advantages. The results highlight the effectiveness of SegCodeNet in learning meaningful representations from wearable camera data and its potential for enabling privacy-aware activity detection in real-world scenarios.
This paper proposes a novel architecture, **Progressive Transformers**, for end-to-end Sign Language Production (SLP). SLP aims to generate continuous sign language video sequences from spoken language input. Existing approaches often struggle with generating temporally coherent and visually realistic sign language. Our Progressive Transformer addresses these challenges by employing a multi-stage decoding process. We introduce a progressive decoding strategy where each stage refines the generated sign language sequence, starting from a coarse initial prediction and iteratively adding detail and improving temporal alignment with the input spoken language. Specifically, we utilize multiple Transformer decoders, each conditioned on the output of the previous stage and the input text, allowing for a hierarchical refinement of the generated motion. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on benchmark SLP datasets, showing significant improvements in generation quality, measured by both quantitative metrics and qualitative evaluation. The results indicate that our Progressive Transformer architecture effectively learns to generate more fluent, accurate, and visually appealing sign language sequences compared to existing end-to-end SLP models.
Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) have emerged as a powerful representation for novel view synthesis, achieving impressive photorealistic results. However, their computational cost during rendering hinders real-time applications. This paper presents a novel approach to significantly accelerate NeRF rendering by "baking" the learned radiance field into a structured data format. Instead of querying the NeRF network directly during rendering, we pre-compute and store key properties, such as density and view-dependent color, within a voxel grid or other efficient spatial data structure. This baked representation allows for real-time rendering through efficient lookups and interpolation, bypassing the computationally expensive neural network evaluation. We demonstrate that our method achieves a substantial speedup compared to standard NeRF rendering while maintaining high visual quality. Our approach enables interactive exploration and manipulation of complex 3D scenes represented by NeRFs, paving the way for real-time applications such as virtual reality, augmented reality, and interactive content creation.
This paper introduces a novel image segmentation approach, Scale-Based Gaussian Coverings (SBGC), that leverages both intra-mixture and inter-mixture models to achieve robust and accurate results. SBGC represents an image as a collection of Gaussian mixtures, where each mixture corresponds to a region at a specific scale. The intra-mixture model captures the statistical properties of pixels within a region, while the inter-mixture model defines relationships between mixtures at different scales, enabling hierarchical segmentation. By iteratively refining the Gaussian coverings based on both intra- and inter-mixture similarities, SBGC effectively handles complex image structures, noise, and varying object scales. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that SBGC outperforms existing methods, achieving superior segmentation accuracy and robustness compared to traditional clustering and scale-space techniques. The proposed method offers a promising framework for image segmentation with potential applications in computer vision, medical imaging, and remote sensing.
This paper presents a novel approach for tracking aerial vehicles using hyperspectral imagery. The method leverages the rich spectral information to generate likelihood maps representing the probability of a target being present in each pixel. To address challenges posed by varying illumination, atmospheric conditions, and target appearance, we propose an adaptive fusion strategy for combining multiple likelihood maps derived from different spectral features and classification algorithms. This fusion process dynamically weights the contributions of each map based on their estimated reliability and relevance to the current scene. The performance of the proposed approach is evaluated on real-world hyperspectral datasets, demonstrating significant improvements in tracking accuracy and robustness compared to traditional methods that rely on single spectral features or fixed fusion weights. The results highlight the potential of adaptive hyperspectral likelihood map fusion for reliable aerial vehicle tracking in complex environments.
Estimating Conditional Mutual Information (CMI) is crucial in various machine learning tasks, including feature selection, causal inference, and representation learning. However, accurately estimating CMI, especially in high-dimensional settings, remains challenging. This paper introduces C-MI-GAN, a novel approach for estimating CMI based on a MinMax formulation inspired by Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). C-MI-GAN leverages a discriminator network to distinguish between joint and product distributions, and a generator network to minimize this distinguishability, ultimately providing a lower bound estimate of CMI. We demonstrate that the MinMax formulation provides a theoretically sound and computationally efficient way to approximate CMI. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets show that C-MI-GAN outperforms existing CMI estimation methods, particularly in high-dimensional scenarios, offering a promising alternative for applications requiring accurate and scalable CMI estimation.
Generative models have become increasingly popular for synthesizing realistic data, but evaluating their performance and identifying weaknesses remains a significant challenge. This paper proposes a novel approach to both training and evaluating generative models using an optimized maximum mean discrepancy (MMD). We leverage the power of MMD, a kernel-based non-parametric distance between probability distributions, to simultaneously optimize the generative model's parameters and provide a rigorous framework for model criticism. By learning an optimal kernel for MMD during training, we adaptively emphasize discrepancies between the generated and real data distributions that are most informative for improvement. Furthermore, the learned kernel provides insights into the specific features and modalities where the generative model falls short, enabling targeted model refinement and debugging. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on various benchmark datasets, showing improved generative performance and providing interpretable feedback for model improvement compared to existing MMD-based methods and other generative model evaluation techniques.
Non-intrusive load monitoring (NILM) aims to disaggregate household energy consumption into individual appliance usage, providing valuable insights for energy conservation and grid management. However, traditional NILM approaches often rely on centralized data collection, raising privacy concerns. This paper introduces FedNILM, a novel framework that leverages federated learning (FL) to enable NILM applications at the edge without requiring direct access to sensitive user data. FedNILM allows individual households to train local NILM models using their own energy consumption data, and then collaboratively learns a global model through iterative aggregation of model updates. This decentralized approach enhances data privacy while still achieving accurate appliance disaggregation. We evaluate the performance of FedNILM on benchmark NILM datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in achieving comparable or even superior performance compared to centralized methods, while preserving user privacy and enabling on-device NILM applications. Our results highlight the potential of FedNILM to democratize NILM technology and promote wider adoption of energy-efficient practices.
Light field cameras capture both spatial and angular information, offering potential for enhanced image processing tasks. This paper proposes a novel approach for jointly addressing the challenging problems of blind motion deblurring and depth estimation in light fields. We leverage the inherent redundancy and multi-view consistency within the light field data to simultaneously estimate the blur kernel and depth map. Our method employs a variational framework that integrates a robust blur kernel estimation module with a depth estimation network, enforcing consistency between the estimated blur kernel and the deblurred light field. Furthermore, we incorporate depth-dependent blur modeling to account for varying blur levels across different depths. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world light field datasets demonstrate that our joint approach achieves superior performance in both deblurring quality and depth accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods that tackle these problems independently. This integrated framework significantly improves the visual quality and geometric understanding of light field images captured under motion blur.
Volumetric medical image segmentation is crucial for diagnosis and treatment planning. While deep learning methods have achieved significant progress, they often struggle with capturing fine-grained details and maintaining anatomical consistency, particularly in complex structures. This paper introduces a novel **Positional Contrastive Learning (PCL)** framework to enhance volumetric medical image segmentation. PCL leverages contrastive learning to explicitly enforce positional relationships between voxels. Specifically, we learn feature embeddings that are similar for voxels belonging to the same semantic class and located near each other, while pushing apart embeddings of voxels from different classes or distant locations. By incorporating this positional awareness, PCL enables the model to learn more discriminative and spatially coherent representations. We evaluate PCL on multiple benchmark datasets for volumetric medical image segmentation, demonstrating its ability to significantly improve segmentation accuracy and robustness compared to state-of-the-art methods. The results highlight the effectiveness of PCL in capturing fine-grained details and maintaining anatomical consistency, leading to more accurate and reliable medical image segmentation.
## ImVoteNet: Boosting 3D Object Detection in Point Clouds with Image Votes

3D object detection in point clouds is crucial for autonomous driving and robotics. While point cloud-based methods have shown promising results, they often struggle with noisy data, occlusion, and limited contextual information. In this paper, we propose ImVoteNet, a novel approach that leverages complementary information from 2D images to enhance 3D object detection. ImVoteNet extends the VoteNet architecture by incorporating "image votes" generated from 2D object detections. Specifically, we project 2D bounding boxes from images onto the 3D point cloud and generate votes that point towards the center of the corresponding 3D object. These image votes are then aggregated with the point cloud-based votes to refine object proposals and improve localization accuracy. We demonstrate that ImVoteNet significantly boosts the performance of VoteNet, particularly for small and occluded objects. Extensive experiments on the challenging KITTI dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving state-of-the-art results and highlighting the benefits of fusing 2D image and 3D point cloud information for robust 3D object detection.
Understanding and modeling sharing behaviors are crucial for developing effective multi-agent systems, particularly in resource allocation and cooperative tasks. This paper presents a novel approach to constrained image generation using binarized neural networks (BNNs) integrated with decision procedures. Generating images that adhere to specific constraints remains a challenging task, often requiring computationally expensive methods. We leverage the efficiency of BNNs, which offer significantly reduced memory footprint and computational cost compared to their full-precision counterparts, to facilitate constraint satisfaction. Our framework employs a decision procedure, such as Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT), to encode the desired constraints and guide the generation process. By integrating the BNN's output with the decision procedure, we can effectively steer the image generation towards solutions that satisfy the specified constraints. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on various image generation tasks with diverse constraints, showcasing its ability to generate high-quality images while adhering to the defined specifications. The results indicate that our method offers a promising balance between computational efficiency, constraint satisfaction, and image quality in constrained image generation.
Real-time Human-Object Interaction (HOI) detection is crucial for various applications, including robotics, surveillance, and augmented reality. However, existing methods often struggle to achieve the necessary speed and accuracy for real-time performance. This paper presents PPDM, a novel **P**arallel **P**oint **D**etection and **M**atching framework designed for real-time HOI detection. PPDM leverages parallel processing to accelerate both the detection of relevant points representing human and object features and the matching of these points to infer interactions. Specifically, we employ a lightweight point detection module based on [mention specific architecture/technique briefly] that is parallelized across multiple processing units. ## Abstract: Dynamical Pose Estimation

Dynamical pose estimation focuses on tracking and predicting the pose (position and orientation) of an object or agent over time, leveraging the inherent temporal coherence and physical constraints governing its motion. Unlike static pose estimation, which treats each frame independently, dynamical approaches incorporate motion models, filtering techniques, and prior knowledge of the object's dynamics to achieve more robust and accurate results, particularly in challenging scenarios involving noise, occlusions, and rapid movements. This abstract outlines the key challenges and approaches in dynamical pose estimation, including the use of Kalman filters, particle filters, and recurrent neural networks to model and predict pose trajectories. We discuss the benefits of incorporating temporal information, such as smoothing noisy estimates, improving robustness to occlusions, and enabling predictive tracking for applications ranging from robotics and autonomous navigation to human motion analysis and augmented reality. The abstract concludes by highlighting current research directions, including the development of robust dynamic models, efficient inference algorithms, and methods for incorporating environmental context to further enhance the accuracy and reliability of dynamical pose estimation.
Accurate energy consumption prediction is crucial for optimizing Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC) system performance and reducing energy waste in buildings. This study proposes an XGBoost-based model for predicting HVAC energy consumption using multi-system data. The model integrates diverse data sources, including environmental factors, building characteristics, occupancy patterns, and HVAC system operational parameters, to capture complex relationships influencing energy demand. The XGBoost algorithm, known for its high prediction accuracy and robustness, is employed to learn these relationships and generate reliable energy consumption forecasts. The performance of the proposed model is evaluated using real-world data from a multi-system HVAC environment. Results demonstrate that the XGBoost-based model achieves superior prediction accuracy compared to traditional methods, highlighting its potential for proactive energy management and optimized HVAC system control.
This paper explores the challenging problem of medical image segmentation using only scribble annotations as supervision. Scribble-based supervision offers a practical alternative to pixel-wise annotations, significantly reducing annotation effort while still providing sufficient information for training accurate segmentation models. We propose a novel framework that leverages scribble annotations to guide the learning process, focusing on robustly propagating information from the scribbled regions to unannotated areas. Our approach incorporates [mention key techniques, e.g., a novel loss function, a specific network architecture, or a unique training strategy]. We evaluate our method on [mention specific datasets] and demonstrate that it achieves competitive performance compared to methods requiring more extensive supervision, while significantly reducing annotation burden. The results highlight the potential of scribble-supervised learning for efficient and accurate medical image segmentation, paving the way for wider adoption of deep learning models in clinical practice.
This paper investigates the application of a Large Margin K-Nearest Neighbors (LMKNN) classifier for fault diagnosis in helical gearboxes using sound signal analysis.  Helical gearboxes are critical components in many industrial applications, and early fault detection is crucial for preventing costly downtime and ensuring operational safety.  This study utilizes sound signals acquired from a gearbox under various operating conditions and fault scenarios.  The sound signals are processed to extract relevant features.  The extracted features are then used to train and test an LMKNN classifier, which aims to improve classification accuracy by maximizing the margin between different classes.  The performance of the LMKNN classifier is compared against traditional K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) and other benchmark classification algorithms.  Results demonstrate that the LMKNN classifier achieves superior performance in identifying different fault types and severity levels in helical gearboxes, highlighting its potential for reliable and effective condition monitoring.  This approach provides a promising solution for automated fault diagnosis in industrial machinery, contributing to improved maintenance strategies and reduced operational costs.
We introduce LEAP: Learning Articulated Occupancy of People, a novel approach for reconstructing and representing clothed human bodies in 3D. Unlike existing methods that focus on surface meshes or volumetric representations, LEAP learns an articulated occupancy field that explicitly encodes the occupancy probability for each point in space, conditioned on the pose and shape of the underlying articulated skeleton. This representation allows us to capture fine-grained geometric details and handle complex clothing deformations beyond the limitations of traditional parametric models. Our method leverages a neural network architecture trained on a combination of synthetic and real data to predict the occupancy value for a given 3D point and articulated pose. We demonstrate that LEAP outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in terms of reconstruction accuracy, especially in challenging scenarios with loose clothing and complex poses. Furthermore, the articulated occupancy representation facilitates downstream tasks such as pose editing and animation, enabling realistic and controllable human body modeling.
This paper presents a novel approach for learning 3D semantic scene graphs from 3D indoor reconstructions. We leverage the rich geometric and semantic information contained within these reconstructions to automatically generate comprehensive scene graphs that capture the relationships between objects and rooms within an indoor environment. Our method involves a multi-stage process: first, we perform semantic segmentation on the 3D mesh to identify individual objects and room regions. Next, we analyze the spatial relationships between these entities, including adjacency, containment, and support, to construct an initial scene graph. Finally, we employ a graph neural network to refine the graph structure and node embeddings, learning to predict and reinforce meaningful relationships based on contextual cues and geometric properties. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on publicly available datasets, showing significant improvements in scene graph accuracy and completeness compared to existing methods. Furthermore, we explore the potential of these learned scene graphs for downstream tasks such as scene understanding, object localization, and robot navigation.
Learning Generalizable Physiological Representations from Large-scale Wearable Data

Wearable devices are generating unprecedented volumes of physiological data, offering the potential to revolutionize personalized healthcare and well-being. However, effectively leveraging this data requires learning robust and generalizable representations that capture underlying physiological states and patterns across diverse individuals and contexts. This paper explores methods for learning such representations from large-scale wearable datasets. We investigate techniques ranging from traditional feature engineering combined with machine learning to deep learning approaches that can automatically extract hierarchical features directly from raw sensor data. We address challenges associated with data heterogeneity, noise, and inter-individual variability by incorporating techniques like domain adaptation, transfer learning, and contrastive learning. Furthermore, we evaluate the generalizability of learned representations across different tasks, populations, and sensor modalities. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of learning robust and transferable physiological representations from large-scale wearable data, leading to improved performance in downstream tasks such as activity recognition, stress detection, and early disease prediction. This work contributes to the development of more personalized and proactive healthcare solutions powered by wearable technology.
Image Super-Resolution (SR) aims to reconstruct high-resolution (HR) images from their low-resolution (LR) counterparts. We propose a novel and efficient deep learning approach for image SR based on Laplacian Pyramid Networks (LapSRN). Our method leverages a cascade of convolutional neural networks to progressively refine the HR image details at multiple pyramid levels. This hierarchical structure allows for learning both global structure and fine-grained textures effectively. By predicting the Laplacian pyramid residuals, our network focuses on learning the high-frequency details crucial for visual quality. Furthermore, we introduce architectural improvements that significantly reduce computational complexity without sacrificing accuracy. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of both perceptual quality and quantitative metrics, while maintaining a competitive inference speed, making it suitable for practical applications requiring fast and accurate image super-resolution.
This paper presents an attention-based neural network model for the automated detection of trash in water channels. Addressing the crucial issue of environmental pollution, our approach utilizes deep learning to efficiently identify and localize various types of trash within complex aquatic environments. The proposed model leverages an attention mechanism to selectively focus on relevant features within input images, mitigating the challenges posed by varying illumination, water turbidity, and diverse trash appearances. By highlighting crucial image regions, the attention mechanism improves the model's robustness and accuracy in distinguishing trash from background clutter. Experimental results on a newly curated dataset of water channel images demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed attention-based network compared to traditional convolutional neural network architectures, highlighting its potential for real-time monitoring and efficient trash removal in water channels.
## T-CNN: Tubelets with Convolutional Neural Networks for Object Detection from Videos

Object detection in videos presents significant challenges due to motion blur, occlusion, and changing viewpoints. This paper introduces T-CNN, a novel approach that leverages the temporal context within video sequences by operating on **tubelets**, short spatio-temporal volumes of the video. T-CNN extends the successful framework of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for image-based object detection to the temporal domain. We first generate candidate tubelets using a motion-based proposal mechanism. Then, a 3D CNN is employed to extract spatio-temporal features from each tubelet. These features are used to classify the tubelet as containing an object of interest and to refine its spatio-temporal boundaries. By explicitly modeling the temporal relationships within tubelets, T-CNN is able to achieve improved object detection performance, particularly in challenging video scenarios. Experimental results on benchmark video object detection datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, showing significant gains in accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods that process individual frames independently.
Graph-structured data is prevalent across diverse domains, necessitating effective methods for learning representations that capture complex relational information. This paper introduces Convolutional Kernel Networks (CKNs) for graph-structured data, a novel framework that combines the strengths of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and kernel methods. CKNs leverage learnable convolutional kernels to extract local features from graph neighborhoods, subsequently mapping these features into a high-dimensional kernel space where non-linear relationships are captured. Unlike traditional graph neural networks (GNNs) which primarily rely on message passing, CKNs employ convolutional operations that are inherently parallelizable and can capture more complex patterns within local graph structures. We demonstrate that CKNs offer a powerful and flexible approach to graph representation learning, achieving competitive performance on various graph classification and node classification tasks while providing theoretical insights into the expressive power of the learned convolutional kernels. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of different kernel choices and convolutional architectures on the performance of CKNs, highlighting the potential for further optimization and application to a wide range of graph-based problems.
Continuous lip-reading, the automatic decoding of speech from lip movements in continuous video, faces challenges due to the inherent ambiguity in visual speech and the difficulty in defining a comprehensive and robust viseme vocabulary. This paper proposes a novel approach for **automatic viseme vocabulary construction** to enhance the performance of continuous lip-reading systems. Our method leverages unsupervised clustering techniques applied to a large corpus of visual speech features extracted from video data. This allows for the discovery of a data-driven viseme set, optimized for the specific characteristics of the training data, rather than relying on predefined, potentially suboptimal, vocabularies. We evaluate the effectiveness of the automatically generated viseme vocabulary within a continuous lip-reading framework, demonstrating significant improvements in word recognition accuracy compared to systems utilizing traditional, hand-crafted viseme sets. The results highlight the potential of automatic viseme vocabulary construction to improve the robustness and accuracy of continuous lip-reading systems, particularly in challenging acoustic environments.
Deep transfer learning has become a powerful technique for image classification, particularly when labeled data is scarce. However, traditional transfer learning approaches often assume a binary transfer scenario: a single source domain is used to improve performance on a single target domain. This assumption can be limiting in real-world applications where multiple, diverse source domains are available. This paper proposes a novel **non-binary deep transfer learning (NBDTL) framework** for image classification. NBDTL leverages information from multiple source domains simultaneously, adaptively weighting their contributions based on their relevance to the target domain.  We introduce a novel weighting mechanism that considers both the feature similarity and the discriminative power of each source domain. Furthermore, we explore different strategies for aggregating knowledge transferred from multiple sources, including feature-level fusion and model-level ensemble techniques.  Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that NBDTL significantly outperforms traditional binary transfer learning methods and other multi-source transfer learning approaches, especially when the source domains exhibit varying degrees of similarity to the target domain. This highlights the effectiveness of NBDTL in harnessing the collective knowledge from diverse sources for improved image classification performance.
This paper addresses the challenge of optimizing multi-label ranking models by rethinking and reweighting univariate losses. Traditional approaches often decompose the multi-label ranking problem into independent univariate classification tasks, optimizing each label separately. However, this ignores the inherent dependencies and ranking relationships between labels. We argue that a naive application of univariate losses can lead to inconsistencies and suboptimal generalization performance. To overcome this, we propose a novel framework that analyzes the consistency of different univariate losses within the multi-label ranking context. Based on this analysis, we introduce a reweighting scheme that dynamically adjusts the importance of each univariate loss based on its contribution to the overall ranking performance. We provide theoretical guarantees on the consistency and generalization ability of our proposed approach. Empirical results on several benchmark multi-label datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art multi-label ranking algorithms, highlighting the benefits of rethinking and reweighting univariate losses for improved performance.
