This allows us to learn SFs that are less sensitive to environment-specific details, enabling more robust transfer performance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on a suite of challenging transfer learning benchmarks involving environments with varying dynamics and reward structures. Our results show that the proposed representation significantly outperforms traditional SF-based transfer and other baseline methods, highlighting its potential for enabling efficient and reliable RL in complex and dynamic environments.
Learning complex policies from limited data, particularly a single demonstration, remains a significant challenge in reinforcement learning. This paper introduces a novel approach to augment policy learning by leveraging the inherent structure within a single demonstration. We propose a method for automatically discovering reusable, temporally extended action sequences – which we term "routines" – from the demonstration. These routines are then integrated into the policy learning process by serving as building blocks for exploration and exploitation. By explicitly incorporating these pre-defined routines, we can guide the agent to explore promising regions of the state space, accelerate learning, and improve the overall performance compared to learning directly from the demonstration or using standard exploration strategies. We evaluate our approach on challenging control tasks, demonstrating that augmenting policy learning with discovered routines significantly improves sample efficiency and achieves superior performance compared to baseline methods.
This paper presents a novel approach for 3D object detection that leverages view aggregation to jointly generate 3D proposals and perform object detection. Current methods often suffer from limitations in proposal quality, especially when dealing with occlusions or sparse point clouds. Our proposed framework addresses this by aggregating information from multiple perspectives, enabling a more robust and complete understanding of the 3D scene. Specifically, we introduce a network architecture that learns to fuse features from different views to generate high-quality 3D proposals. These proposals are then refined and classified into object categories, simultaneously predicting their 3D bounding boxes. By jointly optimizing proposal generation and object detection, our method achieves improved performance compared to approaches that treat these tasks separately. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on challenging benchmark datasets, showing significant improvements in both proposal recall and overall 3D object detection accuracy. The results highlight the benefits of view aggregation and joint optimization for robust and accurate 3D scene understanding.
Attention mechanisms have become a cornerstone of deep learning, enabling models to focus on relevant input features and improve performance across various tasks. This work explores the integration of attention within a brain-inspired deep neural network architecture. We investigate how principles of neural computation, such as lateral inhibition and recurrent connections, can be leveraged to create more efficient and biologically plausible attention mechanisms. Our approach aims to mimic the selective attention processes observed in the brain, leading to models that are not only performant but also more interpretable and robust. We present a novel architecture incorporating these brain-inspired principles and evaluate its performance on benchmark tasks. Results demonstrate that this approach can achieve competitive accuracy while offering insights into the underlying mechanisms of attention and potentially leading to more energy-efficient and adaptable deep learning models.
Recognizing structural data, such as tables, forms, and diagrams, from document images is a challenging task crucial for information extraction and document understanding. This paper presents a novel approach, **Graph Model Boosting (GMB)**, for robust and accurate structural data recognition. GMB leverages the inherent relational structure of these document components by representing them as graphs. We propose a boosting framework that iteratively refines the graph representation through the combination of weak graph learners. Each learner focuses on capturing specific structural features and relationships between document elements. The final model integrates these individual learners, resulting in a strong graph model capable of accurately identifying and classifying structural components. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that GMB significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and robustness, particularly in handling complex and noisy document layouts. This highlights the effectiveness of our graph-based boosting approach for advancing the state-of-the-art in structural data recognition.
## IRLAS: Inverse Reinforcement Learning for Architecture Search

Architecture search (NAS) automates the process of discovering optimal neural network architectures for specific tasks. Traditional NAS methods often rely on reinforcement learning (RL) with a reward signal based on validation performance. However, this can be inefficient, requiring extensive training and evaluation of numerous architectures. This paper introduces IRLAS, a novel approach leveraging **Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) for Architecture Search**. Instead of directly optimizing for performance, IRLAS aims to learn the reward function that underlies the decisions of expert architects or pre-defined architectural principles. By observing a set of "expert" architectures and their corresponding performance, IRLAS infers the underlying reward function that best explains these choices. This learned reward function can then be used within a standard RL framework to efficiently explore the architecture space and identify high-performing architectures. We demonstrate that IRLAS can effectively learn meaningful reward functions from limited data and achieve competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art NAS methods, while significantly reducing the computational cost associated with architecture evaluation. Our results highlight the potential of IRL to guide architecture search by leveraging existing architectural knowledge and expertise.
Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across decentralized devices without sharing raw data. However, many FL applications, such as personalized recommendations and dynamic resource allocation, require adapting to diverse and changing environments, making traditional supervised learning approaches insufficient. In this work, we propose a novel **Federated Bandit (FB)** framework that combines FL with multi-armed bandit (MAB) algorithms to facilitate decentralized exploration and exploitation. Specifically, we introduce a **gossiping approach** to efficiently aggregate bandit feedback and model parameters across clients. This gossiping mechanism allows clients to learn from the experiences of their peers without direct data sharing, thereby preserving privacy and reducing communication overhead. We theoretically analyze the regret performance of our proposed FB algorithm and demonstrate its effectiveness through extensive simulations on various bandit tasks, showing that it achieves superior regret compared to existing federated and decentralized bandit approaches while maintaining privacy.
Person re-identification (Re-ID) aims to identify individuals across non-overlapping camera views, a crucial task in video surveillance and smart city applications. This paper provides an introduction to the application of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) within the field of person Re-ID. We explore the fundamental concepts of GANs, highlighting their ability to generate realistic data and learn complex data distributions. We then delve into various GAN-based approaches utilized for Re-ID, categorizing them based on their primary function, such as data augmentation, feature learning, and domain adaptation. We discuss the strengths and limitations of each approach, emphasizing how GANs address key challenges in Re-ID, including viewpoint variations, illumination changes, and occlusions. Finally, we outline future research directions and potential advancements in leveraging GANs for improved person re-identification performance. This paper serves as a comprehensive overview for researchers and practitioners interested in understanding the role of GANs in advancing the state-of-the-art in person Re-ID.
Self-supervised learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for learning representations from unlabeled data. In the context of graph data, this often involves designing pretext tasks that leverage inherent graph structure. This paper proposes a novel self-supervised graph representation learning approach based on bootstrapping. Our method learns graph embeddings by maximizing the agreement between representations of the same graph under different views. These views are generated through graph augmentations, such as node dropping, edge perturbation, and attribute masking. We introduce a bootstrapping objective that encourages consistency between the representations learned from these augmented views, thereby learning robust and generalizable graph embeddings. Through extensive experiments on a variety of graph classification and node classification tasks, we demonstrate that our approach achieves competitive or superior performance compared to existing self-supervised and supervised graph representation learning methods. Our results highlight the effectiveness of bootstrapping as a self-supervised strategy for capturing meaningful structural and attribute information from graphs.
Image super-resolution (SR) techniques aim to enhance the resolution of low-resolution images, potentially improving the performance of downstream vision tasks. This work investigates the extent to which SR benefits various vision applications beyond simple visual inspection. We explore the impact of applying SR as a pre-processing step for tasks such as object detection, semantic segmentation, and image classification. By evaluating the performance of these tasks on both low-resolution images and their SR-enhanced counterparts, we quantify the potential gains offered by SR. Our results reveal that the effectiveness of SR varies significantly depending on the specific vision task, the SR algorithm employed, and the degree of degradation in the original low-resolution images. We discuss the conditions under which SR proves beneficial, highlighting scenarios where it can effectively mitigate the negative effects of low resolution and lead to improved accuracy and robustness in downstream vision tasks. Furthermore, we analyze the limitations of SR, identifying instances where it fails to provide significant improvements or even introduces artifacts that hinder performance. This study provides valuable insights into the practical utility of SR as a pre-processing step for diverse vision applications, informing the design and deployment of robust and efficient image processing pipelines.
Time series classification models are increasingly used in critical applications, demanding explainability alongside accuracy. While traditional feature-based methods struggle to capture the complex temporal dependencies inherent in time series data, counterfactual explanations offer a promising alternative by identifying the minimal changes required to flip a model's prediction. In this paper, we propose a novel instance-based approach to generating counterfactual explanations for time series classification. Our method leverages the concept of finding the nearest "counterfactual" instance in the training data that belongs to a different class than the original instance. By identifying and analyzing these counterfactual instances, we provide interpretable explanations that highlight the specific temporal patterns and subsequences responsible for the initial classification. We introduce a similarity metric tailored for time series data that considers both shape and temporal alignment, enabling the discovery of meaningful counterfactual examples. We evaluate our approach on several benchmark time series datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in generating concise and intuitive counterfactual explanations that offer valuable insights into the model's decision-making process and facilitate trust and understanding.
Graph Contrastive Learning (GCL) has emerged as a powerful technique for learning node representations in a self-supervised manner. However, the performance of GCL heavily relies on the quality and diversity of the graph augmentations used to generate contrastive views. Existing augmentation strategies often employ fixed, hand-crafted rules that can be suboptimal or even detrimental for specific graphs. To address this limitation, we propose a novel adversarial graph augmentation framework that dynamically learns to generate challenging and informative graph augmentations for GCL. Our approach introduces an adversarial generator that perturbs the graph structure to maximize the contrastive loss, thereby forcing the encoder to learn more robust and discriminative representations. Simultaneously, a discriminator guides the generator to produce realistic and semantically consistent augmentations. We evaluate our method on a variety of benchmark datasets, demonstrating significant improvements in node classification and clustering tasks compared to state-of-the-art GCL approaches with traditional augmentation strategies. Our results highlight the benefits of adversarial learning in automatically discovering effective graph augmentations for enhancing the performance of GCL.
Tabular data remains a prevalent and challenging domain for machine learning. While deep learning models have achieved impressive results in other areas, their application to tabular data often suffers from high computational cost and complex architectures. We present a novel approach, Augmented Distillation, for creating fast, accurate, and simple models specifically tailored for tabular data. Our method leverages knowledge distillation from a powerful teacher model to train a lightweight student model. Crucially, we augment the distillation process with carefully designed data augmentations that expose the student to a broader range of synthetic samples, improving its generalization ability and robustness. This augmentation strategy, combined with a simplified student architecture, results in models that achieve comparable or superior accuracy to complex deep learning models, while offering significant improvements in inference speed and model size. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Augmented Distillation on a diverse set of tabular datasets, showcasing its ability to produce high-performing, resource-efficient models suitable for real-world deployment.
This paper presents a novel, robust, and unsupervised deep learning framework for small area change detection in Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery. Existing change detection methods often struggle with SAR's inherent speckle noise and the limited availability of labeled data, particularly when dealing with small area changes. Our proposed approach leverages a deep convolutional autoencoder network trained on the temporal difference of SAR images to learn robust feature representations that are invariant to speckle noise and illumination variations. We introduce a novel loss function incorporating both reconstruction error and a spatial regularization term to enhance the detection of subtle changes while suppressing false alarms. Furthermore, we employ a change magnitude map derived from the learned features to identify and delineate changed areas without relying on any prior training data or manual thresholding. The robustness and effectiveness of the proposed method are demonstrated through extensive experiments on real SAR datasets with varying geographical landscapes and diverse change types, showcasing its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art unsupervised change detection techniques in terms of accuracy and noise resilience, particularly for small area change detection.
## RL-NCS: Reinforcement Learning Based Data-Driven Approach for Nonuniform Compressed Sensing

This paper introduces RL-NCS, a novel data-driven framework for nonuniform compressed sensing (NCS) leveraging reinforcement learning (RL). Traditional NCS methods often rely on predefined sampling patterns, which may not be optimal for specific signal classes. RL-NCS addresses this limitation by learning an adaptive sampling strategy tailored to the underlying data distribution. We formulate the NCS problem as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) where the agent learns to select the optimal subset of samples by interacting with a training dataset. The reward function is designed to encourage accurate signal reconstruction with minimal samples. We demonstrate that RL-NCS outperforms existing NCS methods, including both uniform and heuristic-based nonuniform sampling techniques, in terms of reconstruction accuracy and sample efficiency. The results highlight the potential of RL to learn optimal sampling strategies in data-driven NCS, paving the way for improved performance in applications such as image and signal acquisition, medical imaging, and sensor networks.
Tree ensembles, such as Random Forests and Gradient Boosting Machines, are powerful predictive models but often suffer from a lack of interpretability. This paper introduces "Tree Space Prototypes," a novel approach to enhance the interpretability of tree ensembles by identifying representative prototypes within the high-dimensional space defined by the ensemble's decision trees. Instead of focusing on individual tree structures or feature importance, we aim to distill the ensemble's knowledge into a smaller set of instances that exemplify its core decision-making process. These prototypes are selected based on their proximity to the cluster centroids in the tree space, where instances are represented by their path through the ensemble. We demonstrate how these prototypes can be used to understand the ensemble's predictions, identify key decision boundaries, and provide a simplified, more human-understandable summary of the model's behavior. We evaluate the effectiveness of Tree Space Prototypes on various datasets, showing that they can provide valuable insights into the model's logic without significantly sacrificing predictive accuracy. Our method offers a complementary perspective to existing interpretability techniques, focusing on instance-level explanations and highlighting the collective behavior of the ensemble.
Efficiently managing large-scale, heterogeneous fleets presents significant challenges in logistics, transportation, and robotics. Traditional optimization methods often struggle with the complexity and dynamic nature of these systems. This paper proposes a novel dynamic dispatching framework leveraging multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (MADRL) to address these challenges. Our approach models each vehicle in the heterogeneous fleet as an independent agent, enabling decentralized decision-making and improved scalability. We design a reward function that incentivizes efficient task completion, reduced idle time, and balanced workload across the fleet, considering the unique capabilities and constraints of each vehicle type. We evaluate our framework in a simulated environment with a diverse fleet and dynamic task requests, demonstrating its superior performance compared to benchmark dispatching strategies. Specifically, our MADRL approach achieves significant improvements in task completion rate, average delivery time, and fleet utilization, highlighting its potential for real-world deployment in large-scale heterogeneous fleet management. The results demonstrate the efficacy of MADRL in addressing the complexity and dynamism inherent in dynamic dispatching problems, paving the way for more efficient and adaptive fleet management solutions.
This paper proposes a novel framework for computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) using longitudinal images, leveraging a multi-task dictionary learning based convolutional neural network (MTDL-CNN).  Longitudinal imaging provides valuable temporal information about disease progression, but effectively integrating this information into a CAD system remains challenging. Our approach addresses this challenge by first employing multi-task dictionary learning to extract shared and task-specific features from longitudinal image sequences, capturing both common anatomical structures and disease-specific temporal patterns. These learned dictionaries are then used to initialize and guide the training of a CNN architecture. By learning multiple diagnostic tasks simultaneously (e.g., disease classification and staging), the MTDL-CNN leverages shared representations and improves generalization performance, particularly in the presence of limited longitudinal data. Experimental results on [Mention Dataset Here, e.g., a longitudinal Alzheimer's disease dataset] demonstrate that the proposed MTDL-CNN outperforms existing methods, achieving higher accuracy in disease diagnosis and improved prediction of disease progression.  The results highlight the effectiveness of combining dictionary learning with CNNs for leveraging longitudinal imaging data in CAD applications.
This abstract summarizes the journey of leveraging deep learning on attributed graphs, focusing on the critical transition between graph structure, node/edge attributes, and learned embeddings. Attributed graphs, rich with both structural and feature information, offer a powerful representation for complex systems. This work explores the landscape of deep learning techniques designed to process these graphs, specifically highlighting methods that generate node or graph embeddings. We examine various approaches, including graph convolutional networks (GCNs), graph attention networks (GATs), and graph autoencoders, analyzing their effectiveness in capturing graph topology and attribute information within low-dimensional vector spaces. Furthermore, we delve into the critical "back" journey – how these learned embeddings are utilized for downstream tasks such as node classification, link prediction, graph clustering, and even graph reconstruction. Finally, we discuss the challenges and future directions in this rapidly evolving field, emphasizing the need for more robust, scalable, and interpretable deep learning models capable of effectively harnessing the full potential of attributed graph data.
## Ripple Walk Training: A Subgraph-based training framework for Large and Deep Graph Neural Network

Training large and deep Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) on massive graphs poses significant challenges due to memory limitations and the vanishing gradient problem. To address these issues, we propose Ripple Walk Training (RWT), a novel subgraph-based training framework that leverages the inherent locality of graph data. RWT iteratively samples node-centric subgraphs by performing a "ripple walk" outwards from a target node, capturing relevant structural information within a limited radius. This approach reduces memory footprint by processing smaller subgraphs instead of the entire graph. Furthermore, RWT mitigates the vanishing gradient problem by strategically sampling shorter, more focused paths during the ripple walk, ensuring effective gradient propagation through deep GNN layers. We empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of RWT on several benchmark datasets, showing significant improvements in training efficiency and generalization performance compared to existing subgraph sampling techniques, especially for large and deep GNN architectures. Our results highlight the potential of RWT as a scalable and effective training framework for handling complex graph learning tasks.
Understanding the dynamics of gradient-based optimization in non-convex high-dimensional landscapes is crucial for the success of modern machine learning. This work investigates the gradient-flow dynamics in a spiked matrix-tensor model, a canonical setting for studying the interplay between signal and noise in high-dimensional inference. The results offer a theoretical framework for understanding the limitations and potential pitfalls of gradient-based methods in high-dimensional non-convex problems.

Time series forecasting is a critical task across various domains. While traditional methods often struggle with complex temporal dependencies and scalability, recent transformer-based models have shown promising results. However, many existing transformer models rely on autoregressive decoding, which can be computationally expensive and limit parallelization. This paper introduces NAST, a novel **N**on-**A**utoregressive **S**patial-**T**emporal Transformer for time series forecasting. NAST leverages a spatial-temporal attention mechanism to capture intricate relationships between different time steps and series without relying on sequential generation. This non-autoregressive approach enables parallel decoding, significantly improving inference speed. We design a dedicated spatial attention module to learn correlations among different series and a temporal attention module to capture long-range temporal dependencies. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that NAST achieves competitive or superior forecasting accuracy compared to state-of-the-art autoregressive and non-autoregressive methods, while offering substantial speedups in inference time, making it a practical and efficient solution for time series forecasting.
Marked Temporal Point Processes (MTPPs) are powerful tools for modeling event sequences with associated time stamps and marks, finding applications in diverse fields like healthcare, finance, and social media. However, training these models often requires a substantial amount of labeled data, which can be expensive and time-consuming to acquire. This paper explores the application of semi-supervised learning techniques to MTPPs, aiming to leverage both labeled and unlabeled event sequences to improve model performance, particularly in scenarios with limited labeled data. We investigate various semi-supervised learning strategies, including consistency regularization, pseudo-labeling, and generative approaches tailored to the temporal and marked nature of point processes. We demonstrate that these techniques can effectively utilize unlabeled data to enhance the accuracy and robustness of MTPP models, leading to improved prediction of future events and their associated marks. Experimental results on benchmark datasets showcase the effectiveness of our proposed semi-supervised learning framework for MTPPs, highlighting its potential to significantly reduce the reliance on labeled data in real-world applications.
This paper proposes a novel approach for trademark retrieval based on learning regional attention over multi-resolution deep convolutional features. Existing methods often rely on global feature representations, which may overlook crucial local details and spatial relationships that are vital for distinguishing trademarks. To address this, we leverage a deep convolutional neural network to extract multi-resolution feature maps, capturing both fine-grained details and broader contextual information. Then, we introduce a regional attention mechanism that learns to selectively attend to discriminative regions within each feature map. This attention mechanism allows the model to focus on the most relevant parts of the trademark image, suppressing irrelevant background noise and emphasizing key visual elements. By integrating regional attention with multi-resolution features, our method achieves superior performance in trademark retrieval, demonstrated through extensive experiments on a large-scale trademark dataset. The results show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods, highlighting the effectiveness of learning regional attention over multi-resolution features for capturing nuanced visual characteristics in trademark images.
Structure learning, the process of discovering causal relationships and dependencies within data, is a fundamental challenge in various fields. Traditional structure learning algorithms often struggle with high-dimensional data and can be computationally expensive. This paper introduces a novel approach to structure learning called "Structure Learning Using Forced Pruning." Our method iteratively refines a candidate structure by aggressively pruning edges deemed less significant according to a chosen scoring function. This "forced pruning" strategy, coupled with a mechanism to recover potentially pruned beneficial edges, allows for efficient exploration of the search space. We demonstrate that forced pruning can significantly reduce computational complexity while maintaining or even improving accuracy compared to existing structure learning algorithms. Empirical evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in discovering accurate and parsimonious structures, highlighting its potential for applications in areas such as causal inference, network analysis, and knowledge discovery.
This paper investigates the use of binary matrices for compressed sensing (CS), focusing on achieving near-optimal sampling complexity. While random matrices are commonly employed in CS, binary matrices offer advantages in terms of storage and computational efficiency. We present a construction of binary matrices with dimensions approaching the theoretical limits for successful sparse signal recovery.  Specifically, we explore the trade-off between matrix size and reconstruction performance, analyzing the conditions under which these matrices satisfy the Restricted Isometry Property (RIP) or similar sufficient conditions for accurate recovery. We provide theoretical analysis and numerical simulations demonstrating the performance of the proposed binary matrix construction compared to other popular CS matrix ensembles, highlighting its potential for applications where resource constraints are significant.  The results demonstrate that carefully designed binary matrices can achieve near-optimal performance in CS, making them a viable and efficient alternative to dense random matrices.
Deep neural networks often struggle to effectively leverage domain-specific knowledge, leading to suboptimal performance and limited interpretability. This paper introduces a novel approach, "Choose Your Neuron" (CYN), which incorporates domain knowledge by explicitly prioritizing the contribution of individual neurons during training. CYN achieves this by assigning neuron-importance scores based on expert understanding of their potential relevance to specific tasks or features. These scores are integrated into the loss function, encouraging the network to learn representations where important neurons are more influential. We demonstrate the effectiveness of CYN on [mention a specific domain, e.g., medical image analysis, financial time series prediction] tasks, showing that incorporating domain knowledge through neuron-importance leads to improved accuracy, faster convergence, and more interpretable network representations compared to standard training methods. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of different neuron-importance assignments, highlighting the potential of CYN to guide network behavior and unlock valuable insights into the learned representations.
3D object detection is a critical task for autonomous driving and robotics. Existing methods often rely solely on LiDAR point clouds, which can be susceptible to performance degradation in adverse weather conditions or sparse environments. This paper introduces MVX-Net, a novel multimodal 3D object detection network that effectively fuses information from LiDAR point clouds and RGB images. MVX-Net extends the VoxelNet architecture by incorporating a parallel image feature extraction branch. The extracted image features are then projected onto the 3D voxel grid, allowing for voxel-level feature fusion. This fusion strategy leverages the complementary strengths of both modalities: the geometric precision of LiDAR and the semantic richness of RGB images. We evaluate MVX-Net on the KITTI 3D object detection benchmark, demonstrating significant performance improvements over state-of-the-art LiDAR-only methods, particularly for challenging object categories and long-range detection. The results highlight the effectiveness of our multimodal fusion approach for robust and accurate 3D object detection.
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Transformers have demonstrated remarkable performance on various computer vision tasks. However, their robustness to subtle input variations remains a critical concern. This work investigates the vulnerability of both CNNs and Transformers to small, in-distribution changes in 3D perspective and lighting conditions. We demonstrate that even minor alterations to these factors, well within the range of naturally occurring variations, can significantly degrade the performance of both architectures. Through controlled experiments, we highlight the sensitivity of these models to these seemingly innocuous perturbations, suggesting a potential lack of true understanding of 3D scene geometry and illumination. Our findings underscore the need for developing more robust and invariant vision models capable of generalizing across a wider range of realistic environments and viewpoints, even when faced with subtle changes in perspective and lighting.
Accurate optical flow estimation in real-world scenarios remains challenging due to the presence of occlusions, which significantly degrade performance. This paper introduces OAS-Net, an Occlusion Aware Sampling Network, designed to explicitly address this issue. OAS-Net leverages a novel sampling strategy guided by an occlusion probability map, allowing the network to focus on reliable regions while mitigating the influence of occluded areas. Specifically, the network learns to predict an occlusion map and utilizes this map to adaptively sample correspondence candidates during the correlation computation. By prioritizing samples from non-occluded regions, OAS-Net reduces ambiguity and improves the accuracy of the estimated optical flow. We demonstrate the effectiveness of OAS-Net on several challenging benchmark datasets, including Sintel and KITTI, achieving state-of-the-art performance, particularly in regions affected by occlusions. The results highlight the importance of occlusion awareness in robust optical flow estimation and validate the efficacy of our proposed sampling approach.
JavaScript, a dynamically typed language, suffers from the lack of static type information, leading to runtime errors and hindering code maintainability and optimization. This paper explores the application of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for inferring JavaScript types. We represent JavaScript code as a graph structure, capturing semantic relationships between variables, functions, and operators. Nodes in the graph represent program entities, and edges encode data flow, control flow, and other relevant dependencies. We then train a GNN model to predict the type of each node based on the graph structure and node features. Our approach leverages the inherent relational reasoning capabilities of GNNs to effectively propagate type information across the code. We evaluate our model on a benchmark dataset of JavaScript code and demonstrate its effectiveness in accurately inferring types, achieving competitive results compared to existing type inference techniques. This work provides a novel approach to static analysis for dynamically typed languages and opens avenues for improved code understanding, error detection, and optimization in JavaScript.

Semantic segmentation, a crucial task in computer vision, requires understanding both low-level image features and high-level contextual information. While Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable success in capturing low-level details, effectively incorporating high-level priors remains a challenge. This paper proposes a novel approach to explicitly learn high-level priors using CNNs for improved semantic segmentation. We introduce a dedicated module designed to extract and represent abstract semantic knowledge from the input image. This module, integrated within a standard segmentation architecture, learns to predict a high-level prior map that encodes global contextual relationships and object distributions. This learned prior is then fused with the feature maps extracted by the main segmentation network, guiding the segmentation process with valuable contextual cues. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our proposed method effectively captures and utilizes high-level priors, leading to significant performance improvements compared to state-of-the-art segmentation networks. The learned prior maps also provide valuable insights into the network's reasoning process and its understanding of scene context.
HoHoNet proposes a novel approach to holistic understanding of 360° indoor scenes by leveraging latent horizontal features. Existing methods often struggle with the unique challenges of panoramic imagery, including significant distortion and the lack of a clear global perspective. Our method introduces a learnable module that extracts and encodes horizontal features, effectively capturing the circular structure and contextual relationships inherent in 360° indoor environments. These latent horizontal features are then integrated into a multi-task learning framework, enabling simultaneous prediction of semantic segmentation, room layout estimation, and object detection. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, HoHoNet demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods, showcasing its effectiveness in capturing holistic indoor scene understanding from 360° imagery. The proposed approach offers a robust and efficient solution for applications such as virtual reality, robotics, and indoor navigation.
This research explores the application of reinforcement learning (RL) to the challenging problem of molecular design, leveraging the accuracy of quantum mechanical (QM) calculations. Traditional molecular design methods often rely on computationally expensive QM calculations for evaluating molecular properties. This work proposes a novel RL framework where an agent iteratively designs novel molecules, guided by rewards derived from QM-calculated properties such as binding affinity, stability, or desired electronic characteristics. By training the RL agent to navigate the vast chemical space, we aim to discover novel molecules with targeted properties while minimizing the reliance on exhaustive QM simulations. The agent learns to predict the impact of structural modifications on molecular properties, effectively amortizing the cost of QM calculations over multiple design iterations. This approach holds promise for accelerating the discovery of new materials and drug candidates with tailored functionalities, offering a powerful alternative to traditional computational design workflows. The development of robust and reliable autonomous driving systems relies heavily on large-scale, diverse, and accurately annotated datasets.  This paper introduces ONCE (One Million Scenes for Autonomous Driving), a novel dataset designed to address limitations in existing datasets.  ONCE comprises one million scenes, each spanning 3 seconds, collected using a sensor suite including LiDAR, cameras, and GPS/IMU.  A key feature of ONCE is its focus on long-range perception, capturing objects and scenes at distances relevant for safe autonomous navigation.  The dataset provides 3D bounding box annotations for common objects, such as vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists, enabling training and evaluation of object detection, tracking, and scene understanding algorithms.  Furthermore, we present comprehensive statistics and benchmarks based on state-of-the-art algorithms, highlighting the challenges and opportunities presented by the scale and diversity of the ONCE dataset for advancing autonomous driving research.  The ONCE dataset is publicly available to facilitate research and development in the field.
Bar charts are a ubiquitous visual representation of data, yet extracting the underlying data values from these charts, especially in the absence of accompanying data files, can be a time-consuming and error-prone task. This paper explores the feasibility of reverse-engineering bar charts using neural networks. We propose a novel approach leveraging convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to automatically identify and extract data values from bar chart images. Our model is trained to detect bars, segment them from the background, and estimate their heights, which are then translated into numerical values based on the chart's axis scales. We investigate different CNN architectures and training strategies to optimize performance, focusing on robustness to variations in chart style, color, and noise. Experimental results on a diverse dataset of synthetically generated and real-world bar charts demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving high accuracy in recovering the original data values. This work contributes to automating data extraction from visual representations and opens up possibilities for enhancing data accessibility and analysis.
Understanding human interaction within a 3D spatial-temporal context is crucial for egocentric perception. This paper proposes a novel approach for learning 3D-aware egocentric spatial-temporal interaction patterns using Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs). We leverage egocentric videos and associated 3D scene reconstructions to construct a dynamic graph representing the spatial relationships between the ego-agent, interacting humans, and surrounding objects over time. Our GCN-based model then learns to aggregate features from these interacting entities, effectively capturing the evolution of their spatial configurations and enabling the prediction of interaction outcomes. By explicitly incorporating 3D information, our method overcomes limitations of 2D image-based approaches, providing a more robust and interpretable representation of interactions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a challenging egocentric interaction prediction task, showing significant improvements over existing methods and highlighting the importance of 3D spatial-temporal reasoning for understanding human behavior in complex environments.
Skeleton-based human action recognition is a challenging task that requires effectively modeling both spatial dependencies between joints and temporal dynamics of movements. While Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have shown promise in capturing spatial relationships, incorporating temporal information and adapting to varying importance of different temporal frames remains a challenge. This paper proposes a Temporal Attention-Augmented Graph Convolutional Network (TA-GCN) for efficient skeleton-based human action recognition. Our approach leverages GCNs to learn spatial features and introduces a novel temporal attention mechanism that dynamically weights the contribution of each frame to the overall action representation. This attention mechanism allows the network to focus on the most salient temporal segments, improving robustness to noise and irrelevant frames. We demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of TA-GCN through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, achieving competitive performance with significantly fewer parameters compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. The results highlight the benefits of incorporating temporal attention for efficient and accurate skeleton-based action recognition.
This paper explores the use of semantic text encoding for improved text classification, drawing an analogy to how humans perceive and differentiate objects based on their "color" (semantic features). We propose a novel approach to learn enriched semantic representations of text that capture nuanced meaning beyond simple word embeddings. Our method focuses on learning a text encoder that effectively maps input text to a high-dimensional semantic space where different classes are well-separated. Our results highlight the importance of learning "color-aware" semantic text encodings for achieving robust and accurate text classification.
This paper presents a lightweight implementation of Mask R-CNN specifically designed for object detection and segmentation in long-range wireless power transfer (WPT) systems. Accurate and efficient object recognition is crucial for optimizing beam steering and power delivery in such systems, especially when dealing with complex and dynamic environments. Traditional Mask R-CNN models, while accurate, are computationally expensive and unsuitable for resource-constrained embedded platforms often employed in WPT applications. To address this, we propose a modified architecture that incorporates techniques such as depthwise separable convolutions, channel pruning, and knowledge distillation to significantly reduce the model's size and computational complexity without sacrificing accuracy. We evaluate the performance of our lightweight Mask R-CNN on a custom dataset consisting of images captured from a simulated long-range WPT environment. The results demonstrate that our approach achieves a substantial reduction in model parameters and inference time compared to the standard Mask R-CNN, while maintaining acceptable levels of object detection and segmentation accuracy, making it a viable solution for real-time object recognition and power delivery optimization in long-range WPT systems.
Adaptive object detection aims to transfer knowledge from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain, often plagued by distribution shifts. Existing methods typically assume a similar distribution between the source and target domains, which is often unrealistic. In this paper, we address the challenge of **Strong-Weak Distribution Alignment** in adaptive object detection, where the target domain exhibits a significantly weaker or more impoverished distribution compared to the source domain. We propose a novel framework that explicitly models and aligns these differing distributions. Our approach leverages a combination of [mention key techniques, e.g., adversarial feature alignment, self-training with confidence-aware pseudo-labeling, or contrastive learning]. By focusing on aligning the strong and weak distributions, we effectively bridge the domain gap and improve the robustness and generalization ability of the detector in the target domain. Extensive experiments on [mention relevant datasets, e.g., cross-domain object detection benchmarks like Cityscapes to Foggy Cityscapes] demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method, achieving significant performance gains over state-of-the-art domain adaptation techniques, particularly in scenarios with substantial distribution disparities.
Incremental few-shot learning presents a significant challenge, requiring models to rapidly adapt to new classes with limited data while mitigating catastrophic forgetting of previously learned knowledge. This paper introduces Attention Attractor Networks (AANs), a novel approach designed to address this challenge. AANs leverage a memory-augmented architecture where learned representations are attracted towards class-specific "attractors" in a feature space. These attractors are dynamically updated during each incremental learning step, allowing for efficient adaptation to new classes with only a few examples. Furthermore, an attention mechanism focuses on the most relevant features for each class, improving discriminative power and reducing interference between old and new knowledge. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that AANs achieve state-of-the-art performance in incremental few-shot learning scenarios, outperforming existing methods in terms of accuracy, knowledge retention, and adaptation speed. The results highlight the effectiveness of attractor-based learning and attention mechanisms in enabling robust and efficient incremental learning from limited data.
This paper introduces a novel attention-based aggregation function designed to effectively combine visual and linguistic information. Leveraging the strengths of both modalities, our approach learns to dynamically attend to relevant features from each domain before fusing them into a unified representation. Unlike traditional concatenation or element-wise operations, our aggregation function utilizes a learned attention mechanism to weigh the contribution of each visual and linguistic feature based on their relevance to the overall context. Our results highlight the importance of adaptive feature weighting for effective multi-modal fusion and offer a promising direction for future research in vision and language understanding.
Self-supervised monocular depth estimation has shown significant promise for learning depth from unlabeled video sequences. However, performance often degrades in challenging lighting conditions, particularly during dawn and dusk, leading to inconsistent and inaccurate depth predictions. This paper proposes a novel approach to improve depth estimation accuracy across all day images using domain separation within a self-supervised framework. We leverage the observation that images captured during different times of day exhibit distinct statistical characteristics. Our method explicitly separates the image domain into day and non-day categories, utilizing a domain classifier to guide the learning process. We then train separate depth estimation networks, each specialized for its respective domain, enabling them to learn domain-specific features and mitigate the adverse effects of varying illumination. A domain adaptation module ensures consistency between the domains and facilitates robust depth prediction across all times of day. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly improves depth estimation accuracy, especially in challenging low-light conditions, outperforming existing state-of-the-art self-supervised methods and achieving more consistent and reliable depth maps for all-day image sequences.
Image-to-image translation aims to transform an input image from one domain to another while preserving its underlying structure. Existing methods often struggle with complex transformations and may lack fine-grained control over the generated output. This paper proposes a novel **Generative Transition Mechanism to Image-to-Image Translation via Encoded Transformation (GTM-EIT)**.  Our approach introduces a learnable transformation encoder that maps the input image into a latent transformation code, representing the desired domain shift. This encoded transformation is then fed into a generative network, guiding the image generation process.  We hypothesize that encoding the transformation explicitly allows for more nuanced control over the translation process and facilitates the generation of higher-quality and more diverse outputs.  Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that GTM-EIT achieves state-of-the-art performance in image quality, fidelity, and diversity, outperforming existing methods, particularly in scenarios involving complex and subtle transformations. The proposed mechanism provides a powerful and flexible framework for image-to-image translation, enabling fine-grained control and superior generation capabilities.
## SVT-Net: Super Light-Weight Sparse Voxel Transformer for Large Scale Place Recognition

Large-scale place recognition, the task of identifying previously visited locations from sensor data, remains a challenging problem due to the computational demands of processing large point clouds and the difficulty of achieving robust viewpoint invariance. This paper introduces SVT-Net, a **S**uper **V**oxel **T**ransformer **Net**work, a novel and highly efficient architecture designed specifically for large-scale place recognition using sparse voxel representations of 3D point clouds. SVT-Net leverages a lightweight voxelization scheme to minimize memory footprint and computational overhead. Crucially, it employs a transformer-based architecture to effectively capture long-range dependencies between voxels, enabling robust viewpoint invariance and accurate place recognition even in the presence of significant perceptual changes. We propose a novel sparse attention mechanism tailored for voxel-based data, further reducing computational complexity and improving efficiency. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that SVT-Net achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of both accuracy and speed, outperforming existing methods while requiring significantly less memory and computational resources. This makes SVT-Net a promising solution for real-time place recognition in resource-constrained environments.
Accurate and efficient medical image segmentation is crucial for various clinical applications, including diagnosis, treatment planning, and disease monitoring. Deep learning models have demonstrated remarkable performance in this area, but often struggle with complex anatomical structures and varying image qualities. This paper proposes a novel two-layer ensemble approach to improve the robustness and accuracy of medical image segmentation. The first layer consists of multiple diverse deep learning models, each trained on the same dataset with different architectures and/or training parameters. The outputs of these models are then fed into a second layer, which employs a learned fusion strategy to combine the individual segmentations into a final, refined segmentation map. We evaluate our approach on [mention specific medical imaging modality and anatomical structure, e.g., CT scans of the lungs] and demonstrate that the proposed two-layer ensemble outperforms individual deep learning models and traditional ensemble methods, achieving significant improvements in segmentation accuracy, robustness, and generalization ability. The results suggest that this approach offers a promising solution for enhancing the performance of medical image segmentation systems.
## Abstract: Structural Compression of Convolutional Neural Networks

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable success in various computer vision tasks, but their high computational cost and memory footprint often hinder deployment on resource-constrained devices. Structural compression techniques offer a promising solution by directly manipulating the network architecture to reduce its complexity. This abstract explores the landscape of structural compression methods for CNNs, focusing on approaches that prune entire filters, channels, or layers, thereby leading to hardware-friendly acceleration. We categorize these techniques based on their pruning granularity and the strategies employed for identifying and removing redundant structures. Furthermore, we discuss the impact of different pruning criteria, such as weight magnitude, activation statistics, and gradient information, on model performance and recovery. Finally, we highlight the challenges and future directions in structural compression, including the development of more efficient search algorithms, automated architecture design for compressed models, and hardware-aware compression strategies to maximize real-world performance gains.
This paper presents a novel two-stream appearance transfer network for high-quality person image generation. Our approach addresses the challenging problem of transferring the appearance (e.g., clothing, texture) from a source person image onto a target person image while preserving the target's pose and identity. The proposed network leverages a two-stream architecture: a **structure stream** that focuses on preserving the target's structural information, including pose and shape, and an **appearance stream** that concentrates on transferring the source's appearance details. These two streams operate in parallel, allowing for independent feature extraction and processing.  Specifically, the structure stream encodes the target's pose and shape information using a pose-guided deformation module.  The appearance stream extracts appearance features from the source image, focusing on clothing and texture information.  Finally, a fusion module effectively combines the features from both streams to generate a realistic person image with the target's pose and the source's appearance. Experimental results on publicly available datasets demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in terms of visual quality, identity preservation, and appearance transfer accuracy. This highlights the effectiveness of our two-stream architecture for disentangling and recombining structural and appearance information in person image generation.
Electronic Health Records (EHRs) often contain multivariate time series data with pervasive missing values. While traditional imputation methods may introduce bias, assuming Missing At Random (MAR) can be leveraged to improve model performance. This paper introduces a novel kernel function designed to exploit informative missingness patterns within multivariate time series derived from EHR data. Our kernel explicitly incorporates the presence and absence of data points across different features and time steps, allowing the model to learn relationships between observed values and missingness indicators. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed kernel in a kernel-based machine learning framework for [mention specific application, e.g., predicting disease progression, classifying patient subtypes]. Empirical results on real-world EHR datasets show that our kernel significantly outperforms traditional kernels and imputation-based approaches, highlighting the value of explicitly modeling informative missingness in multivariate time series analysis. We believe this approach provides a valuable tool for researchers and clinicians seeking to extract meaningful insights from incomplete EHR data.
Resource allocation problems are ubiquitous in various domains, often requiring adaptive and efficient solutions. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a promising approach, but its application is hindered by the curse of dimensionality and the need for extensive training for each specific instance. This paper introduces a novel framework for efficient RL in resource allocation by leveraging **permutation invariant multi-task learning**. We propose training a single RL agent on a diverse set of resource allocation instances, ensuring the agent's policy is invariant to the ordering of resources and agents. This allows for effective knowledge transfer across different problem instances, significantly accelerating learning and improving generalization performance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on benchmark resource allocation problems, showing that it achieves superior performance compared to traditional RL methods and other transfer learning techniques, particularly in scenarios with limited training data and varying problem sizes. Our results highlight the potential of permutation invariant multi-task learning to significantly improve the practicality of RL for solving complex resource allocation problems.
Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are powerful but often opaque, making it challenging to understand which input features contribute most to their predictions. Existing attribution methods often highlight irrelevant features, hindering the interpretability and reliability of DNNs. This paper introduces "Attribution Mask," a novel approach for filtering out irrelevant features by recursively focusing attention on the most influential regions of the input. Attribution Mask iteratively refines an attention mask that highlights relevant features based on the attribution scores generated in each iteration. This recursive process allows the network to progressively ignore less important information, leading to more focused and interpretable attribution maps. Experiments on image classification tasks demonstrate that Attribution Mask effectively filters out irrelevant features compared to existing attribution methods, resulting in improved attribution accuracy, better visual explanations, and enhanced robustness against adversarial attacks. The proposed method provides a more targeted and reliable approach to understanding the decision-making process of DNNs.
Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) offers a powerful non-invasive method for studying brain functional connectivity. However, effectively capturing the complex spatio-temporal dynamics within rs-fMRI data remains a challenge. This paper proposes a novel approach using Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolution (ST-GCN) for analyzing rs-fMRI data. We construct a graph representation of the brain, where nodes represent brain regions and edges represent functional connections derived from rs-fMRI time series. The ST-GCN then leverages graph convolutional layers to model spatial dependencies between brain regions, while simultaneously employing temporal convolutional layers to capture the temporal evolution of functional connectivity patterns. This framework allows for learning both static and dynamic features within the brain network. We evaluate the performance of our proposed ST-GCN on a benchmark dataset for identifying subjects with different cognitive states. Our results demonstrate that the ST-GCN outperforms traditional methods and other graph-based approaches, highlighting its effectiveness in capturing the intricate spatio-temporal relationships within rs-fMRI data and its potential for improving the accuracy of brain state decoding and other rs-fMRI analysis tasks.
This study explores the potential of machine learning and sentiment analysis to predict Airbnb listing prices. We leverage a comprehensive dataset of Airbnb listings, incorporating traditional features like location, property type, amenities, and occupancy, alongside novel sentiment-based features extracted from listing descriptions and reviews. We employ various machine learning models, including linear regression, random forest, and gradient boosting, to predict prices. Furthermore, we utilize natural language processing techniques to analyze textual data, quantifying sentiment expressed in reviews and descriptions. Our results demonstrate that the inclusion of sentiment features significantly improves the accuracy of price prediction models compared to models relying solely on traditional features. This highlights the importance of considering subjective perceptions and emotional content in understanding and predicting Airbnb pricing dynamics. This research provides valuable insights for both Airbnb hosts seeking to optimize their pricing strategies and potential guests seeking to understand the factors influencing listing prices.
This paper introduces a novel deep generative model for sparse graphs, leveraging text-based learning and augmentation within a Generative Examination Network (GEN) framework. Generating realistic and diverse sparse graphs remains a challenge due to their complex structural dependencies and limited connectivity. Our approach tackles this by encoding graph substructures into textual descriptions, enabling the use of powerful pre-trained language models for learning graph generation rules. The GEN architecture further enhances the generation process by incorporating an examination network that evaluates the generated graphs based on predefined graph properties and provides feedback for refinement. To address the data scarcity often encountered in graph generation tasks, we propose a novel augmentation strategy that leverages the learned textual representations to generate new, plausible graph substructures. Experimental results on various benchmark datasets demonstrate that our model outperforms existing graph generation methods, particularly in generating sparse graphs with high fidelity and diversity. The incorporation of text-based learning and augmentation within the GEN framework offers a promising avenue for advancing the field of deep generative models for graphs.
Deep neural networks have demonstrated remarkable success in various tasks, yet their performance can be significantly affected by subtle image distortions and variations. Traditional loss functions often focus on pixel-wise differences, neglecting the crucial structural information that the human visual system relies on. To address this limitation, we introduce SSIMLayer, a novel layer that integrates the Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) directly into the network architecture. By leveraging a differentiable approximation of SSIM, SSIMLayer captures nonlinear structural similarities between feature maps, promoting the learning of more robust and perceptually relevant deep representations. We demonstrate that incorporating SSIMLayer into existing network architectures improves performance on image classification and image quality assessment tasks, particularly under conditions of image degradation and adversarial attacks. Our results highlight the effectiveness of SSIMLayer in guiding deep networks to learn representations that are less sensitive to irrelevant variations and more aligned with human visual perception, leading to improved generalization and robustness.
The wide-minima density hypothesis posits that neural networks converging to wider minima in the loss landscape exhibit better generalization performance. This work explores the connection between this hypothesis and the learning rate schedule used during training. We propose that a specific learning rate schedule, termed the "Explore-Exploit" schedule, can effectively guide the optimization process towards regions of the loss landscape characterized by higher wide-minima density. This schedule consists of an initial "exploration" phase with a relatively high learning rate, promoting exploration of the loss landscape and escape from sharp, local minima. This is followed by an "exploitation" phase with a decaying learning rate, encouraging convergence to a wider minimum within the identified region. We present empirical evidence on standard benchmark datasets demonstrating that the Explore-Exploit learning rate schedule consistently leads to improved generalization performance compared to traditional decaying schedules, suggesting its efficacy in navigating the loss landscape towards regions with higher wide-minima density. This work provides a practical approach to leveraging the wide-minima density hypothesis for training more robust and generalizable neural networks.
Accurate segmentation of histopathology images is crucial for computer-aided diagnosis and prognosis. However, stain variations across different laboratories and staining protocols pose a significant challenge to the generalization ability of segmentation models. To address this issue, we propose a **Dual Adaptive Pyramid Network (DAPN)** for cross-stain histopathology image segmentation. DAPN leverages a dual pyramid architecture to capture multi-scale contextual information while adapting to stain variations. The first pyramid branch employs a standard convolutional pyramid to extract hierarchical features. The second adaptive pyramid branch incorporates learnable stain style normalization modules at each scale to mitigate stain discrepancies. These normalized features are then fused with the corresponding features from the first branch to provide stain-invariant and context-aware representations. Furthermore, we introduce a novel adaptive fusion strategy that dynamically weights the contributions of each scale based on the input image's stain characteristics. Extensive experiments on multiple cross-stain histopathology datasets demonstrate that DAPN significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of segmentation accuracy and generalization capability, highlighting its potential for robust and reliable histopathology image analysis.
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have emerged as a powerful tool for medical image segmentation, offering the potential for automated and accurate delineation of anatomical structures, lesions, and other regions of interest. This abstract presents an overview of CNN-based approaches for medical image segmentation, highlighting their advantages over traditional methods. We discuss various CNN architectures commonly employed, including U-Net, V-Net, and their variants, which are designed to effectively capture both local and global contextual information crucial for accurate segmentation. The abstract further explores challenges specific to medical image segmentation, such as limited labeled data, class imbalance, and high inter-subject variability. This abstract aims to provide a concise introduction to the applications and advancements of CNNs in the field of medical image segmentation.
## FiGLearn: Filter and Graph Learning using Optimal Transport

FiGLearn introduces a novel framework for simultaneously learning graph structure and filter parameters for graph signal processing. This approach leverages the power of Optimal Transport (OT) to bridge the gap between observed graph signals and a desired spectral representation. By formulating graph and filter learning as an OT problem, we minimize the transportation cost between the empirical distribution of the observed graph signal's spectrum and a target distribution reflecting desired filtering characteristics. This allows us to learn graph adjacency matrices that promote signals with the target spectral properties. Furthermore, FiGLearn optimizes the filter parameters directly within the OT framework, ensuring consistency between the learned graph and the designed filter. We demonstrate the effectiveness of FiGLearn on various synthetic and real-world datasets, showcasing its ability to learn meaningful graph structures and effective filters for tasks such as signal denoising and classification, outperforming existing methods that treat graph and filter learning separately. Our results highlight the potential of OT as a powerful tool for joint graph and filter learning in graph signal processing.
Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) is a crucial imaging modality for diagnosing retinal diseases. However, inter-frame eye movements during OCT volume acquisition often introduce distortions and artifacts, hindering accurate analysis. This paper proposes a novel unsupervised approach for correcting these distortions using a Dueling Deep Q-Network (DDQN). Our method learns a policy to sequentially align OCT B-scans within a volume without requiring ground truth alignment or manual intervention. The DDQN agent learns to apply transformations to each B-scan based on the observed differences between adjacent frames, aiming to maximize a reward function that reflects the structural consistency and smoothness of the aligned volume. The dueling architecture allows the agent to efficiently learn the value of different states and the advantage of different actions, leading to improved alignment performance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on real-world OCT volumes, showing significant reduction in artifacts and improved structural integrity compared to existing methods, paving the way for more reliable and automated retinal analysis.
Deep Active Learning (DAL) aims to efficiently train deep neural networks by strategically selecting the most informative data points for labeling. However, traditional DAL methods often rely on heuristics or uncertainty estimates that can be unreliable or computationally expensive. This paper introduces a novel approach, **Diffusion-based Deep Active Learning (D-DAL)**, which leverages diffusion models to address these limitations. D-DAL utilizes a pre-trained diffusion model to generate synthetic data points that are structurally similar to the unlabeled pool. By analyzing the diffusion process and the reconstruction error associated with these synthetic samples, we can identify regions in the data space where the model struggles to generalize. This information is then used to guide the active learning query strategy, prioritizing the selection of unlabeled samples that lie in these challenging regions. We demonstrate that D-DAL effectively explores the data distribution and improves the efficiency of DAL, achieving superior performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines on several benchmark datasets across different classification tasks. Our results highlight the potential of leveraging diffusion models for robust and efficient active learning in deep learning.
This paper presents an automatic system for accurately counting cells with elliptical shapes in microscopy images. This paper presents an adaptive fuzzy-based system designed to simulate, quantify, and compensate for color blindness. The system utilizes fuzzy logic to model the subjective perception of color deficiencies, allowing for a more nuanced and personalized representation of various colorblindness types and severities. The simulation module accurately replicates the visual experience of individuals with protanopia, deuteranopia, and tritanopia, offering a valuable tool for designers and developers to assess the accessibility of their products. Furthermore, the system incorporates a novel fuzzy-based quantification method to objectively measure the degree of color deficiency based on user input. Finally, an adaptive compensation algorithm leverages the fuzzy representation to selectively adjust colors in images and interfaces, enhancing visibility and improving the overall user experience for colorblind individuals without significantly altering the intended color palette for those with normal vision. The effectiveness of the system is demonstrated through simulations and user studies, highlighting its potential to improve accessibility and inclusivity across a wide range of applications.
This paper explores a linear model for the removal of rain streaks from single images. Rain streaks often appear as linear structures, and leveraging this characteristic, we propose a method that utilizes a linear model to represent and subsequently subtract these streaks from the input image. The model aims to differentiate between the underlying background scene and the additive rain component. We investigate different linear model formulations and optimization techniques to effectively estimate the rain streak parameters. Experimental results demonstrate the potential of this approach in mitigating the visual impact of rain streaks and improving the overall clarity of images captured in rainy conditions. The simplicity and computational efficiency of the linear model make it a promising solution for real-time rain removal applications.
Accurate uncertainty estimation is crucial for reliable decision-making in regression tasks. Traditional regression objectives like Mean Squared Error (MSE) primarily focus on minimizing the error between predicted and ground truth values, often neglecting the quality of the predicted uncertainty. This work introduces **Second-Moment Loss (SML), a novel regression objective explicitly designed to improve the calibration and sharpness of predicted uncertainties.** SML leverages the second moment of the predictive distribution to directly penalize discrepancies between the predicted variance and the actual variance of the target variable around its prediction. By incorporating this second-moment regularization, SML encourages models to produce more confident and accurate uncertainty estimates. We demonstrate, through experiments on a range of benchmark datasets and model architectures, that SML consistently outperforms MSE and other commonly used uncertainty-aware losses in terms of calibration metrics such as Negative Log-Likelihood and Calibration Error. Furthermore, SML leads to sharper predictive distributions, enabling more informed and risk-aware decision-making. Our results highlight the efficacy of SML as a simple yet powerful tool for enhancing the reliability of uncertainty quantification in regression tasks.
This paper explores the application of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for temporal super-resolution of radar rainfall products. High temporal resolution rainfall data is crucial for various applications, including flood forecasting, hydrological modeling, and nowcasting. However, radar rainfall data is often acquired at coarser temporal resolutions. We propose a CNN-based approach to enhance the temporal resolution of radar rainfall data by learning the complex spatiotemporal relationships inherent in rainfall patterns. Our model leverages a deep convolutional architecture to predict finer-grained rainfall intensities from a sequence of lower-resolution radar images. The performance of the proposed method is evaluated against traditional interpolation techniques and other deep learning-based approaches using a comprehensive dataset of radar rainfall observations. Experimental results demonstrate that the CNN-based temporal super-resolution method significantly improves the accuracy and realism of the reconstructed high-resolution rainfall data, offering potential benefits for a wide range of hydrological and meteorological applications.
This work introduces a novel approach for generating molecular graphs hierarchically, leveraging the concept of structural motifs as building blocks. Instead of generating molecules atom-by-atom or bond-by-bond, our method constructs molecules by sequentially assembling and connecting pre-defined or learned molecular fragments (motifs).
