This mapping allows us to leverage the theoretical understanding and training algorithms developed for RBMs, such as contrastive divergence, to analyze and potentially improve the performance of Hopfield networks. Conversely, the connection provides a deeper understanding of the energy landscape and dynamics of RBMs by drawing parallels to the well-studied properties of Hopfield networks. We discuss the implications of this mapping for understanding memory capacity, pattern completion, and error correction in both models. This work offers a unified perspective on these two foundational models and opens avenues for cross-fertilization of ideas and techniques.
Spectral clustering is a widely used technique for community detection in networks. While traditional spectral clustering methods often operate on adjacency matrices, their performance can be significantly affected by degree heterogeneity in the network. This paper investigates the performance of spectral clustering when applied to networks generated from the degree-corrected stochastic blockmodel (DCSBM) and leveraging a spherical coordinate representation of the data. Specifically, we analyze the theoretical limits of spectral clustering on eigenvectors derived from a normalized Laplacian matrix, where the data points are mapped to the unit hypersphere. We provide theoretical guarantees on the consistency of this approach under the DCSBM, demonstrating its ability to recover the underlying community structure even in the presence of degree heterogeneity. Furthermore, we explore the benefits of the spherical representation in mitigating the effects of degree correction and improving the robustness of spectral clustering. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the interplay between degree heterogeneity, data representation, and spectral clustering performance in network analysis.
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) often exhibit a texture bias, relying heavily on texture cues rather than shape information for object recognition, a stark contrast to human perception which prioritizes shape. This paper introduces CognitiveCNN, a novel architecture designed to mitigate this texture-shape bias by incorporating principles from human cognitive models. CognitiveCNN integrates mechanisms inspired by hierarchical processing, attention, and object-based representations, mimicking the way humans prioritize structural information during visual perception. We hypothesize that by embedding these cognitive constraints, the network will learn more robust and shape-sensitive feature representations. We evaluate CognitiveCNN on challenging datasets known to exacerbate texture bias, demonstrating a significant improvement in shape recognition accuracy compared to standard CNN architectures. Our results suggest that incorporating cognitive principles into deep learning can lead to more human-aligned and robust visual recognition systems, reducing the undesirable reliance on texture and promoting a stronger shape bias.
Catastrophic forgetting, the abrupt degradation of performance on previously learned tasks when training on new ones, remains a significant challenge in continual learning. This work proposes a novel approach to dissecting the mechanisms underlying catastrophic forgetting through deep visualization techniques. We leverage methods like t-SNE, UMAP, and class activation mapping (CAM) to visualize the evolution of feature representations, decision boundaries, and salient image regions across different tasks within a continually learning model. By visualizing these aspects of the learned representations, we identify specific patterns and shifts that contribute to forgetting, such as feature space overlap between tasks, instability of critical neurons, and drift in decision boundaries. Our visualizations provide insights into the internal dynamics of catastrophic forgetting, enabling a deeper understanding of its root causes and offering potential avenues for developing more robust and effective continual learning strategies. We present experimental results on benchmark datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of our visualization-based approach in elucidating the complex interplay between task interference and knowledge retention in continual learning scenarios.
Large-scale recommendation models, particularly those employing deep learning, are highly dependent on the quality and relevance of their input features. While feature engineering has traditionally relied on domain expertise and manual exploration, this process becomes increasingly challenging and time-consuming as models grow in complexity and data volume. This paper introduces a novel neural input search (NIS) framework designed to automatically discover and optimize input features for large-scale recommendation models. NIS leverages a neural architecture search (NAS) paradigm, employing a dedicated search network to explore the vast space of potential input feature combinations and transformations. The search network learns to predict the performance of different input configurations, guiding the discovery process towards high-performing features. We demonstrate the effectiveness of NIS on large-scale real-world recommendation datasets, showing significant improvements in recommendation accuracy and efficiency compared to manually engineered features and traditional feature selection methods. Our results highlight the potential of NIS to automate and enhance the feature engineering process for modern recommendation systems, enabling the development of more accurate and scalable models.
The complexity of software code presents a significant challenge for many machine learning tasks, including code generation, code summarization, and bug prediction. Traditional sequence-to-sequence models often struggle to effectively capture the intricate relationships and structural information inherent in code. This paper introduces code2seq, a novel approach that leverages the Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) representation of code to generate sequences. Instead of directly processing the raw code, code2seq encodes paths within the AST, capturing the relationships between distant tokens and preserving structural context. By learning representations of these paths and aggregating them, code2seq effectively encodes the code's semantic meaning. We demonstrate the effectiveness of code2seq in the task of method name prediction, showing significant improvements over state-of-the-art sequence-to-sequence models trained on raw code. This work highlights the benefits of incorporating structured code representations into neural models for code-related tasks.
## Abstract: Learning to Maximize Influence

Maximizing influence, the ability to affect the beliefs, behaviors, or decisions of others, is a central goal in diverse domains ranging from marketing and politics to social network analysis and public health. This paper explores the problem of **learning to maximize influence in complex, dynamic environments.** We investigate approaches that enable agents to autonomously learn effective strategies for influencing a target population, without relying on complete knowledge of the underlying influence network or individual susceptibilities. We consider various learning paradigms, including reinforcement learning and imitation learning, and discuss their applicability to different influence maximization scenarios. Furthermore, we explore the challenges associated with learning in environments with delayed feedback, partial observability, and strategic adversaries. Finally, we present promising directions for future research, including the development of robust and adaptable influence learning algorithms that can effectively navigate the complexities of real-world influence dynamics.
This paper introduces BeCAPTCHA-Mouse, a novel approach to bot detection leveraging synthetic mouse trajectories generated using a behavior-based model.  CAPTCHAs, while ubiquitous for distinguishing humans from bots, often suffer from usability issues and evolving bot techniques. BeCAPTCHA-Mouse addresses these challenges by analyzing the fine-grained characteristics of mouse movements during CAPTCHA interaction. We present a method for generating realistic synthetic mouse trajectories that mimic human behavior, enabling the training of robust machine learning models for bot detection.  Our approach allows for the creation of diverse and controllable datasets, mitigating the limitations of relying solely on real-world data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of BeCAPTCHA-Mouse in accurately classifying bots based on subtle deviations from human-like mouse behavior, achieving improved detection rates compared to traditional CAPTCHA methods while maintaining a user-friendly experience.  Furthermore, we analyze the key features that differentiate human and bot mouse trajectories, providing insights into the underlying mechanisms driving bot automation and informing future CAPTCHA design.
## HySTER: A Hybrid Spatio-Temporal Event Reasoner

HySTER is a novel reasoning system designed to infer relationships between events based on both their spatial and temporal contexts. Existing event reasoners often focus primarily on temporal ordering or abstract spatial relationships, neglecting the crucial interplay between these dimensions. HySTER addresses this limitation by employing a hybrid approach that combines symbolic reasoning with probabilistic modeling. The symbolic component utilizes a knowledge base of event schemas and domain constraints to establish logical connections and potential causal pathways. Simultaneously, the probabilistic component leverages statistical models trained on event data to quantify the likelihood of different spatial and temporal co-occurrences. HySTER integrates these two perspectives, allowing it to reason about events with incomplete or uncertain information, disambiguate multiple possible interpretations, and generate explanations that incorporate both spatial and temporal justifications. We demonstrate the effectiveness of HySTER through experiments on real-world event datasets, showcasing its superior performance in inferring event causality, predicting future events, and providing more comprehensive and informative explanations compared to state-of-the-art spatio-temporal reasoning systems.
This paper introduces a novel, nature-inspired modularity function specifically designed for unsupervised learning in spatially embedded networks. Existing modularity functions often fail to adequately capture the inherent structure and constraints imposed by spatial embedding, leading to suboptimal community detection. Our proposed function leverages principles observed in natural systems, such as proximity-based interaction and resource sharing, to better represent the relationships within these networks. We perform a comparative analysis against established modularity functions, including the Louvain method and variations adapted for spatial data, using both synthetic and real-world spatially embedded networks. Results demonstrate that our approach consistently identifies more meaningful and coherent communities, particularly in networks with strong spatial dependencies. Furthermore, we illustrate the advantages of our method in uncovering hidden patterns and improving the interpretability of network structure in applications such as urban planning, ecological modeling, and social network analysis. This new modularity function offers a promising tool for researchers seeking to extract valuable insights from spatially embedded network data through unsupervised learning.
## Abstract: Overcoming Multi-Model Forgetting

Multi-model systems, which leverage diverse models for improved performance, often suffer from a phenomenon we term "multi-model forgetting." This occurs when training a new model within the system negatively impacts the performance of previously trained models, hindering the overall effectiveness of the ensemble. This abstract outlines the problem of multi-model forgetting, highlighting its potential causes such as catastrophic forgetting in individual models and interference between models during training. We explore potential solutions, including regularization techniques designed to preserve existing knowledge, specialized training strategies to mitigate interference, and knowledge distillation methods to transfer knowledge between models without compromising individual performance. This work aims to provide a framework for understanding and addressing multi-model forgetting, ultimately leading to more robust and adaptable multi-model systems capable of continuously learning and improving without sacrificing prior knowledge.
This paper presents a novel reinforcement learning (RL)-based multi-agent cooperative approach for adaptive speed regulation on a metallurgical pickling line. Traditional methods often struggle with the dynamic and complex interactions within the pickling process, leading to suboptimal performance in terms of throughput, acid consumption, and strip quality. Our approach decomposes the pickling line into multiple interacting agents, each responsible for regulating the speed of a specific section. These agents cooperatively learn an optimal policy through decentralized training and execution, leveraging a shared reward function that encourages overall pickling line efficiency. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through simulations, comparing its performance against conventional control strategies. Results show that the proposed RL-based multi-agent system achieves significant improvements in production throughput while maintaining desired strip quality and minimizing acid consumption, highlighting its potential for real-world implementation in metallurgical pickling lines.
Distributional Reinforcement Learning (DRL) aims to learn the full distribution of future returns rather than just the expected value, enabling more nuanced decision-making and improved risk awareness. This work investigates the application of Unconstrained Monotonic Neural Networks (UMNNs) within a DRL framework to represent and learn these return distributions. UMNNs offer a powerful and flexible approach to modeling probability densities without imposing restrictive assumptions, particularly beneficial when dealing with complex, potentially multi-modal return distributions. We propose a novel DRL algorithm leveraging UMNNs for value distribution approximation and demonstrate its effectiveness in capturing the intricacies of return distributions. Our empirical evaluation on a suite of benchmark environments shows that the proposed approach achieves competitive performance compared to existing DRL algorithms, while also providing valuable insights into the learned return distributions and their impact on policy optimization. Furthermore, we analyze the benefits of using unconstrained monotonicity in the context of DRL, highlighting its ability to represent complex distributions and facilitate stable learning.
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown remarkable performance in learning representations from graph-structured data. However, GNN performance is often highly dependent on the underlying graph structure, which may be noisy, incomplete, or simply suboptimal for the learning task. This work explores methods for **learning discrete structures** that enhance GNN performance. We investigate techniques to dynamically adapt the graph structure during training by learning to **modify, add, or remove edges** based on node features and task-specific objectives. This allows GNNs to operate on improved graph representations that better capture relevant relationships and facilitate information propagation. We present [mention specific techniques, e.g., a differentiable relaxation of discrete edge selection, a reinforcement learning approach for graph evolution, etc.]. Experimental results on [mention datasets and tasks] demonstrate that learning discrete graph structures significantly improves the performance and robustness of GNNs compared to using fixed, pre-defined graphs. This approach offers a promising direction for leveraging the power of GNNs in scenarios where the underlying graph structure is not inherently optimal.
Text-to-image generation models have achieved remarkable progress, but often struggle to precisely capture subtle details and nuanced relationships described in the input text. This work proposes a novel approach to improve text-to-image generation by grounding the process with **fine-grained user attention**. Our method allows users to specify regions of interest within the input text and associate them with corresponding areas in the generated image. This explicit attention mechanism guides the model to focus on specific aspects of the text, resulting in more accurate and controllable image generation. We introduce a framework that incorporates user-provided attention maps into the image generation process, leveraging them to refine the feature representations and guide the generation of relevant image regions. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly enhances the fidelity and consistency of generated images compared to existing methods, particularly in scenarios requiring precise object placement, attribute binding, and complex scene composition. Furthermore, we show that this fine-grained control empowers users to effectively refine and personalize the generated images to better align with their desired visual outcomes.
Longitudinal electronic health record (EHR) data is frequently characterized by missing values, often treated as a nuisance requiring imputation or deletion. This work challenges that perspective, proposing that the structure of missingness itself can reveal underlying stability or instability in patient health trajectories. We investigate patterns of missingness in longitudinal EHR data, demonstrating that certain types of missingness are associated with periods of relative stability in patient health, while others indicate periods of instability or significant health events. Furthermore, we examine the impact of explicitly modeling missingness patterns on the performance of reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms in healthcare. By leveraging missingness as a signal, we demonstrate that RL agents can learn more effective treatment policies, leading to improved outcomes compared to agents that ignore or naively impute missing data. This research highlights the potential to transform missingness from a problem into a valuable source of information for understanding patient dynamics and improving decision-making in healthcare.
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable success in learning on graph-structured data. However, their performance often degrades significantly on non-homophilous graphs, where connected nodes tend to have dissimilar labels. This is due to the prevalent assumption in many GNN architectures that neighboring nodes share similar features and labels. To facilitate research and development of more robust GNNs for non-homophilous settings, we introduce a suite of new benchmark datasets specifically designed to exhibit varying degrees and types of non-homophily. These datasets encompass diverse real-world scenarios and provide a comprehensive evaluation platform. We analyze the performance of several existing GNN models on these benchmarks, highlighting their limitations and identifying key challenges in learning on non-homophilous graphs. Furthermore, we propose novel metrics and evaluation protocols tailored to assess the effectiveness of GNNs in capturing complex relationships and overcoming the homophily bias. Our contribution provides a valuable resource for the community, enabling the development and rigorous evaluation of future GNN architectures capable of effectively learning on non-homophilous graphs.
## FAIM -- A ConvNet Method for Unsupervised 3D Medical Image Registration

This paper introduces FAIM (Feature-Aligned Image Matching), a novel unsupervised convolutional neural network (ConvNet) method for 3D medical image registration. Unlike traditional registration algorithms that rely on hand-crafted features or iterative optimization, FAIM learns a registration network directly from image data without requiring ground truth transformations.  The core of FAIM lies in a feature-alignment objective that encourages the learned deformation field to align corresponding feature representations extracted from the moving and fixed images. This alignment is achieved by minimizing a feature-based similarity metric between the warped moving image features and the fixed image features.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of FAIM on challenging 3D medical image registration tasks, showcasing competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art unsupervised and traditional methods.  Our results highlight the potential of FAIM as a robust and efficient solution for unsupervised medical image registration, enabling accurate anatomical alignment without the need for laborious manual annotation.
Ranking similar artists for new or emerging artists (the "cold start" problem) is a challenging task in music recommendation. Traditional collaborative filtering approaches struggle due to the lack of historical interaction data. This paper introduces a novel approach leveraging a Gravity-Inspired Graph Autoencoder (GIGAE) to address this cold start challenge. We construct a graph representing artist relationships based on publicly available knowledge such as genre, shared influences, and lyrical similarity. The GIGAE then learns node embeddings that capture the underlying structure and semantic relationships within this graph. Crucially, we incorporate a gravity-inspired loss function during training, encouraging artists with stronger connections (e.g., shared genres and high lyrical overlap) to have closer embeddings. These learned embeddings are then used to rank similar artists for cold start artists based on proximity in the embedding space. We evaluate our approach on a benchmark dataset, demonstrating that the GIGAE significantly outperforms existing methods in accurately ranking similar artists for cold start scenarios, highlighting the effectiveness of incorporating gravity-inspired principles into graph representation learning for knowledge-aware music recommendation.
We propose a novel approach to learning structural edits on tree-structured data by framing the problem as incremental tree transformations. Instead of predicting a complete target tree directly, our model learns a sequence of local, structure-preserving edits that progressively transform an initial tree towards the desired output. This incremental approach offers several advantages, including improved interpretability, reduced complexity compared to generating entire trees at once, and the ability to leverage intermediate states for better guidance. We introduce a model architecture that learns to predict these incremental tree transformations, incorporating contextual information from the current tree state and the target structure. We evaluate our approach on [mention specific tasks or datasets, e.g., program repair, semantic parsing, or code generation] and demonstrate its effectiveness in learning complex structural edits, achieving significant improvements over baselines that directly predict the target tree. Our results highlight the benefits of learning structural transformations incrementally and pave the way for more efficient and accurate manipulation of tree-structured data.
Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) is a popular algorithm for continuous control, known for its ability to learn effective policies in high-dimensional environments. However, the performance of DDPG actors can be sensitive to hyperparameter tuning and often suffers from limitations in exploration and exploitation. This work introduces a novel approach to refine the continuous control capabilities of DDPG actors through **Parametrised Activation**. Instead of relying on fixed activation functions in the actor network, we propose learning the parameters of activation functions, effectively shaping the output space and influencing the exploration-exploitation trade-off. By adapting the activation function, the actor can learn more nuanced and tailored control strategies. We evaluate our method on a range of benchmark continuous control tasks and demonstrate significant improvements in performance compared to standard DDPG and other relevant baselines. Our results indicate that learning activation function parameters offers a promising avenue for enhancing the robustness, efficiency, and adaptability of DDPG actors in complex environments.
This paper proposes a novel approach to weakly supervised semantic segmentation by leveraging cross-image semantics.  Our method addresses the challenge of limited pixel-level annotations by mining relationships between images based on shared object instances and contextual similarities. We introduce a framework that first establishes a cross-image correspondence network, identifying potential semantic connections between images using global image features and object proposals.  These connections are then used to propagate weak supervision signals, such as image-level labels, across the network, generating pseudo-labels for unlabeled pixels.  Specifically, we utilize a graph-based propagation algorithm that refines the initial pseudo-labels by considering the consistency of semantic assignments within and across images. Finally, a standard segmentation network is trained using the propagated pseudo-labels.  Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly improves segmentation performance compared to existing weakly supervised methods, highlighting the effectiveness of mining cross-image semantics for learning with limited supervision.  The proposed method offers a promising direction for reducing annotation costs while achieving competitive segmentation accuracy.
Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) often suffer from performance degradation when applied to new subjects due to inter-subject variability in EEG data. Data augmentation techniques can mitigate this issue by increasing the diversity of training data. This paper proposes a novel data augmentation method for cross-subject BCI based on Common Spatial Pattern (CSP) transformed EEG data and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). We introduce Common Spatial Generative Adversarial Networks (CSGANs), which leverage CSP to extract task-relevant features and then employ a GAN architecture to generate synthetic EEG data in the CSP space. By training the generator on CSP features extracted from multiple subjects, we aim to capture the underlying commonalities across subjects while generating realistic and diverse samples. We evaluate the effectiveness of CSGANs for cross-subject BCI performance on a benchmark EEG dataset. Our results demonstrate that augmenting the training data with CSGAN-generated samples significantly improves the classification accuracy on unseen subjects compared to baseline data augmentation techniques and training without augmentation, highlighting the potential of CSGANs for robust and generalizable BCI systems.
This study explores the application of interpretable machine learning (IML) techniques to predict COVID-19 severity.  Leveraging a real-world dataset, we investigate the performance of various IML models in predicting patient outcomes, focusing on identifying key clinical features associated with increased severity.  Beyond predictive accuracy, our emphasis lies on understanding the reasoning behind model predictions, providing insights into the complex interplay of factors influencing disease progression. We compare the performance of inherently interpretable models with post-hoc explanation methods applied to black-box models, evaluating their ability to reveal clinically relevant patterns and potential biases. This empirical study contributes to a more transparent and trustworthy approach to COVID-19 risk stratification, potentially aiding clinicians in making informed decisions and improving patient management strategies. The findings highlight the importance of incorporating IML for not only accurate predictions but also for fostering a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms driving COVID-19 severity.
This paper proposes a novel dimensionality reduction technique for stationary time series data based on stochastic nonconvex optimization. Traditional dimensionality reduction methods often struggle to capture the temporal dependencies inherent in time series, leading to suboptimal representations. Our approach leverages a stochastic gradient descent algorithm to learn a low-dimensional embedding that preserves the essential characteristics of the time series, while simultaneously minimizing a nonconvex loss function designed to capture temporal relationships such as autocorrelation and spectral properties. This nonconvex formulation allows for greater flexibility in modeling complex dependencies compared to linear methods. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on both synthetic and real-world time series datasets, showcasing its ability to achieve superior performance in tasks such as time series classification and anomaly detection compared to existing dimensionality reduction techniques. Furthermore, we provide theoretical insights into the convergence properties of the proposed stochastic nonconvex optimization algorithm within the context of time series analysis.
## BERT2DNN: BERT Distillation with Massive Unlabeled Data for Online E-Commerce Search

Online e-commerce search demands both high accuracy and low latency. While BERT-based models achieve state-of-the-art accuracy, their computational complexity hinders their deployment in online systems. This paper introduces BERT2DNN, a novel knowledge distillation framework that leverages massive unlabeled e-commerce data to compress a pre-trained BERT model into a lightweight Deep Neural Network (DNN) for efficient online search. Our approach utilizes BERT as a teacher model to generate pseudo-labels for a large corpus of unlabeled search queries and product descriptions. These pseudo-labels are then used to train a DNN student model, effectively transferring BERT's rich semantic understanding to a computationally efficient architecture. Experimental results on a real-world e-commerce search dataset demonstrate that BERT2DNN achieves comparable accuracy to BERT while significantly reducing inference latency, making it suitable for deployment in high-throughput online environments. We show that BERT2DNN provides a practical solution for bridging the accuracy-latency gap in e-commerce search by effectively utilizing readily available unlabeled data.
This paper presents the 2nd place solutions for the HC-STVG (Hierarchical Classification of Spatial-Temporal Video Groups) track of the Person in Context Challenge 2021. The HC-STVG track focuses on classifying video segments depicting human actions into a hierarchical taxonomy. Our approach leverages a combination of [mention the key techniques, e.g., 3D Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for spatio-temporal feature extraction, attention mechanisms for focusing on relevant frames, and hierarchical classification strategies for improved accuracy]. We detail the architecture of our models, the training methodology, and the specific strategies employed to address the challenges of fine-grained action recognition and hierarchical classification. Furthermore, we analyze the performance of our system on the challenge dataset, highlighting its strengths and weaknesses, and discuss potential avenues for future research in this domain. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach in achieving high accuracy in the HC-STVG task.
This paper introduces a novel approach to high-fidelity image generation using cascaded diffusion models. We address the challenge of generating realistic and detailed images by proposing a multi-stage framework where multiple diffusion models are sequentially applied, refining the image quality at each stage. The initial diffusion model generates a low-resolution image, which is then progressively upscaled and enhanced by subsequent diffusion models conditioned on the output of the previous stage. This cascaded approach allows us to leverage the strengths of diffusion models for both global structure generation and fine-grained detail synthesis. We demonstrate that our method significantly improves image quality compared to single-stage diffusion models, achieving state-of-the-art results on benchmark datasets. Our results highlight the effectiveness of cascaded diffusion models for generating high-resolution images with exceptional fidelity and realism, opening new avenues for image synthesis and manipulation.
This paper presents a novel approach to batch reinforcement learning (RL) that leverages a nonparametric policy gradient method for off-policy learning. In batch RL, learning is constrained to a fixed dataset of experience, necessitating robust off-policy techniques. Our method addresses this challenge by directly estimating the policy gradient from the batch data using a nonparametric kernel estimator. This allows us to avoid explicit policy evaluation, a common source of instability in off-policy algorithms, and learn directly from observed returns. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a suite of benchmark tasks, showing that it can achieve competitive performance compared to existing batch RL algorithms, while offering potential advantages in terms of stability and ease of implementation due to its nonparametric nature. The proposed method offers a promising avenue for learning effective policies from limited and potentially biased datasets, a crucial requirement for real-world RL applications.
Many real-world phenomena exhibit asymmetric distributions, posing challenges for traditional statistical modeling. This work introduces a novel approach to generating asymmetric distributions through **constrained mixtures**. We demonstrate how imposing specific constraints on the mixing proportions and/or component parameters of a mixture model can induce significant skewness and control its shape. Unlike existing methods that rely on specific asymmetric distributions or transformations, our approach offers flexibility and interpretability by leveraging the inherent properties of mixture models. We explore various constraint strategies and analyze their impact on the resulting distribution's shape, skewness, and kurtosis. Furthermore, we present examples of how these constrained mixtures can be applied to model data exhibiting asymmetry in diverse fields, showcasing their potential for improved model fit and inference compared to symmetric alternatives. This framework provides a powerful and adaptable tool for representing and understanding asymmetric data patterns across various disciplines.
This abstract outlines a study focused on modeling directional data using Kent distributions. Directional data, representing orientations or directions in two or three dimensions, arises in various scientific fields. The Kent distribution, a generalization of the von Mises-Fisher distribution, offers a flexible framework for modeling such data, particularly when dealing with elliptically contoured datasets exhibiting non-uniform concentrations around the mean direction. This work explores the properties of the Kent distribution and investigates its application in modeling diverse directional datasets. Specifically, we discuss parameter estimation techniques, including maximum likelihood estimation, and evaluate the performance of the Kent distribution in comparison to other common directional distributions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the utility of the Kent distribution through real-world examples, showcasing its ability to capture complex directional patterns and provide valuable insights into the underlying phenomena. This research contributes to the development of more accurate and robust statistical methods for analyzing directional data.
Reinforcement learning (RL) agents often struggle to generalize learned policies to new environments or tasks. This paper investigates the integration of working and episodic memory mechanisms to improve generalization capabilities in RL. We propose a novel architecture that combines a working memory module for short-term task-specific information storage with an episodic memory module for storing and retrieving past experiences. The working memory allows the agent to adapt to variations within an environment, while the episodic memory provides a framework for leveraging knowledge gained from previously encountered, similar situations to accelerate learning and improve performance in novel scenarios. We evaluate the proposed architecture on a suite of challenging reinforcement learning tasks with varying degrees of environmental similarity. Results demonstrate that the integration of working and episodic memory significantly enhances generalization performance compared to traditional RL algorithms and agents utilizing only one type of memory, leading to faster adaptation and improved overall reward in unseen environments. This work highlights the potential of combining different memory systems to create more robust and adaptable RL agents.
Few-shot classification aims to recognize novel classes with limited labeled examples. Existing methods often struggle to extract robust features from scarce data, hindering generalization. To address this, we propose a novel approach, **Boosting Few-Shot Classification with View-Learnable Contrastive Learning (BVCL)**. BVCL enhances feature representation by learning multiple diverse views of each instance and leveraging contrastive learning to maximize agreement within views of the same instance while minimizing similarity between different instances. Crucially, instead of relying on handcrafted transformations to generate views, we introduce a **view-learning module** that dynamically generates informative views tailored to the specific task and data distribution. This view-learning module is trained jointly with the feature extractor and contrastive loss, allowing for adaptive and optimized view generation. We further boost performance by incorporating a multi-stage training strategy that progressively refines the feature extractor and view-learning module. Extensive experiments on benchmark few-shot datasets demonstrate that BVCL significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, showcasing its effectiveness in learning robust and generalizable features for few-shot classification.
This study presents a comparative analysis of the clinical application of motion analysis derived from Kinect skeleton data. While Kinect sensors offer a low-cost and accessible alternative to traditional motion capture systems, their accuracy and reliability in clinical settings remain a subject of investigation. This research compares different approaches for extracting clinically relevant kinematic parameters from Kinect skeleton data, including filtering techniques, joint angle calculations, and spatiotemporal gait analysis. The comparative analysis focuses on the applicability of these methods for assessing specific clinical conditions, such as gait disorders, postural instability, and rehabilitation progress. We evaluate the strengths and limitations of each approach, considering factors such as accuracy, sensitivity to noise, computational complexity, and ease of clinical interpretation. The findings provide valuable insights for clinicians and researchers seeking to leverage Kinect-based motion analysis for improved patient assessment and treatment monitoring, while also highlighting areas for future development and validation.
Real-Time Reinforcement Learning (RTRL) addresses the challenge of learning optimal policies in dynamic environments where decisions must be made with strict time constraints. Unlike traditional reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms that often rely on offline training and computation-intensive updates, RTRL focuses on enabling agents to learn and adapt online, reacting immediately to incoming sensory information. This abstract explores the key challenges and opportunities within RTRL, including the need for efficient exploration strategies, computationally feasible policy update mechanisms, and robust handling of noisy or incomplete data. We examine various approaches to achieving real-time performance, such as model-free methods with incremental updates, approximate dynamic programming techniques, and the utilization of specialized hardware for accelerated computation. Furthermore, we discuss the application of RTRL in domains like robotics, autonomous driving, and financial trading, where timely decision-making is critical. This abstract highlights the growing importance of RTRL in enabling intelligent agents to operate effectively in complex and time-sensitive real-world scenarios.
Night environmental perception poses significant challenges for autonomous systems due to limited visibility. This paper introduces IR2VI, a novel unsupervised thermal image translation framework designed to enhance night environmental perception by converting infrared (IR) images into visually representative (VI) images. Our approach leverages a generative adversarial network (GAN) architecture coupled with carefully designed loss functions to learn the complex mapping between IR and VI domains without requiring paired training data. We employ a combination of content, texture, and perceptual losses to ensure that the translated VI images preserve crucial structural information and realistic details from the IR input while resembling natural visible light images. Experimental results demonstrate that IR2VI effectively generates high-quality VI images from IR images, significantly improving the performance of downstream tasks such as object detection and semantic segmentation in low-light conditions. This unsupervised translation method offers a practical and scalable solution for enhancing night environmental perception, contributing to safer and more reliable autonomous navigation in challenging environments.
3D semantic segmentation in point clouds often suffers from performance degradation when applied to new, unseen domains due to domain shift. This paper proposes a novel domain adaptation framework, termed "Sparse-to-dense Feature Matching," to address this challenge. Our approach leverages both intra-domain and inter-domain cross-modal learning to bridge the gap between source and target domains. Specifically, we exploit the complementary nature of sparse and dense feature representations, generated from point clouds and their corresponding voxelized representations, respectively. Intra-domain learning encourages consistency between these modalities within each domain, while inter-domain learning aligns corresponding sparse and dense features across domains using a feature matching strategy. This sparse-to-dense feature matching facilitates the transfer of semantic knowledge from the labeled source domain to the unlabeled target domain. We evaluate our method on benchmark datasets, demonstrating significant improvements in 3D semantic segmentation accuracy on the target domain compared to state-of-the-art domain adaptation techniques. Our results highlight the effectiveness of leveraging cross-modal information and feature matching for robust domain adaptation in 3D semantic segmentation.
This paper introduces a novel approach for token-level labeling tasks that leverages Bidirectional Recursive Neural Networks (BRNNs) to explicitly incorporate structural information into the labeling process. Traditional sequence labeling models often treat input as a linear sequence, neglecting underlying hierarchical or tree-like structures present in the data. Our proposed BRNN-based model addresses this limitation by recursively processing input data based on a predefined structure, allowing information to flow both upwards and downwards within the structure. This bidirectional recursive processing enables the model to capture contextual dependencies at various levels of granularity, leading to a richer representation of each token and improved labeling accuracy. We evaluate our approach on [mention specific datasets or tasks, e.g., Named Entity Recognition on parse trees, Part-of-Speech tagging with dependency structures] and demonstrate that it outperforms existing sequence labeling models that do not explicitly incorporate structural information. The results highlight the benefits of utilizing BRNNs for effectively capturing and leveraging structural context in token-level labeling problems.
This paper proposes a novel group-wise semantic mining (GSM) approach for weakly supervised semantic segmentation. Leveraging image-level labels, GSM aims to bridge the gap between image-level classification and pixel-level segmentation by effectively exploring and exploiting inherent semantic relationships within image regions. Specifically, we first partition the image into a set of semantic groups based on feature similarity. Then, we introduce a group-wise contrastive learning strategy to encourage intra-group consistency and inter-group discrimination, thus promoting the discovery of discriminative semantic cues. Furthermore, we develop a group-wise attention mechanism to refine the pseudo labels generated from the weakly supervised classifier, enhancing the accuracy and completeness of the segmentation masks. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our GSM method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art weakly supervised semantic segmentation approaches, proving its effectiveness in mining and leveraging semantic information for improved segmentation performance.
Detecting protective movement behaviors, such as bracing or guarding, is crucial for understanding and predicting potential injury risk. This paper proposes a novel approach to protective movement behavior detection by explicitly learning both bodily and temporal attention mechanisms. Our model learns to focus on relevant body parts within each frame (bodily attention) and identifies critical time segments within the movement sequence (temporal attention). By jointly learning these attention mechanisms, the model can effectively prioritize informative features, leading to improved detection accuracy and robustness. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a dataset of simulated protective movements, showing significant improvements over baseline methods that rely solely on spatial or temporal information. The learned attention maps provide valuable insights into which body parts and movement phases are most indicative of protective behavior, offering potential for further understanding and analysis of human movement strategies.
Arbitrary-oriented object detection (AOOD) is a challenging task crucial for numerous applications, ranging from remote sensing to autonomous driving. While regression-based methods have dominated the field, classification-based approaches offer potential advantages in handling complex object shapes and overlapping instances. This paper revisits classification-based approaches for AOOD, critically examining their strengths and weaknesses in comparison to regression-based counterparts. We analyze existing classification frameworks, focusing on their feature representation, angle discretization strategies, and loss functions. Furthermore, we explore potential improvements to enhance their performance and robustness, including novel feature aggregation techniques and adaptive angle classification schemes. Through comprehensive experiments on benchmark datasets, we demonstrate the viability of classification-based methods and highlight their potential to achieve competitive results with optimized designs. This work aims to revitalize interest in classification-based AOOD and provides insights for future research directions in this important area.
Text-based person retrieval (TBPR) is crucial in forensic applications, where identifying individuals from textual descriptions like witness statements or suspect profiles is paramount. Traditional TBPR methods often rely on supervised learning, requiring substantial labeled data associating text descriptions with identity information. This is problematic in forensic contexts where labeled data is scarce and constantly evolving. This paper explores the potential of generative one-class models for TBPR, offering a novel approach that alleviates the need for extensive labeled data. We propose a generative framework that learns a latent representation of "normal" person descriptions, effectively modeling the distribution of known individuals. During retrieval, the model assesses the likelihood of a novel text description belonging to this learned distribution. Descriptions with high likelihood scores are considered more likely to correspond to known individuals, while outliers may indicate new or unknown subjects. We evaluate our approach on publicly available TBPR datasets and demonstrate its effectiveness in identifying individuals from textual descriptions, particularly in scenarios with limited labeled data. Furthermore, we discuss the applicability of this method to forensic investigations, highlighting its potential to improve efficiency and accuracy in person identification and ultimately aiding in law enforcement efforts.
This paper proposes a novel approach for radar image segmentation using active contours. Radar images, often characterized by speckle noise and low contrast, pose significant challenges for traditional segmentation methods. To address these challenges, we develop an active contour model specifically tailored for radar imagery. The proposed method leverages statistical properties of radar data, incorporating a region-based energy term derived from the Gamma distribution to effectively handle speckle noise. Furthermore, we integrate a gradient-based edge term to enhance the contour's ability to adhere to object boundaries. The active contour is then evolved iteratively to minimize the overall energy function, resulting in accurate and robust segmentation. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world radar images demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in accurately delineating objects, even in the presence of significant noise and clutter, outperforming traditional active contour models and other common segmentation techniques. The results highlight the potential of this approach for various radar image analysis applications, including object detection, target recognition, and change detection.
Robust and accurate 6DoF relocalization in large-scale environments remains a significant challenge for robotics and autonomous navigation. This paper introduces DH3D, a novel approach leveraging deep learning to generate hierarchical 3D descriptors for this task. DH3D employs a deep convolutional neural network to extract multi-scale geometric features from 3D point clouds, encoding them into compact descriptors at different levels of granularity. The hierarchical structure allows for efficient coarse-to-fine matching, enabling fast candidate retrieval and precise pose estimation. We demonstrate that DH3D achieves state-of-the-art performance on challenging benchmark datasets, exhibiting superior robustness to viewpoint changes, occlusions, and noise compared to existing methods. The experimental results highlight the effectiveness of the proposed hierarchical descriptor representation and its potential for enabling reliable large-scale 6DoF relocalization in real-world applications.
Semi-supervised graph node classification leverages both labeled and unlabeled nodes to predict labels for the latter. Existing methods often struggle with over-smoothing and inefficient information propagation, particularly when dealing with complex graph structures. This paper introduces Graph Decoupling Attention Markov Networks (GDAMN), a novel framework designed to address these challenges. GDAMN decouples the graph into subgraphs based on node feature similarity, enabling localized information aggregation and mitigating over-smoothing. We then introduce an attention mechanism within a Markov Network framework to selectively propagate information across these subgraphs, allowing nodes to learn from relevant neighbors while filtering out noise. This attention mechanism learns to weigh the influence of different subgraphs based on their relevance to the target node, further enhancing the accuracy and robustness of the node classification. We demonstrate the effectiveness of GDAMN through extensive experiments on benchmark graph datasets, showing significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in semi-supervised node classification. The results highlight the benefits of decoupling the graph structure and leveraging attention-based Markov Networks for efficient and accurate information propagation.
Embedded neural networks are increasingly deployed in resource-constrained environments, necessitating model compression techniques like low-bitwidth quantization. While quantization significantly reduces model size and computational cost, its impact on adversarial robustness remains a critical concern, particularly for security-sensitive applications. This paper investigates the impact of low-bitwidth quantization on the adversarial robustness of embedded neural networks. We empirically evaluate the vulnerability of quantized models to various adversarial attacks, considering different quantization strategies and bitwidths. Our results demonstrate that aggressive quantization can significantly degrade adversarial robustness, making quantized models more susceptible to adversarial perturbations. We analyze the underlying causes of this degradation, linking it to the altered loss landscape and reduced gradient information in quantized models. Furthermore, we explore potential mitigation strategies, including quantization-aware training and adversarial training techniques tailored for low-bitwidth networks, to improve the adversarial robustness of quantized embedded neural networks. Our findings provide valuable insights into the trade-off between model efficiency and security, guiding the design of robust and efficient embedded neural networks for real-world deployment.
This paper introduces a novel lossless compression technique for structured convolutional neural networks (CNNs) based on lifting schemes. By leveraging the inherent structure within CNN filter weights, specifically sparsity induced by techniques like filter pruning or low-rank approximations, we demonstrate that these structures can be transformed and reorganized via lifting to achieve significant entropy reduction without any loss of information. Our approach decomposes the structured filters into a series of invertible lifting steps, enabling efficient representation and reconstruction. We analyze the theoretical bounds on compression performance achievable with this lifting-based approach and empirically evaluate its effectiveness on various CNN architectures and benchmark datasets. Results demonstrate that our method achieves substantial lossless compression ratios compared to traditional compression techniques, while preserving the original model accuracy and offering potential benefits for resource-constrained deployment scenarios.
Counting transient phenomena in complex audio recordings, such as the individual strikes on a steelpan drum, presents a significant challenge for traditional signal processing techniques. This paper explores the application of Convolutional Neural Networks (ConvNets) for object detection of these events. We propose a novel approach leveraging ConvNets to analyze spectrogram representations of steelpan drum recordings, treating each strike as a distinct object within the time-frequency domain. The network is trained to identify and localize these transient events, effectively counting the number of strikes and providing temporal information. The results demonstrate the potential of ConvNets for accurate and robust counting of transient phenomena in steelpan drums, offering a promising avenue for automated analysis and understanding of complex musical performances. This approach can be extended to other musical instruments and acoustic environments where the identification and counting of transient events are crucial.
This paper presents a deep machine learning based system for the recognition of Egyptian vehicle license plates (VLPs). The system leverages convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for both VLP localization and character recognition, addressing the challenges posed by varying lighting conditions, font variations, and plate degradation common in real-world Egyptian traffic environments. The proposed system is divided into two main stages: first, a robust object detection model, trained on a large and diverse dataset of Egyptian vehicle images, accurately locates the VLP region. Second, the extracted VLP is processed using a character segmentation module followed by a CNN-based character recognition model trained to identify the unique Arabic and numerical characters present on Egyptian VLPs. We evaluate the performance of the proposed system on a challenging dataset of real-world images, demonstrating its effectiveness in achieving high accuracy and robustness in VLP recognition. The results highlight the potential of deep learning techniques for building efficient and reliable VLP recognition systems for applications such as traffic management, automated parking, and security surveillance within the Egyptian context.
This paper presents a novel approach to foreground-background segmentation that leverages the strengths of both codebook-based modeling and edge detection. The proposed method utilizes a codebook to model the background scene, capturing variations in pixel intensities over time. To improve robustness and accuracy, we incorporate an edge detector to identify and refine object boundaries. Specifically, edges are used to guide the codebook learning process, preventing the background model from incorporating foreground object pixels. Furthermore, edge information is integrated into the segmentation decision, reinforcing foreground regions and suppressing noise. Experimental results on challenging video sequences demonstrate that our method outperforms traditional codebook-based approaches and achieves competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art segmentation algorithms, particularly in scenarios with complex background motion and gradual illumination changes. The combination of codebook modeling and edge detection effectively enhances the accuracy and robustness of foreground-background segmentation.
This paper explores a novel approach to image synthesis, termed "Generator Versus Segmentor: Pseudo-healthy Synthesis," which leverages the adversarial relationship between a generative model and a segmentation network. Instead of directly generating realistic images, our method focuses on synthesizing "pseudo-healthy" data, meaning images that mimic the appearance of healthy samples but are constructed to challenge a segmentation model trained to identify healthy versus unhealthy regions. The generator is trained to produce images that fool the segmentor into misclassifying unhealthy regions as healthy, thereby forcing the segmentor to learn more robust and subtle features. We hypothesize that this adversarial training paradigm can improve the segmentor's generalization performance and reduce its reliance on spurious correlations present in the training data. We present experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach in [mention specific application area, e.g., medical image analysis, anomaly detection], showing improved segmentation accuracy and robustness compared to traditional generative adversarial networks and standard segmentation training methods. Our work highlights the potential of adversarial training to synthesize targeted data for enhancing the performance of downstream image analysis tasks.
This paper investigates the impact of incorporating a priori information into the structure of deep neural networks (DNNs) designed for wireless communication tasks. While DNNs have demonstrated remarkable performance in complex wireless scenarios, their black-box nature often obscures the underlying mechanisms and limits interpretability. This work explores how injecting domain-specific knowledge about wireless systems directly into the DNN architecture can improve performance, efficiency, and robustness. Specifically, we propose and analyze various structural modifications that leverage a priori information such as channel characteristics, signal processing techniques, and physical layer constraints. Through simulations and analysis, we demonstrate that these structurally informed DNNs can achieve superior performance compared to standard DNN architectures, particularly in challenging wireless environments with limited training data. Furthermore, we show that the resulting networks exhibit improved interpretability and generalization capabilities, paving the way for more efficient and reliable DNN-based wireless communication systems.
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated remarkable performance across various graph-related tasks. However, like many machine learning models, GNNs are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where carefully crafted perturbations to the graph structure or node features can significantly degrade their performance. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the rapidly evolving field of adversarial learning on graphs. We categorize and analyze existing attack and defense strategies, focusing on their underlying principles, strengths, and limitations. Specifically, we examine attack methods that target different aspects of GNNs, including their vulnerability to node-level, graph-level, and edge-level perturbations. Furthermore, we discuss diverse defense mechanisms, such as adversarial training, graph structure modification, and robust feature engineering, designed to enhance the resilience of GNNs against adversarial attacks. Finally, we identify open challenges and future research directions in this critical area, highlighting the need for more robust, scalable, and theoretically grounded approaches to ensure the reliable deployment of GNNs in adversarial environments.
Executing programs often requires navigating complex control flow, represented by the order of instruction execution. This paper introduces Instruction Pointer Attention Graph Neural Networks (IPA-GNNs), a novel approach for learning to execute programs by explicitly modeling the program's control flow graph and attending to the current instruction pointer. IPA-GNNs represent programs as graph structures where nodes are instructions and edges represent control flow dependencies. The core innovation lies in using the instruction pointer to dynamically attend to relevant instructions in the graph, guiding information propagation and enabling the model to reason about the current execution context. We demonstrate the effectiveness of IPA-GNNs on program execution tasks, showing that explicitly modeling the instruction pointer and control flow leads to improved performance compared to existing methods. Our results highlight the potential of graph-based representations and attention mechanisms for learning to execute complex programs.
Similarity models, which quantify the resemblance between data points, are fundamental across various machine learning tasks. While these models excel at identifying similar items, understanding *why* they deem certain instances similar remains a challenge. This work addresses this gap by exploring methods for visually explaining the decisions of similarity models. We propose a framework to generate visual explanations that highlight the features contributing most to a model's similarity score for a given pair of inputs. This framework leverages techniques from explainable AI (XAI) to identify relevant input regions and present them in a user-friendly visual format. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on diverse datasets and similarity models, showcasing its potential to improve user trust, enable model debugging, and facilitate a deeper understanding of the underlying data relationships learned by these models. The ability to visually explain similarity provides valuable insights beyond simple numerical scores, ultimately fostering more informed and effective utilization of these powerful tools.
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have shown remarkable success in generating realistic images, but often require large amounts of labeled data for training. Self-supervised learning offers a promising avenue to alleviate this dependency. This paper introduces a novel self-supervised approach for GAN training by incorporating an auxiliary rotation loss. Our method leverages the inherent structure of images by training the discriminator to predict the degree of rotation applied to input images (e.g., 0°, 90°, 180°, 270°). This auxiliary task forces the discriminator to learn robust feature representations that capture semantic information, which in turn benefits the generator's ability to produce high-quality and diverse images. We demonstrate that the addition of this rotation prediction task to the standard GAN objective leads to improved performance on image generation tasks, achieving better Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) scores and visual quality compared to baseline GANs and other self-supervised GAN methods. Furthermore, we show that the learned representations can be effectively transferred to downstream classification tasks, highlighting the quality of the learned features. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed self-supervised GAN training strategy via auxiliary rotation loss for generating realistic images with minimal supervision.
This paper introduces the Image Registration Optimizer Network (IRON), a novel learning-based optimization algorithm for image registration. Traditional optimization methods for image registration often suffer from computational expense and sensitivity to initialization. IRON addresses these limitations by learning an efficient optimization strategy directly from data. Specifically, IRON employs a neural network to predict the optimal update direction for the transformation parameters at each iteration, guided by the image similarity metric and its gradient. This learned optimization strategy allows for faster convergence and robustness to poor initializations compared to conventional gradient-based approaches. We evaluate IRON on various image registration tasks, demonstrating its superior performance in terms of registration accuracy, computational speed, and convergence stability. Our results highlight the potential of learning-based optimization for image registration and pave the way for more efficient and robust registration pipelines.
Federated Learning (FL) offers a promising approach to training machine learning models on decentralized data residing on numerous edge devices. This paradigm is particularly relevant when dealing with "big data" distributed across networks, where traditional centralized training is infeasible due to communication bottlenecks, privacy concerns, and data ownership restrictions. This paper explores the challenges and opportunities of applying FL in such big data network environments. We analyze the impact of network topology, communication bandwidth limitations, and data heterogeneity on the convergence and performance of FL algorithms. Furthermore, we investigate strategies for addressing these challenges, including communication-efficient aggregation techniques, personalized model adaptation, and privacy-preserving mechanisms. We discuss the theoretical foundations and practical considerations for scaling FL to handle massive datasets and complex network structures, highlighting the potential of FL to unlock valuable insights from distributed big data while preserving data privacy and minimizing communication overhead. This work contributes to the advancement of FL as a viable and effective solution for training models from big data over networks.
This paper presents a novel approach to Automatic Machine Learning (AutoML) through pipeline synthesis using a combination of model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) and a formal grammar. Our method aims to automate the discovery of optimal machine learning pipelines by treating pipeline construction as a sequential decision-making problem. We leverage a grammar to define the space of possible pipelines, ensuring syntactic correctness and enabling efficient exploration. This grammar is then used to train a model-based reinforcement learning agent, which learns to predict the performance of pipelines based on their structure and the characteristics of the dataset. By learning a model of the environment, the agent can efficiently explore promising pipeline configurations, minimizing the need for expensive real-world evaluations. The efficacy of our approach is demonstrated through experiments on benchmark datasets, showing that our method can discover pipelines that achieve competitive or superior performance compared to existing AutoML techniques, while significantly reducing the computational cost associated with pipeline search.
This paper presents a novel approach to inference and prediction in Gaussian Process State-Space Models (GP-SSMs) that leverages closed-form solutions. GP-SSMs combine the flexibility of Gaussian Processes (GPs) for modeling nonlinear dynamics with the structured inference capabilities of state-space models. However, exact inference in general GP-SSMs is intractable. We address this challenge by deriving analytical expressions for the predictive distribution under specific, yet practically relevant, conditions. These conditions involve restricting either the observation model or the GP transition model to be linear Gaussian. We demonstrate that under these constraints, both filtering and smoothing can be performed efficiently and accurately using closed-form updates, avoiding computationally expensive approximations like particle filtering or variational inference. We validate our approach on synthetic and real-world datasets, showcasing its competitive performance in terms of accuracy and computational speed compared to existing approximation methods. The proposed closed-form solutions offer a significant advantage for applications requiring real-time inference and prediction in GP-SSMs.
Accurate prediction of urban vehicle trajectories is crucial for various intelligent transportation applications, including autonomous driving, traffic management, and collision avoidance. This paper proposes an attention-based recurrent neural network (RNN) model for predicting future vehicle trajectories in complex urban environments. The model leverages the ability of RNNs to capture temporal dependencies in trajectory data, while incorporating an attention mechanism to selectively focus on the most relevant historical trajectory points when predicting future movements. The attention mechanism allows the model to dynamically weight the importance of different past states, thereby mitigating the limitations of traditional RNNs in handling long-range dependencies and noisy data. Experimental results on real-world urban driving datasets demonstrate that the proposed attention-based RNN model outperforms existing state-of-the-art trajectory prediction methods, exhibiting improved accuracy and robustness, particularly in challenging scenarios with complex interactions and varying driving behaviors. This highlights the effectiveness of incorporating attention mechanisms for enhancing the performance of RNNs in urban vehicle trajectory prediction.
This paper addresses the challenging problem of changepoint detection in high-dimensional time series data, a prevalent issue in various domains ranging from finance to climate science. A key difficulty arises from the presence of missing data, which can significantly impact the performance of traditional changepoint detection methods. We propose a novel approach that effectively handles both high dimensionality and missing values. Our method leverages [mention the core technique, e.g., a regularized estimator, a robust imputation strategy, or a specific statistical model] to [mention the key advantage, e.g., accurately estimate the covariance structure, impute missing data in a statistically sound manner, or model the time series dynamics]. We develop a computationally efficient algorithm for identifying multiple changepoints and provide theoretical guarantees for its consistency under mild assumptions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method through extensive simulations and real-world data analysis, showing significant improvements in detection accuracy and robustness compared to existing techniques, particularly in the presence of substantial missing data.
This paper explores the application of deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to optimize residential demand-side management (DSM) in smart grids for cost savings. While DRL agents have shown promise in this domain, their inherent "black-box" nature hinders trust and adoption. This work focuses on developing explainable AI (XAI) techniques to provide insights into the decision-making process of DRL agents trained to control household appliances and energy storage systems. By employing methods such as feature importance analysis and rule extraction, we aim to understand the factors influencing the agent's actions and their impact on reducing electricity bills. The proposed approach not only demonstrates the effectiveness of DRL for DSM but also enhances its transparency, enabling users and grid operators to understand and trust the agent's strategies for achieving cost-effective energy consumption. The results highlight the potential of XAI to bridge the gap between high-performance DRL agents and practical deployment in residential smart grid environments.
Conformal Prediction (CP) offers a powerful and distribution-free framework for quantifying uncertainty in machine learning predictions. Unlike many methods that rely on distributional assumptions or require extensive calibration, CP provides prediction sets or intervals with guaranteed coverage probabilities, regardless of the underlying data distribution. This paper provides a gentle introduction to the core concepts of conformal prediction, focusing on its simplicity and practical applicability. We explore the fundamental principles of exchangeability, nonconformity measures, and the construction of valid and efficient prediction sets. The paper aims to demystify the methodology, making it accessible to researchers and practitioners seeking robust and reliable uncertainty quantification in their machine learning workflows. We illustrate the concepts with clear examples and discuss the advantages and limitations of CP, highlighting its potential for enhancing the trustworthiness and interpretability of predictive models across various domains.
Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) is a crucial imaging modality for diagnosing various retinal diseases. However, training deep learning models for accurate OCT-based diagnosis requires large, expertly labeled datasets, a resource often limited in clinical settings. This work addresses the challenge of achieving accurate OCT-based diagnosis with limited labeled data, reflecting the reality of clinical practice. We propose a novel approach leveraging [mention the key technique/methodology used - e.g., semi-supervised learning, transfer learning, data augmentation] to effectively learn from a small set of labeled OCT images. Our results demonstrate that our method achieves [mention key performance metrics - e.g., comparable accuracy, significantly improved F1-score] to models trained with significantly more labeled data, showcasing its potential for practical clinical application. This research contributes to the development of robust and accurate OCT-based diagnostic tools, even when confronted with the scarcity of labeled data inherent in real-world clinical scenarios.
Segmenting spatio-temporal point clouds is crucial for applications like autonomous driving and robotics, but remains computationally expensive. This paper introduces LatticeNet, a novel and efficient architecture for spatio-temporal point cloud segmentation based on permutohedral lattices. By leveraging the inherent structure of permutohedral lattices, LatticeNet facilitates efficient neighborhood aggregation and feature propagation across both spatial and temporal dimensions. This allows for significant computational savings compared to traditional point-based methods, enabling real-time performance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of LatticeNet on challenging spatio-temporal segmentation datasets, achieving competitive accuracy while significantly reducing processing time. Our results highlight the potential of permutohedral lattices for efficient processing of large-scale spatio-temporal point clouds, paving the way for real-time applications.
## Capturing Omni-Range Context for Omnidirectional Segmentation

Omnidirectional segmentation, a crucial task for understanding 360° scenes, demands effective exploitation of contextual information due to the distorted perspective and global connectivity inherent in equirectangular projection (ERP) images. Existing methods often struggle to capture both short-range and long-range contextual dependencies effectively, leading to fragmented segmentation results. This paper proposes a novel approach to address this challenge by explicitly capturing **omni-range context** for omnidirectional segmentation. Our method leverages a multi-scale contextual aggregation module that integrates information from varying receptive fields. Specifically, we employ dilated convolutions with increasing dilation rates to capture long-range dependencies, while retaining local details through standard convolutions. Furthermore, we introduce a spherical-aware attention mechanism to weigh the importance of contextual features based on their spatial relationships on the sphere, mitigating distortion artifacts. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our proposed method significantly outperforms existing approaches in terms of segmentation accuracy and boundary consistency, showcasing the effectiveness of capturing omni-range context for robust omnidirectional scene understanding.
## Abstract: Learning Representations from Audio-Visual Spatial Alignment

This paper explores a novel approach to learning powerful, multimodal representations by leveraging the inherent spatial alignment between audio and visual signals. We propose a method that encourages a model to learn embeddings where spatially corresponding audio and visual features are closely aligned in a shared representation space. By exploiting the natural co-occurrence and spatial relationships between sounds and their sources in the visual world, our model learns to associate audio events with their visual counterparts, even without explicit labels.
