Points identified as belonging to dynamic objects are down-weighted during optimization, minimizing their impact on the estimated camera trajectory and the reconstructed static scene. We evaluate our system on challenging RGB-D datasets featuring significant dynamic elements, demonstrating improved accuracy and robustness compared to existing SLAM methods in dynamic environments. The results highlight the effectiveness of our point correlation-based approach for decoupling static scene reconstruction from the disruptive effects of moving objects, ultimately enabling more reliable and accurate SLAM performance in real-world scenarios.
Achieving systematic generalization, the ability to apply learned skills to novel situations with compositional variations, remains a significant challenge for deep reinforcement learning (DRL). This paper proposes a novel approach to address this challenge by integrating Task Temporal Logic (TTL) with DRL. We leverage TTL to formally specify task goals, enabling a structured representation of compositional task variations. Our method trains a DRL agent to satisfy TTL specifications, promoting the learning of reusable skills and their compositional structures. By encoding task goals in a formal language, we facilitate the transfer of learned knowledge to unseen tasks with different temporal requirements. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a set of complex, compositional tasks, showcasing its ability to generalize to novel task variations with significantly improved performance compared to traditional DRL methods and other generalization techniques. Our results suggest that explicitly representing task temporal structure with TTL, coupled with DRL, provides a promising avenue for achieving robust systematic generalization in reinforcement learning.
Accurate segmentation of anatomical structures in medical volumes is crucial for diagnosis, treatment planning, and image-guided interventions. However, variations in image acquisition parameters and patient anatomy across different modalities pose significant challenges. This paper introduces a novel approach for translating and segmenting multimodal medical volumes using a Cycle- and Shape-Consistency Generative Adversarial Network (CS-GAN). Our CS-GAN leverages cycle consistency to learn bidirectional mappings between different modalities, enabling the generation of synthetic images that retain essential anatomical information. Furthermore, we incorporate a shape consistency loss that encourages the generated images to maintain the shape characteristics of the original images, leading to improved segmentation accuracy. The proposed method allows for leveraging information from multiple modalities to improve segmentation performance, even when one modality is missing or of poor quality. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on [mention specific dataset(s) if applicable, e.g., brain MRI and CT scans], showing significant improvements in segmentation accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods. Our results highlight the potential of CS-GAN for accurate and robust multimodal medical image analysis.
Data fusion aims to combine information from multiple sources to achieve a more accurate and comprehensive understanding of a phenomenon. However, traditional data fusion techniques can be computationally expensive, hindering their applicability in resource-constrained environments. This paper presents a novel approach to lightweight data fusion using conjugate mappings. We leverage the properties of conjugate functions to efficiently transform and combine data from heterogeneous sources, minimizing computational overhead while preserving essential information. By mapping source data into a shared domain via conjugate transformations, we enable simple and effective fusion operations, such as averaging or weighted averaging. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experimental results on [mention specific application domain, e.g., sensor networks, image processing, etc.], showcasing significant reductions in computational complexity compared to existing methods, while maintaining comparable or improved fusion accuracy. This lightweight approach facilitates data fusion in resource-limited applications, opening possibilities for real-time and embedded systems.
This paper introduces a novel "Plug-in, Trainable Gate" designed to streamline arbitrary neural networks by dynamically controlling information flow. Existing methods for network pruning and compression often require extensive retraining or introduce significant architectural changes. Our approach offers a flexible and minimally invasive solution: a learnable gate that can be seamlessly inserted into existing network architectures. This gate, implemented as a lightweight module, learns to selectively forward or block information based on the input, effectively deactivating redundant or less impactful connections. Crucially, the gate is end-to-end trainable alongside the original network, allowing for efficient adaptation and optimization of the network's computational graph. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach across diverse network architectures and datasets, showcasing significant improvements in model size and inference speed while maintaining or even improving accuracy. Our results highlight the potential of plug-in, trainable gates as a powerful tool for automated network streamlining and efficient deployment of complex neural networks.
Large motion in video sequences poses a significant challenge for video super-resolution (VSR) due to severe misalignment and blur. This paper introduces a novel VSR framework, termed "Large Motion Video Super-Resolution with Dual Subnet and Multi-Stage Communicated Upsampling," designed to effectively address this issue. Our approach employs a dual subnet architecture: one subnet focuses on motion estimation and compensation to align frames, while the other aims to reconstruct high-frequency details. To handle large displacements, we propose a multi-stage communicated upsampling module. This module progressively refines the reconstructed resolution through multiple upsampling stages, exchanging information between adjacent stages to ensure consistency and reduce artifacts. Specifically, the output of each stage is communicated to both the subsequent stage and the final reconstruction module, enabling a more robust and accurate upsampling process. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art VSR algorithms, particularly in scenarios with significant motion, achieving superior performance in terms of both quantitative metrics and visual quality.
This paper proposes a novel graph-based approach for approximating the geodesic distance on statistical manifolds, with application to multimedia information retrieval (MIR). Calculating the exact geodesic distance, a crucial metric for comparing probability distributions represented as points on a manifold, is often computationally prohibitive. Our method constructs a graph representation of the manifold, where nodes correspond to data points and edges are weighted based on local similarity. By leveraging shortest path algorithms on this graph, we efficiently estimate the geodesic distance between any two distributions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach within the context of MIR, specifically for content-based image and audio retrieval. Experimental results on benchmark datasets show that our graph-based geodesic distance approximation achieves comparable accuracy to computationally expensive methods while offering significant speed improvements, leading to enhanced retrieval performance. This work offers a practical and scalable solution for harnessing the power of geodesic distances in various statistical manifold learning applications, particularly in the realm of multimedia analysis.
This paper proposes a novel approach for logo detection, leveraging a Discriminative Semantic Feature Pyramid Network (DSFPN) with Guided Anchoring. The DSFPN enhances the standard Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) by incorporating discriminative semantic information at each pyramid level, enabling the network to better distinguish logos from cluttered backgrounds and similar objects. This is achieved through [mention specific mechanism, e.g., attention mechanisms or semantic segmentation]. Furthermore, we introduce a Guided Anchoring strategy that learns to predict the optimal location and shape of anchors, effectively addressing the challenges posed by varying logo aspect ratios and scales. This guided anchoring mechanism improves recall by reducing the reliance on pre-defined anchor boxes. Experimental results on [mention datasets, e.g., Logo-32, FlickrLogos-32] demonstrate that our proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance in logo detection, surpassing existing methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. The combination of DSFPN and Guided Anchoring significantly improves the robustness and precision of logo detection, making it a promising solution for real-world applications.
Geometric registration of medical images is crucial for various clinical applications, enabling comparison and integration of multi-modal or longitudinal data. Traditional registration methods often rely on visual features, which can be susceptible to variations in image intensity, contrast, and noise. This work explores the potential of deep learning-based registration without explicitly extracting visual features. We investigate the limits of registration accuracy achievable by training deep neural networks to learn direct mappings from image coordinates to deformation fields, effectively bypassing feature extraction. Our approach utilizes only spatial information derived from the image grid itself, allowing the network to learn implicit geometric relationships between images. We evaluate the performance of our proposed method on a variety of medical imaging modalities and demonstrate the attainable accuracy, highlighting the potential for robust and efficient registration even in the absence of reliable visual features. This study provides insights into the fundamental geometric information encoded within medical images and demonstrates the capability of deep learning to leverage this information for accurate and feature-agnostic registration.
## Faster-LTN: A Neuro-Symbolic, End-to-End Object Detection Architecture

Object detection, a crucial task in computer vision, often struggles with reasoning and incorporating prior knowledge. This paper introduces Faster-LTN, a novel neuro-symbolic object detection architecture leveraging Logic Tensor Networks (LTNs) to enhance performance and interpretability. Faster-LTN builds upon a Faster R-CNN backbone, augmenting it with an LTN layer that enforces logical constraints and incorporates symbolic knowledge about object relationships and scene context. This end-to-end trainable architecture allows for seamless integration of neural perception and symbolic reasoning. We demonstrate that Faster-LTN achieves superior performance compared to traditional object detection models, particularly in scenarios with limited data or complex relationships between objects. Furthermore, the LTN layer provides insights into the model's reasoning process, improving transparency and enabling more reliable predictions. Our results showcase the potential of neuro-symbolic approaches for object detection, offering a pathway towards more robust, interpretable, and knowledge-aware vision systems.
Deep neural networks are known to be vulnerable to adversarial examples, raising concerns about their robustness and generalization capabilities. This paper investigates the impact of adversarial training on the transferability of deep models, specifically focusing on image classification tasks. We hypothesize that adversarial training not only improves robustness but also leads to better feature representations that generalize more effectively to unseen datasets. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that adversarially-trained models exhibit significantly improved transfer learning performance compared to standardly-trained counterparts, even when transferring to datasets with differing distributions. Our findings suggest that adversarial training acts as a regularizer, forcing the model to learn more robust and transferable features, thereby enhancing its ability to adapt to new and potentially adversarial environments. This work provides compelling evidence for the benefits of adversarial training beyond robustness, highlighting its potential for improving the overall generalization and transferability of deep learning models.
This paper explores the integration of logical specifications of objectives within the framework of Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning (MORL). Traditional MORL often relies on scalarized reward functions or Pareto front approximations to guide the learning process. However, this can be limiting when dealing with complex, non-linear preferences or when objectives are best expressed through logical relationships. We propose a novel approach that allows agents to learn policies that satisfy objectives defined using temporal logic, specifically Linear Temporal Logic (LTL). By translating LTL formulas into reward shaping functions, we enable the agent to directly optimize for the satisfaction of these logical constraints alongside other numerical objectives. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments in diverse environments, showcasing the ability to learn policies that adhere to complex temporal goals while simultaneously optimizing for multiple quantitative rewards. Our results suggest that incorporating logical specifications provides a more expressive and intuitive way to define and achieve desired behaviors in MORL, leading to more interpretable and controllable learning outcomes.
## Cycle-IR: Deep Cyclic Image Retargeting

Image retargeting aims to adapt an image to a different aspect ratio or resolution while preserving its visual content. This paper introduces Cycle-IR, a novel deep learning framework for image retargeting that leverages a cyclic consistency loss to ensure high-quality and content-preserving results. Unlike traditional methods that often rely on heuristics or local operations, Cycle-IR employs a cycle-consistent generative adversarial network (CycleGAN) architecture. This allows the model to learn bidirectional mappings between different aspect ratios, forcing the retargeted image to be reconstructible to the original image through an inverse mapping. This cyclic constraint significantly reduces artifacts and distortions typically associated with image retargeting. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Cycle-IR through extensive experiments on various datasets, showing its superior performance in terms of both quantitative metrics and qualitative visual assessment compared to state-of-the-art approaches. Our results highlight the benefits of cyclic consistency in achieving robust and visually pleasing image retargeting.
Medical image segmentation is a crucial task for accurate diagnosis, treatment planning, and disease monitoring. While convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable success in this domain, they often struggle with capturing long-range dependencies and global contextual information. Transformers, with their self-attention mechanism, offer a potential solution to address these limitations. This paper introduces the Pyramid Medical Transformer (PMT), a novel architecture designed specifically for medical image segmentation. PMT leverages a hierarchical pyramid structure to extract multi-scale features, effectively capturing both local details and global context. Specifically, we integrate transformer blocks within each pyramid level to model long-range relationships and enhance feature representation. This allows the model to effectively capture contextual information across different scales, leading to improved segmentation accuracy. We evaluate PMT on benchmark medical image segmentation datasets, demonstrating its superior performance compared to state-of-the-art CNN-based and transformer-based methods. The experimental results highlight the effectiveness of the proposed pyramid structure and transformer integration in achieving precise and robust medical image segmentation.
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable success in various graph-related tasks. However, many existing GNN architectures treat all nodes and edges equally within a neighborhood, neglecting the rich structural information present in a node's immediate ego-network. This paper introduces Ego-GNNs, a novel framework that explicitly exploits the ego structures within each node's neighborhood to enhance GNN performance. Ego-GNNs leverage the inherent connections and relationships within a node's ego-network, such as cliques, stars, and other recurring motifs, to learn more informative node embeddings. We propose a novel aggregation mechanism that considers the structural properties of the ego-network, allowing the model to differentiate between nodes based on their position and role within the local graph. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Ego-GNNs on several benchmark datasets for node classification and graph classification, showing significant improvements over state-of-the-art GNN models. Our results highlight the importance of incorporating ego-structural information in GNN architectures for a more nuanced and effective representation learning process.
Automated Machine Learning (AutoML) systems have emerged as powerful tools for simplifying and accelerating the development of machine learning models. However, even within AutoML, the selection of the best AutoML system for a given task remains a challenge. This paper introduces "Ensemble Squared," a meta-AutoML system designed to address this problem. Ensemble Squared leverages an ensemble of diverse base AutoML systems, strategically combining their individual predictions to achieve superior performance and robustness. Crucially, the system learns to dynamically weight the contributions of each base AutoML system based on the characteristics of the input data and the performance of the individual systems on similar tasks. We present empirical results demonstrating that Ensemble Squared consistently outperforms individual state-of-the-art AutoML systems across a range of benchmark datasets, highlighting its effectiveness in adapting to diverse data distributions and model complexities. This work offers a novel approach to meta-AutoML, significantly enhancing the accessibility and performance of automated machine learning for a broader audience.
Anomaly detection in attributed networks, where nodes and edges possess feature information, is a challenging task. Traditional anomaly detection methods often struggle to effectively leverage the complex relationships and feature interactions inherent in such networks. This paper proposes a novel anomaly detection framework based on **One-Class Graph Neural Networks (OCGNN)**. Our approach learns a compact and representative embedding space for normal nodes by training a Graph Neural Network (GNN) using only normal data. This one-class learning paradigm allows the model to capture the underlying structure and feature characteristics of normal nodes, enabling it to distinguish them from anomalous nodes. Specifically, we leverage a GNN architecture to aggregate information from neighboring nodes and features, followed by a one-class objective function that encourages the GNN to map normal nodes close to a central point in the embedding space. Anomaly scores are then computed based on the distance of each node's embedding from this learned center. We evaluate our OCGNN framework on several real-world attributed network datasets, demonstrating its superior performance compared to existing anomaly detection methods. The experimental results highlight the effectiveness of our approach in capturing the complex dependencies within attributed networks and accurately identifying anomalous nodes.
Local-surrogate explainers, such as LIME and SHAP, have become popular tools for understanding individual predictions made by complex machine learning models. However, the process of selecting and defining the specific explanation objective is often overlooked. This abstract argues that the implicit assumptions and choices made in defining what constitutes a "good" explanation for a single instance significantly impact the resulting explanation and its utility. We highlight the importance of explicitly defining explanation objectives, considering factors such as feature sensitivity, counterfactual reasoning, and user-specific needs. By examining the limitations of current practices and proposing avenues for more nuanced and objective-driven approaches, this work aims to contribute to a more robust and reliable application of local-surrogate explainers, ultimately leading to more trustworthy and actionable insights.
This paper presents a comprehensive performance evaluation of deep generative models for generating hand-written character images. We investigate the ability of various architectures, including Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), and their variants, to synthesize realistic and diverse hand-written character images. The evaluation encompasses both qualitative and quantitative metrics. Qualitatively, we visually assess the generated images for clarity, resemblance to real hand-written characters, and the presence of artifacts. Quantitatively, we employ metrics such as Inception Score (IS), Fréchet Inception Distance (FID), and pixel-wise similarity to evaluate the quality, diversity, and fidelity of the generated images. Furthermore, we explore the impact of different hyperparameters and training strategies on the performance of these models. The results highlight the strengths and weaknesses of each architecture in generating hand-written character images and provide insights into selecting the most suitable model for specific applications requiring realistic and diverse character generation. Our findings contribute to the advancement of deep generative models for image synthesis and offer a valuable benchmark for future research in this domain.
This paper explores various defect detection techniques applicable to the sewing stages of airbag production. The critical nature of airbag functionality necessitates robust quality control measures to identify and eliminate defects arising during the sewing process. This abstract outlines a review of both traditional and emerging methods for defect detection, including visual inspection, automated optical inspection (AOI), pressure testing, and advanced techniques like machine learning-based image analysis. The paper analyzes the strengths and limitations of each technique in detecting common sewing defects such as skipped stitches, loose threads, misaligned seams, and fabric damage. Furthermore, it discusses the potential for integrating these techniques to create a comprehensive defect detection system that enhances the reliability and safety of airbags, contributing to improved passenger safety outcomes.
This paper introduces Contrastive Multivariate Singular Spectrum Analysis (CMSSA), a novel method for extracting and enhancing shared oscillatory patterns across multiple time series datasets. Building upon the foundation of Multivariate Singular Spectrum Analysis (MSSA), CMSSA leverages a contrastive learning framework to identify and amplify the common temporal dynamics present in the input data while simultaneously suppressing noise and dataset-specific variations. By constructing positive and negative pairs based on temporal alignment and dataset membership, CMSSA learns a low-dimensional embedding space that emphasizes the shared underlying oscillatory structure. We demonstrate the efficacy of CMSSA through simulations and real-world applications, showcasing its ability to effectively extract coherent signals, improve pattern recognition, and outperform traditional MSSA in scenarios with high noise levels or heterogeneous datasets. The proposed method offers a robust and versatile approach for analyzing complex multivariate time series data and uncovering hidden shared dynamics.
## Abstract: Lip Reading Sentences in the Wild

Automatic lip reading, also known as visual speech recognition, has traditionally focused on constrained environments with controlled lighting and clear articulation. However, real-world applications demand robustness to variations in speaking style, head pose, illumination, and occlusion. This paper addresses the challenging problem of lip reading sentences "in the wild," where such constraints are absent. We explore techniques for robust feature extraction and sequence modeling that can handle the inherent variability and noise present in uncontrolled video data. We introduce InfoBot, a novel reinforcement learning (RL) agent that leverages the Information Bottleneck (IB) principle for improved transfer and exploration. InfoBot learns a compressed representation of its state that captures only the information relevant to predicting future rewards. This compressed representation promotes transfer learning by disentangling task-specific information from irrelevant sensory details, allowing the agent to generalize more effectively to new environments. Simultaneously, the information bottleneck encourages exploration by forcing the agent to discover and represent only the most important features of the environment, thereby reducing the complexity of the learning problem and enabling more efficient exploration strategies. We evaluate InfoBot on a suite of benchmark RL tasks demonstrating its superior performance compared to standard RL algorithms in both transfer learning and exploration settings. Our results highlight the effectiveness of the information bottleneck as a powerful tool for building robust and efficient RL agents.
This paper explores knowledge distillation techniques to improve the efficiency of 3D object detection by transferring knowledge from a multi-frame to a single-frame detector. Multi-frame detectors leverage temporal information to achieve superior accuracy but suffer from increased computational cost and latency. We propose a novel knowledge distillation framework that enables a lightweight, single-frame detector to learn from a more accurate, multi-frame teacher. Our approach focuses on distilling not only the final detection output but also intermediate features and temporal relationships learned by the teacher network. We evaluate our method on benchmark datasets and demonstrate significant performance gains for the single-frame student detector, achieving comparable accuracy to the multi-frame teacher while maintaining real-time processing speeds. This work offers a practical solution for deploying high-performance 3D object detection in resource-constrained environments by effectively bridging the performance gap between multi-frame and single-frame approaches.
