The results highlight the potential of 3D model assistance in achieving more accurate and reliable image segmentation for various applications.
Deep learning has shown remarkable success in robotics, yet its reliance on large, labeled datasets presents a significant bottleneck. Generating realistic synthetic data offers a promising solution to alleviate this data scarcity problem. This paper introduces Stillleben, a novel scene synthesis framework specifically designed to create high-fidelity, labeled images for training deep learning models in robotics. Stillleben leverages physically-based rendering and sophisticated object placement algorithms to generate realistic scenes containing diverse objects, lighting conditions, and camera perspectives. It provides precise control over scene parameters, enabling the creation of tailored datasets optimized for specific robotic tasks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Stillleben by training deep learning models for object detection and pose estimation on synthetic data and evaluating their performance on real-world datasets. Our results show that models trained with Stillleben-generated data achieve significant performance improvements compared to training on limited real-world data alone, highlighting the potential of our framework for accelerating the development of robust and generalizable robotic systems. We also provide open-source access to Stillleben, fostering further research and development in realistic scene synthesis for robotics.
Referring Expression Comprehension (REC) tasks aim to ground natural language descriptions to specific objects in an image. Existing REC datasets often lack complexity in both language and visual scenes. This paper introduces Cops-Ref, a new dataset and task focusing on **Compositional Referring Expression Comprehension**. Cops-Ref features synthetically generated images with multiple objects possessing diverse attributes (color, shape, size, material) and spatial relationships, enabling the creation of more complex and compositional referring expressions. The task requires models to understand the interplay of these attributes and relationships to accurately identify the target object. We provide a detailed analysis of the dataset's characteristics and benchmark the performance of several state-of-the-art REC models. Our results demonstrate that Cops-Ref poses a significant challenge for existing methods, highlighting the need for models capable of robust compositional reasoning and fine-grained visual understanding. We believe Cops-Ref will serve as a valuable resource for advancing research in REC and related areas like visual reasoning and natural language grounding.
Outdoor position recovery using telecommunications (telco) data offers a cost-effective alternative to traditional GPS-based solutions. However, the performance of models trained on telco data is often limited by data scarcity and variations across different geographical regions and network configurations. This paper proposes a transfer learning-based approach to improve outdoor position recovery accuracy by leveraging knowledge from a source domain with abundant telco data to enhance performance in a target domain with limited data. We investigate different transfer learning strategies, including fine-tuning and feature-based approaches, to adapt pre-trained models to the specific characteristics of the target domain.  Experimental results on [mention datasets if applicable, e.g., real-world telco datasets] demonstrate that our transfer learning approach significantly improves the accuracy of outdoor position recovery compared to training models from scratch in the target domain. This work highlights the potential of transfer learning for addressing data scarcity challenges in telco-based location estimation and enabling more accurate and reliable location-aware services.
This paper explores the application of Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) to solve the classic supply chain management challenge known as the Beer Game. Specifically, we propose a Deep Q-Network (DQN) agent to optimize inventory ordering decisions in a simulated Beer Game environment. The DQN agent learns to minimize costs associated with inventory holding and backorders by interacting with the game environment and receiving reward signals. We detail the design and implementation of the DQN agent, including the state space, action space, and reward function. We then evaluate the performance of the DQN agent against traditional heuristic strategies and benchmark results from previous studies. Our findings demonstrate that the DQN agent can effectively learn optimal ordering policies, achieving lower total costs compared to the baselines. This work highlights the potential of DRL, and specifically DQN, as a powerful tool for addressing complex inventory optimization problems in supply chain management and provides a foundation for future research in applying DRL to more realistic and dynamic supply chain scenarios.
Robust and reliable lane detection is crucial for autonomous driving systems. This paper presents a deep learning approach for robust lane detection from continuous driving scenes. Our method leverages a deep neural network architecture, specifically tailored to address the challenges of varying illumination, occlusions, and complex road geometries encountered in real-world driving environments. We propose a novel network design and training strategy that enhances the model's ability to generalize to unseen conditions. Furthermore, we incorporate temporal information from consecutive frames to improve the stability and accuracy of lane detection. The performance of our proposed approach is evaluated on publicly available datasets and demonstrates superior robustness and accuracy compared to state-of-the-art lane detection methods, even under challenging driving scenarios. The results highlight the potential of our method for enabling safer and more reliable autonomous navigation.
## Abstract: Self-Similarity Based Time Warping

Time warping is a powerful technique for aligning time series data that exhibit variations in temporal speed. This abstract introduces a novel approach to time warping based on the principle of self-similarity. By leveraging the inherent repetitive patterns within a single time series, we propose a method that identifies and aligns corresponding segments based on their self-similarity characteristics. This approach avoids the need for external templates or manually defined features, making it suitable for situations where such information is unavailable or unreliable. We present a framework for computing self-similarity matrices and utilizing them to derive optimal warping paths that minimize the distortion between self-similar regions. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in aligning time series with varying temporal distortions, showcasing its potential for applications in areas such as speech recognition, gesture recognition, and bioinformatics. The proposed self-similarity based time warping offers a robust and adaptable solution for aligning time series data by exploiting the inherent structural information present within the data itself.
The Information Bottleneck (IB) principle provides a powerful framework for learning compressed representations that are predictive of relevant information. However, traditional IB methods often struggle with complex data distributions and can lead to suboptimal compression. This paper introduces the Adversarial Information Bottleneck (AIB), a novel approach that leverages adversarial training to improve the performance of IB. In AIB, we train an encoder to minimize the mutual information between the input and the bottleneck representation while simultaneously training an adversary to maximize the same mutual information. This adversarial objective encourages the encoder to discard irrelevant information and retain only the most crucial features for prediction. We demonstrate the effectiveness of AIB on various benchmark datasets, showing that it achieves superior compression and generalization performance compared to existing IB methods. Our results highlight the potential of adversarial learning for enhancing the information bottleneck principle and learning more efficient and robust representations.
Modern object detectors heavily rely on predefined anchor boxes to propose candidate object locations. However, the fixed nature of these anchors often leads to a mismatch between the anchor distribution and the actual object distribution, hindering detection performance. This paper introduces FreeAnchor, a novel anchor matching strategy that learns to dynamically match anchors to target objects. Instead of relying on hand-crafted rules like Intersection-over-Union (IoU) thresholds, FreeAnchor formulates anchor matching as a learning problem. We train the detector to predict the probability of each anchor being matched to a ground-truth object, effectively allowing the network to learn the optimal anchor-to-object assignment. This adaptive matching process enables the detector to focus on the most informative anchors, leading to improved recall and precision, particularly for objects with unusual aspect ratios or sizes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of FreeAnchor on benchmark datasets, showing significant performance gains over existing anchor-based detectors. Our results highlight the importance of learning anchor matching strategies for robust and accurate object detection.
This paper introduces Weather GAN, a novel approach to multi-domain weather translation using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). We address the challenge of transforming weather conditions from one domain (e.g., clear skies) to another (e.g., rainy) without requiring paired training data. Our model leverages a conditional GAN architecture with multiple discriminators, each specialized in a specific weather domain, to enforce realistic and domain-consistent transformations. We demonstrate that Weather GAN can effectively translate between various weather conditions, generating visually plausible and coherent weather maps. Furthermore, we evaluate the performance of our model qualitatively and quantitatively, showing its ability to capture the complex spatial dependencies and inherent characteristics of different weather phenomena. This work has potential applications in weather forecasting, data augmentation for climate modeling, and generating realistic weather scenarios for virtual environments.
This paper presents a novel unsupervised learning framework for visual odometry (VO) from monocular videos, aiming to simultaneously estimate depth and learn a deep representation robust to varying environments. Unlike traditional VO methods that rely on geometric assumptions and feature engineering, our approach leverages deep neural networks trained end-to-end without ground truth depth or pose information. We propose a network architecture that jointly predicts depth maps and camera poses by minimizing a photometric reconstruction loss between consecutive frames. Crucially, we enforce geometric consistency and scale awareness by incorporating a metric scale recovery module, enabling the estimation of VO trajectories in a metric space. The learned deep representation captures salient features relevant for both depth and pose estimation, improving robustness and generalization. We evaluate our method on standard VO benchmarks, demonstrating competitive performance against state-of-the-art unsupervised and even some supervised methods. The results highlight the effectiveness of our approach in learning a robust and scalable monocular VO system capable of operating in a metric space without requiring explicit supervision.
This paper investigates Bayesian algorithms for the decentralized stochastic bandit problem, where multiple agents independently explore and exploit a shared set of stochastic bandit arms with the goal of maximizing cumulative reward across the team. Decentralization introduces challenges due to the lack of direct communication between agents, requiring them to learn and act based solely on their local observations. We propose novel Bayesian algorithms that leverage posterior sampling techniques to balance exploration and exploitation in a distributed manner. These algorithms incorporate mechanisms for implicit coordination, allowing agents to learn about the actions of others indirectly through the observed reward distributions. We analyze the theoretical performance of our algorithms, providing regret bounds that demonstrate their efficiency in minimizing cumulative regret compared to centralized solutions and naive decentralized approaches. Furthermore, we present experimental results on various benchmark bandit environments, demonstrating the practical effectiveness of our Bayesian decentralized algorithms in achieving competitive performance while maintaining communication efficiency.
This paper presents a novel top-down salient object detection approach guided by a pre-trained object classifier. Unlike conventional methods that rely solely on low-level features or bottom-up attention mechanisms, our approach leverages high-level semantic information derived from a classifier to guide the saliency detection process. We first utilize the classifier to identify potential object categories present in the image. This information is then incorporated into a saliency model, effectively biasing the attention towards regions associated with these identified categories. Specifically, we propose a mechanism to modulate the feature maps based on classifier outputs, highlighting features relevant to the predicted object categories. This allows the model to prioritize regions that are not only visually distinct but also semantically meaningful, leading to improved accuracy and robustness in identifying salient objects. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our classifier-guided approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly in challenging scenarios with complex scenes and cluttered backgrounds, showcasing the effectiveness of integrating high-level semantic information into top-down saliency detection.
## Center3D: Center-based Monocular 3D Object Detection with Joint Depth Understanding

Monocular 3D object detection is a challenging task that requires inferring 3D information from a single 2D image. This paper presents Center3D, a novel center-based framework for monocular 3D object detection that leverages joint depth understanding to improve performance. Unlike previous approaches that rely heavily on explicit 3D feature encoding or complex geometric constraints, Center3D directly predicts 3D bounding box parameters from the detected object center. To enhance depth estimation, we propose a joint depth understanding module that integrates semantic information and geometric priors to refine the initial depth prediction. This module implicitly learns the relationship between object semantics, spatial layout, and depth, leading to more accurate and robust 3D localization. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Center3D on the challenging KITTI benchmark, achieving state-of-the-art results compared to existing monocular 3D object detectors. Our experiments highlight the benefits of the center-based approach and the importance of joint depth understanding for accurate 3D object detection from a single image.
Learning the structure of factored Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) from data is a challenging problem with significant implications for efficient reinforcement learning. This paper presents a novel method for learning the structure of factored MDPs using a chi-square tests driven approach. Our method leverages statistical independence tests, specifically chi-square tests, to identify causal relationships between state variables and their influence on reward and next-state transitions. By systematically testing for conditional independence, we construct a graphical representation of the factored MDP, revealing the dependencies between factors and enabling efficient planning and exploration. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on synthetic and benchmark MDP datasets, showcasing its ability to accurately recover the underlying factored structure and outperform existing structure learning algorithms in terms of structural accuracy and computational efficiency. This method offers a promising avenue for scaling reinforcement learning to complex, high-dimensional environments by exploiting the inherent structure present in factored MDPs.
Accurate prediction of human motion is crucial for various applications, ranging from robotics to surveillance. While existing methods have achieved promising results, they often struggle with predicting habit-unrelated, unpredictable movements. This paper introduces Multi-grained Trajectory Graph Convolutional Networks (MG-TGCN), a novel approach designed to capture both fine-grained and coarse-grained relationships within human motion trajectories for improved prediction accuracy, particularly for habit-unrelated actions. MG-TGCN leverages graph convolutional networks to model the spatio-temporal dependencies between different body joints across multiple granularities. We decompose the trajectory into segments of varying lengths, representing both short-term fluctuations and long-term trends. This multi-grained representation, combined with graph convolutions, allows the model to effectively learn intricate motion patterns and better predict future poses, even in the absence of strong habitual behavior. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that MG-TGCN outperforms state-of-the-art methods, especially in scenarios involving unpredictable and habit-unrelated human motions, highlighting its effectiveness in capturing complex and nuanced movement patterns.
This paper introduces a novel approach to improving generalization and exploration in reinforcement learning through the use of randomized value functions. We propose a method that leverages an ensemble of value functions, each initialized with different random parameters, to encourage exploration and facilitate generalization to unseen states. By learning a diverse set of value function estimates, our agent can better represent the uncertainty inherent in the environment and make more informed decisions. We demonstrate that this randomized approach encourages effective exploration by incentivizing the agent to visit states where the value function estimates disagree, thereby reducing epistemic uncertainty. Furthermore, we show that learning from this diverse experience leads to improved generalization performance in unseen environments. We present empirical results across a range of benchmark tasks, demonstrating that our method outperforms existing exploration strategies and achieves state-of-the-art generalization capabilities. Our findings suggest that randomized value functions offer a promising direction for developing more robust and adaptable reinforcement learning agents.
3D multi-object tracking (MOT) is a crucial task in autonomous driving and robotics, requiring robust and efficient object association across time. This paper introduces a novel approach for 3D MOT based on **learnable online graph representations**. We propose to construct a dynamic graph where nodes represent object detections and edges encode their relationships, capturing both spatial and temporal context. Crucially, we learn the graph structure and node/edge features online using a neural network trained end-to-end with the tracking objective. This allows the model to adapt to evolving scene dynamics and learn more informative representations compared to hand-crafted features. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on challenging 3D MOT benchmarks, showing significant improvements in tracking accuracy and robustness, particularly in scenarios with frequent occlusions and identity switches. Our results highlight the benefits of learning online graph representations for achieving robust and efficient 3D MOT.
This paper investigates the inherent perception-distortion tradeoff in super-resolution (SR) image reconstruction. While traditional SR methods prioritize minimizing distortion metrics like PSNR and SSIM, they often result in overly smooth and perceptually unsatisfying results. Conversely, networks optimized for perceptual quality can introduce artifacts and distortions. To address this challenge, we propose an Enhanced Perceptual Super-Resolution Network (EPSRN) that aims to balance both perceptual fidelity and low distortion. EPSRN incorporates novel architectural components and training strategies designed to improve perceptual realism without sacrificing fidelity to the ground truth. We analyze the performance of EPSRN against state-of-the-art SR methods using both quantitative metrics and subjective evaluations, demonstrating its ability to achieve a favorable perception-distortion balance. Our results show that EPSRN generates visually appealing high-resolution images with improved perceptual quality while maintaining competitive distortion metrics, offering a promising solution for real-world SR applications.
Recommender systems often struggle with the "cold start" problem, where new users or items lack sufficient interaction data for accurate predictions. This paper proposes a novel approach to mitigate cold start using Hierarchical Graph Neural Networks (HGNNs). We leverage the inherent hierarchical structure within user-item relationships and item content to construct a multi-level graph representation. This graph captures both fine-grained similarities between entities based on features and coarse-grained relationships based on category or attribute hierarchies. The HGNN then learns embeddings that incorporate information from multiple levels, enabling effective propagation of knowledge from well-established users/items to those with limited interaction history. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed HGNN-based framework through experiments on real-world datasets, showing significant improvements in recommendation accuracy for cold start users and items compared to state-of-the-art methods. Our results highlight the benefits of hierarchical graph modeling in addressing the cold start challenge and improving the overall performance of recommender systems.
Few-shot learning presents a significant challenge for Parkinson's disease (PD) speech recognition, where labeled data is scarce. This paper introduces a novel Deep Double-Side Learning Ensemble (DDSLE) model designed to address this challenge. DDSLE leverages the power of deep learning with a double-side learning strategy, simultaneously focusing on both feature representation learning and classifier adaptation.  On the feature representation side, a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) is employed to extract robust and discriminative speech features. On the classifier adaptation side, a meta-learning based approach is utilized to quickly adapt the classifier to new tasks with limited labeled samples.  Furthermore, an ensemble learning framework combines multiple independently trained DDSLE models to enhance robustness and generalization performance.  Experimental results on a benchmark PD speech dataset demonstrate that the proposed DDSLE model significantly outperforms existing few-shot learning methods, achieving superior accuracy and demonstrating its effectiveness in recognizing PD speech with limited labeled data.
## Retina U-Net: Embarrassingly Simple Exploitation of Segmentation Supervision for Medical Object Detection

This paper introduces Retina U-Net, a novel and surprisingly effective approach to medical object detection that leverages existing segmentation annotations. Instead of relying on complex object detection architectures, we propose a simple modification to the U-Net segmentation model. By directly regressing bounding box parameters (center coordinates, width, and height) from the feature maps of the U-Net decoder, we create a unified framework that simultaneously performs segmentation and detection. This "embarrassingly simple" approach eliminates the need for dedicated detection heads, anchor boxes, or non-maximum suppression. We demonstrate the efficacy of Retina U-Net on [mention a specific medical imaging dataset, e.g., a retinal vessel dataset and a lung nodule dataset], achieving competitive detection performance compared to more complex object detection methods, while maintaining state-of-the-art segmentation accuracy. Our results highlight the potential of exploiting segmentation supervision for object detection in medical imaging, offering a computationally efficient and easily implementable alternative for scenarios where segmentation annotations are readily available.
Deep neural networks, while achieving state-of-the-art performance in various tasks, are vulnerable to adversarial attacks that can easily fool them. This paper investigates the generation of adversarial attacks specifically designed to both mislead the network's prediction (fooling) and simultaneously influence the network's explanation of its decision-making process (explaining). We propose a novel attack strategy that leverages the inherent connection between input features and their contribution to the final prediction, as revealed by explanation techniques such as gradient-based attribution methods. Our approach aims to craft perturbations that not only cause misclassification but also manipulate the explanation maps to highlight misleading or nonsensical features as being critical for the incorrect prediction. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our attack on benchmark image classification datasets, showing that it can successfully fool networks while simultaneously manipulating their explanations. This work highlights the potential for adversaries to not only disrupt deep learning systems but also undermine trust in their interpretability, emphasizing the need for robust and explainable deep learning models.
This paper presents a novel LiDAR ground filtering algorithm tailored for complex urban environments. The proposed approach utilizes scan line based segmentation to effectively separate ground points from non-ground objects. The algorithm first organizes LiDAR point clouds into scan lines, then segments each line based on geometric features such as height difference and slope changes. These segments are then classified as ground or non-ground through a progressive filtering process that leverages contextual information within and between scan lines. The algorithm is designed to handle the challenges posed by urban landscapes, including varying terrain, buildings, vegetation, and elevated road structures. Performance evaluation on real-world urban LiDAR datasets demonstrates the algorithm's ability to accurately extract ground points while preserving terrain details and minimizing misclassification of low-lying objects. The results indicate that the scan line based segmentation provides a robust and efficient method for ground filtering in densely built environments.
Multi-domain image segmentation aims to develop models capable of accurately segmenting images from diverse and unseen domains. However, domain shifts in image appearance and statistical properties often lead to significant performance degradation when applying models trained on limited source domains to new target domains. To address this, we propose **Adversarial Normalization** (AN), a novel approach that leverages adversarial learning to promote domain-invariant feature representations. AN introduces a domain discriminator trained to distinguish between features extracted from different domains after normalization. By adversarially training the segmentation network to fool the discriminator, we encourage the normalization layers to align feature distributions across domains, thereby reducing domain-specific biases. We evaluate our approach on several challenging multi-domain image segmentation benchmarks and demonstrate that AN significantly improves generalization performance on unseen target domains compared to existing domain adaptation and generalization techniques. Our results highlight the effectiveness of adversarial normalization in learning robust and domain-agnostic feature representations for multi-domain image segmentation.
Underwater images often suffer from poor visibility due to light absorption and scattering, hindering visual perception and limiting the effectiveness of underwater robotics and marine research. This paper presents a fast and effective image enhancement method specifically designed to address these challenges. The proposed approach leverages [mention key technique, e.g., a simplified dark channel prior, a frequency-domain transformation, a lightweight neural network] to efficiently estimate and compensate for the effects of light attenuation and color distortion. By minimizing computational complexity while maximizing perceptual quality, the method enables real-time or near-real-time processing of underwater imagery. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed technique significantly improves image contrast, color fidelity, and overall visual clarity compared to existing methods, while maintaining a significantly faster processing speed. This enhanced visual quality facilitates improved object recognition, navigation, and situational awareness in underwater environments.
This paper proposes an attention-aware cost volume pyramid-based multi-view stereo (MVS) network for accurate and efficient 3D reconstruction. Building upon the cost volume pyramid approach, we introduce an attention mechanism to adaptively refine the cost volume at each pyramid level, focusing on informative features and suppressing irrelevant noise. This attention module leverages both spatial and channel-wise attention to effectively guide the network towards regions with high photometric consistency and discriminative features. Furthermore, we employ a cascaded architecture with progressive refinement to gradually improve the depth map estimation. Experiments on standard MVS datasets demonstrate that our proposed network achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of accuracy and completeness while maintaining competitive efficiency, showcasing the effectiveness of the attention mechanism and the cost volume pyramid architecture for robust 3D reconstruction from multiple views.
## TSPNet: Hierarchical Feature Learning via Temporal Semantic Pyramid for Sign Language Translation

Sign language translation (SLT) aims to automatically translate sign language videos into spoken language. Existing approaches often struggle with capturing the multi-scale temporal dependencies and semantic relationships crucial for accurate translation. To address this, we propose TSPNet, a novel hierarchical feature learning framework leveraging a Temporal Semantic Pyramid (TSP) for SLT. TSPNet constructs a pyramid of features at different temporal resolutions, enabling the model to capture both fine-grained movements and long-range dependencies within the sign language sequence. Specifically, we employ a hierarchical convolutional network to extract local features, followed by a multi-stage temporal pooling and semantic encoding module to build the TSP. This module progressively aggregates and refines temporal information, generating semantic representations at multiple levels. These multi-scale features are then fused and decoded into the target spoken language. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that TSPNet significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, highlighting the effectiveness of our hierarchical feature learning approach and the benefits of the Temporal Semantic Pyramid for capturing complex temporal and semantic information in sign language videos.
This paper introduces Self-Grouping Convolutional Neural Networks (SGCNNs), a novel approach to dynamic filter grouping within convolutional layers. Traditional convolutional neural networks employ a fixed filter structure, limiting their adaptability to varying input features. SGCNNs address this limitation by enabling filters to self-organize into groups based on learned similarities. This self-grouping mechanism allows the network to dynamically allocate computational resources to relevant feature representations, enhancing feature extraction and improving performance. We propose a differentiable grouping module that learns to assign filters to clusters during training, effectively creating specialized filter banks.  Experimental results on benchmark image classification datasets demonstrate that SGCNNs achieve superior accuracy and efficiency compared to conventional convolutional architectures and other dynamic filter selection methods.  The learned filter groupings provide insights into the network's feature representation and highlight the potential for improved model interpretability.
This paper explores the use of autoencoders for discovering "traveling companions" – individuals or entities exhibiting similar movement patterns across a given spatiotemporal dataset. Traditional methods for identifying such relationships often rely on predefined similarity metrics or clustering algorithms, which can be limited by their sensitivity to noise, varying data densities, and the need for manual parameter tuning. We propose a novel approach leveraging autoencoders to learn a compressed, latent representation of individual movement trajectories. By training an autoencoder on a dataset of trajectories, we capture the underlying structural patterns and reduce the dimensionality of the data. The resulting latent vectors are then used to compute a similarity score between trajectories, effectively revealing individuals or entities that share similar movement characteristics. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on [mention dataset type, e.g., real-world GPS data, synthetic trajectories] and show that it outperforms traditional methods in [mention specific evaluation criteria, e.g., identifying known traveling partners, handling noisy data, capturing complex movement patterns]. This method offers a robust and scalable solution for uncovering meaningful relationships based on movement behavior in various applications, including transportation planning, social network analysis, and wildlife monitoring.
## Abstract: Property Inference for Deep Neural Networks

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success in various applications, but their opaque nature raises concerns about understanding and controlling their behavior. Property inference, the task of inferring attributes or characteristics of the training data or the network itself from the trained model, has emerged as a critical area of research. This abstract explores the landscape of property inference attacks and defenses for DNNs. We discuss various techniques employed to infer properties, including membership inference, attribute inference, and model extraction, highlighting their strengths and limitations. Furthermore, we analyze the underlying vulnerabilities that enable these attacks and review existing defense mechanisms designed to mitigate the risk of property leakage. Finally, we discuss open challenges and future directions in this evolving field, emphasizing the need for robust and privacy-preserving DNN development.
Accurate detection of pelvic fractures in X-ray images is crucial for timely diagnosis and treatment. However, challenges arise from subtle fracture patterns, anatomical variations, and image noise. This paper introduces an Anatomy-Aware Siamese Network that exploits semantic asymmetry within the pelvis to improve fracture detection accuracy. The proposed network leverages a Siamese architecture to compare regions of interest (ROIs) from both sides of the pelvis, enabling the model to learn subtle differences indicative of fractures. Furthermore, we incorporate anatomical prior knowledge by guiding the network to focus on key anatomical structures and their relationships, enhancing its ability to differentiate between normal variations and pathological conditions. Experimental results on a diverse pelvic fracture dataset demonstrate that our Anatomy-Aware Siamese Network significantly outperforms existing methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance in pelvic fracture detection and showcasing the effectiveness of exploiting semantic asymmetry and anatomical awareness in medical image analysis.
Object detection in large images presents a significant challenge due to computational constraints and the prevalence of small or distant objects. This paper introduces a novel **Dynamic Zoom-in Network (DZN)** designed for fast and accurate object detection in such scenarios. DZN employs a multi-stage, coarse-to-fine approach where the network dynamically focuses on promising regions of interest within the large image. Initially, a low-resolution, computationally efficient stage performs a global scan to identify potential object locations. Subsequently, the network dynamically zooms into these regions, progressively increasing resolution and refining object predictions. This dynamic focusing mechanism allows DZN to efficiently allocate computational resources to relevant areas, significantly reducing processing time compared to traditional methods that process the entire image at high resolution. We demonstrate through experiments on challenging large-image datasets that DZN achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of speed and accuracy, particularly for detecting small and distant objects, making it a practical solution for real-time object detection applications in large-scale imagery.
## AlignMix: Improving Representation by Interpolating Aligned Features

This paper introduces AlignMix, a novel approach to improve representation learning by leveraging feature alignment and interpolation. We hypothesize that features corresponding to semantically similar regions across different instances contain valuable information for generalization. AlignMix explicitly aligns features from different instances based on their spatial correspondence and then interpolates these aligned features to generate new, augmented representations. This process encourages the model to learn more robust and generalizable features by exposing it to a richer set of variations within the data. We evaluate AlignMix on various benchmark datasets and demonstrate significant improvements in performance across different tasks, including image classification and semantic segmentation. Our results highlight the effectiveness of feature alignment and interpolation as a powerful technique for enhancing representation learning and achieving state-of-the-art results.
Model inversion attacks aim to reconstruct sensitive training data from a trained machine learning model. Existing attacks often rely on gradient information or specific model architectures. This paper introduces a novel approach to model inversion that leverages explanations, specifically feature importance scores, to guide the reconstruction process. We hypothesize that explanations, by revealing the model's reliance on specific features, provide valuable constraints that can significantly improve the accuracy and efficiency of inversion attacks. We propose a framework that integrates explanation information into the optimization objective of a traditional inversion attack, guiding the search towards data points that not only match the target model's predictions but also exhibit similar feature importance profiles. We evaluate our approach on various datasets and model architectures, demonstrating that exploiting explanations leads to substantial improvements in reconstruction quality, particularly in scenarios where gradient information is limited or noisy. Our findings highlight the vulnerability of models to explanation-guided inversion attacks and underscore the importance of considering explanation methods as potential attack vectors when designing and deploying machine learning models.
## Iterative Bounding MDPs: Learning Interpretable Policies via Non-Interpretable Methods

This paper introduces a novel framework, Iterative Bounding MDPs (IB-MDPs), for learning interpretable policies in complex environments. We address the challenge of balancing performance and interpretability by leveraging powerful, but often opaque, reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms. Our approach involves iteratively constructing simpler, bounded Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) that approximate the original environment. These bounded MDPs are designed to be amenable to interpretable policy extraction methods, such as decision trees or rule-based systems. We train a high-performing, potentially non-interpretable RL agent on the original environment, and then use its behavior to define the state and action spaces of the bounded MDP. Subsequently, we learn an interpretable policy within this simplified environment. This iterative process allows us to refine the bounded MDP based on the performance of the interpretable policy, gradually increasing its complexity while maintaining interpretability. We demonstrate the effectiveness of IB-MDPs on a variety of benchmark tasks, showing that we can achieve competitive performance with significantly more interpretable policies compared to directly applying interpretable RL methods to the original environment. Our results highlight the potential of IB-MDPs to bridge the gap between performance and interpretability in RL, enabling the deployment of trustworthy and understandable AI systems.
Disentangled representation learning aims to discover independent factors underlying observed data, often with the promise of improved generalization and interpretability. However, many existing methods struggle to produce representations that are robust to interventions or distributional shifts. In this work, we propose a framework for learning and validating **robustly disentangled causal mechanisms**. We leverage causal modeling to explicitly define the relationships between latent factors and observed variables, focusing on identifying representations where interventions on one latent factor lead to predictable and localized changes in the observed data. We introduce a novel validation procedure that uses interventional data to assess the faithfulness of the learned causal graph and the robustness of the disentangled factors. This procedure measures the consistency of observed changes with predicted causal effects based on the learned representation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on synthetic and real-world datasets, showing that it can learn representations that are both disentangled and robust to interventions, leading to improved performance on downstream tasks requiring interventional reasoning. Our findings provide a step towards building reliable and interpretable AI systems that can reason about and adapt to changing environments.

This paper introduces Styleformer, a novel generative adversarial network (GAN) architecture leveraging the power of Transformers for image generation with explicit style control. Unlike traditional GANs, Styleformer employs a Transformer-based generator that modulates image synthesis through a style vector. This style vector, learned from the latent space, is injected into the Transformer layers, enabling fine-grained control over various stylistic attributes of the generated images. The discriminator is also designed to effectively evaluate the generated images while considering the provided style vector. We demonstrate that Styleformer achieves state-of-the-art performance in generating high-resolution images with disentangled style manipulation. Experimental results on benchmark datasets show that Styleformer outperforms existing GAN architectures in terms of image quality, diversity, and style transfer capabilities, offering a promising approach for controllable image generation.
Hierarchical Support Vector Regression (HSVR) is a powerful technique for modeling complex, multi-scale data by decomposing the regression task into a hierarchy of simpler sub-problems. A key challenge in HSVR is determining the optimal number of layers in the hierarchy, as too few layers may fail to capture the data's underlying structure, while too many can lead to overfitting and increased computational cost. This paper investigates the problem of predicting the critical number of layers in HSVR, defined as the point where adding further layers provides diminishing returns in terms of prediction accuracy. We propose a novel approach that leverages [mention key features of your approach, e.g., statistical measures of data complexity, model performance metrics on validation sets, or theoretical bounds]. We evaluate our approach on [mention datasets used] and demonstrate its effectiveness in accurately predicting the critical number of layers, resulting in improved model performance and reduced computational complexity compared to traditional grid search or cross-validation methods. Our findings provide valuable insights for designing efficient and accurate HSVR models for a wide range of applications.
This paper introduces Poet, a novel product-oriented video captioner designed specifically for e-commerce applications. Existing video captioning models often generate generic descriptions, failing to highlight key product features and benefits crucial for online sales. Poet addresses this limitation by leveraging a product-aware architecture that integrates object detection, attribute extraction, and contextual understanding to generate descriptive captions tailored to showcase the product's value proposition. We present a detailed architecture of Poet, including its training methodology and evaluation metrics. Experimental results demonstrate that Poet significantly outperforms state-of-the-art general-purpose video captioning models in generating informative and persuasive captions that are more relevant and engaging for potential e-commerce customers. This work offers a practical solution for automating the creation of compelling product descriptions, ultimately improving online shopping experiences and driving sales.
## Abstract: Deep Representation Learning for Multimodal Brain Networks

Understanding the intricate relationships within and between different brain regions requires the integration of diverse neuroimaging modalities. This work explores the application of deep representation learning techniques to construct informative and compact embeddings of multimodal brain networks. We propose a novel approach that leverages [**mention specific architecture, e.g., graph neural networks, autoencoders, contrastive learning**] to learn latent representations from brain networks derived from [**mention modalities, e.g., fMRI, DTI, EEG**]. ## Abstract: How Many Moments Does MMD Compare?

The Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) is a popular kernel-based non-parametric test for comparing probability distributions. It operates by embedding distributions into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) and measuring the distance between their mean embeddings. A common misconception is that MMD compares a fixed number of moments of the distributions. This work clarifies the relationship between MMD and moment comparisons. We demonstrate that the number of moments effectively compared by MMD is implicitly determined by the choice of kernel. Specifically, we analyze the moment matching properties of different kernels and show how the kernel's smoothness and characteristic properties influence the number and type of moments that contribute to the MMD value. Our analysis provides insights into the sensitivity of MMD to differences in distributions and helps guide the selection of appropriate kernels for specific applications where moment matching is a desirable property. Ultimately, we argue that MMD implicitly compares an infinite number of moments, weighted according to the kernel's properties, making it a powerful tool for detecting subtle distributional differences beyond simple moment disparities.
Medical image classification is crucial for accurate and timely diagnosis, but often suffers from limited labeled data. This paper proposes a novel Unsupervised Deep Transfer Feature Learning (UDTFL) approach to address this challenge. UDTFL leverages knowledge from a large, unlabeled source domain dataset (e.g., natural images) to learn robust and generalizable features, which are then transferred to the target medical image classification task. The core of our method involves training a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) on the source domain using an unsupervised learning objective, such as autoencoding or contrastive learning. The learned feature representations are subsequently transferred to the target domain, where a lightweight classifier is trained using the available, albeit limited, labeled medical images. By decoupling feature learning from the target task and leveraging unsupervised pre-training, UDTFL effectively mitigates the overfitting issues associated with small datasets and improves classification performance. We evaluate our approach on several medical image datasets and demonstrate significant improvements compared to traditional supervised learning methods and other transfer learning techniques. Our results highlight the potential of UDTFL for enhancing medical image classification accuracy in data-scarce environments.
This paper presents a variational Bayesian (VB) approach for parameter estimation and inference in Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) with multivariate Gaussian emission distributions.  Traditional methods, such as Expectation-Maximization (EM), can suffer from overfitting and provide only point estimates of the model parameters.  The proposed VB method addresses these limitations by inferring full posterior distributions over the HMM parameters (transition probabilities, emission means and covariances, and initial state probabilities). This allows for a more robust and principled approach to model selection, uncertainty quantification, and prediction. We derive the variational update equations for each parameter based on the mean-field approximation, leading to a computationally efficient iterative algorithm. The effectiveness of the method is demonstrated through simulated data and compared against EM, showcasing its ability to avoid local optima and provide more accurate estimates of the model parameters and their uncertainties. Furthermore, we explore the benefits of the VB approach in applications where accurate uncertainty estimation is crucial, such as anomaly detection and time series forecasting.
Many real-world phenomena are naturally represented as sets of entities, but analyzing their relationships often requires understanding the underlying graph structure. This paper introduces Set2Graph, a novel framework for learning graphs from sets. Set2Graph leverages set representation learning to encode each set into a latent embedding, which is then used to construct a graph where nodes correspond to sets and edges represent relationships inferred from their embeddings. We explore different methods for edge creation and weighting, including similarity-based and learned approaches. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Set2Graph on various tasks, including node classification and link prediction, showing its ability to capture meaningful relationships between sets and generate graphs that outperform baselines built on simple set overlap. Our results highlight the potential of Set2Graph for applications where graph structure is implicit in set data, enabling graph-based analysis and reasoning in domains such as collaborative filtering, biological network discovery, and document analysis.
Hierarchical Imitation and Reinforcement Learning (HIRL) offers a powerful paradigm for tackling complex, long-horizon tasks by combining the strengths of both imitation learning (IL) and reinforcement learning (RL). This abstract explores the core principles and benefits of HIRL, highlighting how it leverages hierarchical structures to decompose tasks into simpler, more manageable sub-goals. By first learning a hierarchical policy through imitation of expert demonstrations, the system can acquire a strong initial policy and a meaningful task decomposition. Subsequently, RL techniques are employed to refine and optimize the learned hierarchy, improving robustness, generalization, and overall performance. This approach addresses limitations of traditional RL methods in sparse reward environments and allows for efficient exploration and learning. We discuss common approaches to HIRL, including options frameworks, skill discovery, and meta-learning, and outline the potential for HIRL to advance the development of intelligent agents capable of solving intricate real-world problems.
Multi-source domain adaptation (MSDA) aims to transfer knowledge from multiple labeled source domains to an unlabeled target domain. A key challenge in MSDA lies in effectively mitigating the domain discrepancy between the sources and the target. This paper addresses the problem of MSDA under **target shift**, where the target distribution differs significantly from the convex combination of the source distributions. We propose a novel approach based on **optimal transport (OT)** that explicitly models and corrects for this target shift. Our method leverages OT to align each source domain with a **pseudo-target** domain, which is obtained by iteratively refining an initial estimate of the true target distribution. The OT plan minimizes the transportation cost between source and pseudo-target samples, while simultaneously encouraging class consistency. By iteratively updating the pseudo-target and the alignment plans, our method effectively bridges the gap between the source domains and the true target distribution, leading to improved generalization performance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, showing significant improvements over state-of-the-art MSDA methods, particularly in scenarios with pronounced target shift.
The increasing availability of high-resolution 3D data acquired from Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) using LiDAR and Multi-View-Stereo (MVS) techniques presents significant opportunities for automated scene understanding. However, the lack of publicly available, large-scale, and accurately labeled datasets hinders the development and evaluation of semantic segmentation algorithms for these data modalities. This paper introduces the Hessigheim 3D (H3D) benchmark, a novel dataset comprising high-resolution 3D point clouds and textured meshes of the Hessigheim vineyard region, captured using both UAV LiDAR and MVS. The dataset encompasses diverse land cover classes including vegetation, buildings, roads, and terrain, and provides meticulously curated ground truth labels. We describe the data acquisition and labeling process, detail the dataset characteristics, and present baseline results for various semantic segmentation approaches. The H3D benchmark aims to foster research in 3D semantic segmentation, enabling the development and benchmarking of robust and accurate algorithms for processing high-resolution 3D data derived from UAV platforms. The dataset and evaluation tools are made publicly available to facilitate further research and advancements in this field.
This paper explores the application of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to the problem of solid texture synthesis. Solid textures, unlike surface textures, define material properties throughout a volume, enabling realistic rendering of cutaway views and complex shapes. We propose a novel GAN architecture tailored for learning and generating high-quality, three-dimensional solid textures. Our approach leverages a 3D convolutional generator to synthesize volumetric texture data from random noise, while a discriminator learns to distinguish between real and generated textures. By training the GAN adversarially, we achieve the generation of diverse and visually compelling solid textures with complex patterns and structures. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through qualitative and quantitative comparisons with existing solid texture synthesis techniques, highlighting its ability to produce realistic and seamless textures with improved computational efficiency. The results demonstrate the potential of GANs for automating the creation of complex material models in computer graphics and related fields.
Link prediction, the task of inferring missing connections in a knowledge graph, is crucial for various applications. Existing approaches often rely on either inductive or transductive embedding methods. Inductive embeddings learn generalizable representations that can be applied to unseen nodes, while transductive embeddings focus on optimizing representations specifically for the observed graph structure. This paper proposes a novel framework that integrates the strengths of both inductive and transductive embeddings for improved link prediction accuracy. Our approach leverages an inductive embedding model to generate initial node representations and then refines these representations using a transductive learning objective that considers the observed graph structure.  Experimental results on several benchmark datasets demonstrate that our integrated approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art inductive and transductive methods, highlighting the benefits of combining generalizable knowledge with graph-specific structural information for link prediction.
Face recognition has emerged as a crucial technology with widespread applications across various domains. This paper presents a novel multi-level taxonomy-based survey of the face recognition landscape. Unlike existing surveys that often focus on specific aspects or methodologies, this work provides a comprehensive and structured overview of the field. The proposed taxonomy categorizes face recognition techniques at multiple levels, considering factors such as data acquisition methods, feature extraction approaches, classification algorithms, and performance evaluation metrics. This hierarchical classification allows for a deeper understanding of the interrelationships between different techniques and their respective strengths and weaknesses. The survey synthesizes a vast body of research, analyzes recent advancements, and identifies promising directions for future research. By providing a structured and comprehensive framework, this survey aims to serve as a valuable resource for researchers, practitioners, and students seeking to navigate the complex and rapidly evolving field of face recognition.
Unpaired image-to-image translation aims to learn the mapping between two visual domains without requiring explicit correspondence. This paper introduces AttentionGAN, a novel Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) architecture that leverages attention mechanisms to improve the quality and consistency of generated images in unpaired image-to-image translation. AttentionGAN incorporates an attention module within both the generator and discriminator, allowing the model to focus on relevant regions of the input and output images during the translation process. The attention module guides the generator to selectively modify specific image regions based on the characteristics of the target domain, while the discriminator utilizes attention to better distinguish between real and fake images, particularly in regions crucial for domain-specific features. Through extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that AttentionGAN achieves superior performance compared to existing unpaired image-to-image translation methods, generating visually appealing and semantically consistent images with improved detail and reduced artifacts. Our results highlight the effectiveness of attention mechanisms in guiding the translation process and enhancing the capabilities of GANs for unpaired image-to-image translation.
Visual Question Answering (VQA) requires understanding both the visual content of an image and the semantic meaning of a natural language question to generate an accurate answer. A crucial step in this process is identifying the relevant regions within the image that are most pertinent to answering the given question. This paper investigates the problem of *where to look* in VQA, focusing on the development and evaluation of methods for predicting and leveraging *focus regions* – areas of the image that are highly informative for answering specific questions. We explore different approaches for generating these focus regions, including attention mechanisms, object detection, and salient region segmentation. We then analyze how incorporating these focus regions into existing VQA models impacts performance, examining the effectiveness of different strategies for weighting and integrating region-specific information. Our results demonstrate that explicitly focusing on relevant image regions significantly improves VQA accuracy, highlighting the importance of targeted visual grounding for effective question answering. We further identify the strengths and weaknesses of different focus region generation techniques, providing insights for future research in this area.
Neural Discrete Representation Learning focuses on learning representations of data where information is encoded in discrete, rather than continuous, latent variables. This approach offers several advantages, including enhanced interpretability, efficient memory usage, and the ability to perform symbolic reasoning. This abstract provides an overview of the key techniques and challenges in this rapidly evolving field. We discuss various methods for inducing discreteness in neural networks, such as vector quantization, Gumbel-Softmax, and variational approaches. We also highlight the challenges associated with training discrete models, particularly the non-differentiability of discrete operations and the resulting difficulties in gradient-based optimization. Furthermore, we explore applications of neural discrete representation learning across diverse domains, including image compression, natural language processing, reinforcement learning, and program synthesis. Finally, we discuss future research directions and potential advancements in this area, emphasizing the growing importance of discrete representations for building more robust, interpretable, and efficient AI systems.
Reinforcement Learning (RL) often struggles to generalize effectively to unseen environments or tasks, particularly when dealing with variable-sized input sets representing observations, state spaces, or action spaces.  This paper explores the application of Deep Sets, a class of neural networks specifically designed to handle unordered sets of elements, to improve generalization in RL. We hypothesize that by leveraging the permutation invariance and expressive power of Deep Sets, we can build RL agents that are more robust to variations in the composition and size of input sets. We investigate different architectures based on Deep Sets within the context of both policy-based and value-based RL, focusing on tasks with set-structured observations. Our experiments demonstrate that agents utilizing Deep Sets exhibit superior generalization performance compared to traditional approaches like fully connected networks when faced with variations in the input set size and distribution.  We analyze the learned representations and discuss the implications of Deep Sets for developing more generalizable and robust RL agents in complex environments.
This paper introduces a novel batch transform for Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) called "Whitening and Coloring (WC) batch transform." This transform aims to improve GAN training stability and sample diversity by decoupling and reshaping the feature distribution within each batch. First, a whitening operation decorrelates and normalizes the features, preventing feature collapse and promoting more independent feature representations. Subsequently, a coloring operation learns to re-introduce correlations based on a learned color matrix, allowing the GAN to learn complex dependencies between features and generate more realistic and diverse samples. We demonstrate the effectiveness of WC batch transform on various benchmark datasets, showing significant improvements in Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) and Inception Score (IS) compared to baseline GAN architectures and other batch normalization techniques. The results suggest that WC batch transform effectively promotes both feature diversity and realistic image generation, leading to more robust and high-quality GAN models.
This paper explores a novel approach to visual learning that leverages ambient sound as a form of supervision. Traditionally, visual learning relies on large, labeled datasets, which are expensive and time-consuming to acquire. We propose "Learning Sight from Sound" (LSFS), a framework that exploits the inherent correlation between visual scenes and their corresponding auditory environments. By training a visual model to predict the characteristics of the ambient sound associated with an image, we can implicitly teach the model to recognize and understand visual features relevant to the soundscape. We demonstrate that LSFS can learn meaningful visual representations from unlabeled image-sound pairs, achieving comparable performance to supervised methods in tasks such as object recognition and scene classification. Our findings suggest that ambient sound offers a readily available and scalable source of supervision for visual learning, paving the way for more efficient and robust visual models.
LiDAR-based object detection is crucial for autonomous systems, but vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper investigates the generation of physically realizable adversarial examples that can fool LiDAR-based object detectors in real-world scenarios. We propose a novel method for crafting adversarial point clouds that are constrained by physical limitations, such as sensor noise and object placement, ensuring they can be plausibly deployed in the physical world. Our approach optimizes for imperceptibility and effectiveness, balancing the magnitude of added adversarial noise with the resulting degradation in detection performance.  We demonstrate the feasibility of our method through simulations and present experimental results showing a significant reduction in detection accuracy for state-of-the-art LiDAR object detectors when subjected to our physically realizable adversarial examples. This work highlights the vulnerability of LiDAR-based perception systems and emphasizes the need for robust defense mechanisms against physical adversarial attacks.
Hyperparameter Optimization (HPO) plays a crucial role in achieving optimal performance for machine learning models. However, the landscape of HPO benchmarks often lacks realistic scenarios and efficient evaluation methods. In this work, we introduce YAHPO Gym, a novel HPO benchmark suite designed to address these limitations. We outline the design criteria guiding YAHPO Gym, emphasizing realism, flexibility, and extensibility. Continuous-depth models, such as Neural ODEs, offer compelling advantages in terms of memory efficiency and adaptive computation. However, their reliance on numerical integration for evaluation introduces computational overhead and challenges in analysis. This work introduces a novel class of continuous-depth models termed "Closed-Form Continuous-Depth Models" (CF-CDMs), which achieve the benefits of continuous-depth dynamics while possessing a closed-form solution for their evolution. By carefully designing the underlying vector field to admit an analytical solution, we eliminate the need for numerical integration during inference and training. We present a theoretical framework for constructing CF-CDMs and demonstrate their applicability across various tasks, including image classification and time series forecasting. Our experiments show that CF-CDMs achieve comparable performance to traditional Neural ODEs while significantly reducing computational cost and enabling direct analysis of the model's dynamics. This approach opens new avenues for developing efficient and interpretable continuous-depth models.
This paper explores the challenging problem of automatically translating spoken language into photo-realistic sign language video.  Bridging the communication gap between hearing and Deaf communities requires accurate and accessible sign language interpretation. While existing approaches often rely on avatar-based representations, they often lack the expressiveness and naturalness crucial for effective communication.
